noteTitle: Session 2026-05-14 — hypoDD at scale: monolithic vs. pruned + sub-cluster
sectionPath: Session 2026-05-14 — hypoDD at scale: monolithic vs. pruned + sub-cluster
text:
Question: did the events farther from the OBS network disappear from the relocated catalogs? Quantitative check:
| Source | Total events | At >60 km from any station |
|---|---|---|
| pyocto (input) | 42,040 | ~3,460 (≈8 %) |
| GrowClust year (relocated) | 11,033 | 194 |
| hypoDD Stage B | 5,064 | 0 |
| hypoDD Stage B-jan2019 | 3,579 | 0 |
| hypoDD Stage A | 676 | 0 |
| hypoDD Jan 2019 v2 | 5,610 | 0 |
Every hypoDD catalog drops all 3,460 regional events. GrowClust keeps ~6 % of them. Two causes:
DD linking is intrinsically pair-coupled. Regional events arrive at only a handful of stations and rarely satisfy MINLNK/MINOBS. They're dropped at the ph2dt stage and never enter the LSQR.
Stage B sub-region radii (max 3 km from a backbone centroid) don't reach regional event locations. The Stage A backbone is entirely inside the OBS array; K-means partitioning around it can't include far events.
This is expected DD behaviour, not a bug. The events still exist in catalogs/pyocto_events_picker_only.csv at their absolute-method (pyocto) positions. Maximum event-station distance in the pyocto catalog is 127 km -- everything is local-to-regional, no teleseismic.
Double-difference methods can't refine regional events; they need absolute-location methods that solve each event independently from its own picks:
NLLoc (NonLinLoc) -- probabilistic oct-tree, per-event posterior PDF. Already on the project roadmap (see next_steps_after_full_year.md ). Best fit for the regional 8 % of the catalog.
HYPOELLIPSE / HYPOINVERSE -- classic deterministic absolute locators.
Trust pyocto -- pyocto's octree association is itself an absolute method, so its positions for regional events are already reasonable. No-effort fallback.
Recommendation: for the final catalog, tag each event with a location_method column ( pyocto , hypodd , growclust ) and use pyocto positions for events that no DD method relocated. Optionally run NLLoc as a one-pass cross-check for everything; this also calibrates absolute-frame drift in the DD result.
scripts/22_pyocto_to_hypodd_input.py:58 assigns hypodd_id = row_index + 1 after a per-label reset_index . The same physical event therefore gets a different hypodd_id in each sub-region label. Consequences:
Cross-catalog joins on id are invalid ( Stage A vs Stage B only shows 6 overlapping ids when there should be many).
The Stage B merge step in scripts/26_merge_stage_b.py deduplicates bridge events by id -- it currently fails to detect a physical event that appeared in two sub-regions (different ids), so the final 5,064 / 3,579 event counts are upper bounds . Real unique-event counts after a proper dedup will be lower.
Fix:
ev["hypodd_id"] = (ev["event_idx"] + 1).astype(int)
Then re-run scripts 22 -> 23 -> 24 for every sub-region label and re-merge. The relocation positions are unaffected; only the merged-catalog event count and the cross-catalog comparisons change.
Year-long monolithic hypoDD is intractable on serial hardware when one cluster has ~20 k events and ~8 M dt observations. LSQR convergence is single-iteration-bound and each iteration takes >11 h. Stop trying that path.
The two-stage (pruned backbone + dense sub-clusters) approach is what's recommended in the field. Same scientific question, dramatically tractable: ~10 min total wall on this catalog.
Always capture stderr in subprocess wrappers and don't impose a Python-level timeout on long-running Fortran jobs unless you really want them killed.
Subprocess timeouts kill the binary, not just disconnect. If you need to bail out without losing work, kill the parent (python) and the child (hypoDD) reparents to init and keeps running.
K-means on a backbone catalog gives a fine spatial partition , but radius-capping is essential -- otherwise one outlier point gives a region 22 km wide that swallows the swarm and reproduces the monolithic problem.
Bridge events (overlap between sub-regions) preserve inter-region coupling and let the merge step resolve conflicts cleanly. Each event is kept once, from the sub-region for which it is most interior.
Compare Stage B (Stage A-seeded) vs Stage B (jan2019-seeded). Are they materially different where they overlap? Does the denser seed give a tighter swarm core?
Compare hypoDD Stage B vs GrowClust year-long on the same input -- algorithm-level comparison on identical pyocto picks.
Should we re-run Stage B with graph-based partitioning (METIS or networkx community detection on the dt.ct edge weights), as the expert suggested? Spatial K-means is a coarser proxy.
Paper-level question: how to phrase Stage B in methods? Cite the partitioning approach (Yano et al.-style) and report the bridge-event overlap fraction.
Related memory: [[jupyterhub-pod-memory-limit]] , [[session_handoff_2026-05-13]] , [[session_handoff_2026-05-14]] .

sectionPath: Session 2026-05-15 — Shot discrimination (temporal + spectral) and pipeline cleanup
text:
Yesterday left us with:
Three Stage B variants (Stage B, Stage B-jan2019, Stage C) all plotted with -1000 m contour and seafloor profile overlays.
An animation showing a rotating NW-SE → SW-NE lineation through the Jan 2019 swarm that I had flagged as "possibly real, possibly a resolution-kernel artifact."
User identified that BRAVOSEIS 2019 cruise fired active-source shots during the same time window as the catalog. Found shotfiles/ directory with 5 survey files:
| File | Survey | Shots | Time span |
|---|---|---|---|
| orca_mcs_shotfile_final.txt | Orca MCS (NW–SE) | 14,892 | Jan 21 – Jan 26 |
| orca_tomo_shotfile_final.txt | Orca Tomo (SW–NE) | 2,426 | Jan 26 – Jan 29 |
| rift_mcs_shotfile_final.txt | Rift Lines MCS | 3,265 | Jan 31 – Feb 4 |
| eda_mcs_shotfile_final.txt | Edifice-A MCS | 4,699 | Feb 1 – Feb 4 |
| other_mcs_shotfile_final.txt | Other Lines MCS | 1,541 | Jan 31 – Feb 4 |
| Total | | 26,823 | Jan 21 – Feb 4 |
The two perpendicular lineations were the Orca MCS NW–SE survey track and the Orca Tomo SW–NE perpendicular. The "rotation" was just the survey schedule (MCS first, then Tomo after Jan 26).
Logic: for each pyocto event, find the nearest shot in time via pd.merge_asof(..., direction="nearest", tolerance="N s") . If within ±tol-sec → flag as shot.
| Tolerance | Events flagged | Phase-2 catch rate |
|---|---|---|
| ±1 s | 4,610 (11.0 %) | Poor — most Phase 2 missed |
| ±2 s | 6,175 (14.7 %) | Better |
| ±3 s | 6,809 (16.2 %) | Better |
| ±5 s | 8,982 (21.4 %) | Still incomplete |
Diagnostic plot notes/figures/phase2_shot_residuals.png shows Phase-2 (Jan 31–Feb 4) red unflagged events sitting directly on top of black shot tracks even at ±5 s — confirming missed shots.
Two physical causes that user pinpointed:
Pyocto origin-time error grows with shot-to-array distance. Orca surveys are in the middle of the OBS array (sub-second origin-time fits); Phase 2 surveys (Rift, EDA, Other) are 20-50 km offshore (origin-time error can be 10-30 s).
Water-column multiples and P/S converted phases. A single airgun pulse produces P, water-multiples, Moho refractions, and basement P→S conversions, each arriving as separate coherent pulses up to ~30 s after the shot. PhaseNet picks them; pyocto associates them as "events."

noteTitle: Session 2026-05-15 — Shot discrimination (temporal + spectral) and pipeline cleanup
sectionPath: Session 2026-05-15 — Shot discrimination (temporal + spectral) and pipeline cleanup
text:
User's insight: shots have a distinct narrow-band spectrum (airgun bubble pulses) vs broadband earthquakes. Plan:
Extract per-event spectra ( scripts/extract_event_spectra.py ): Reuse growclust/picker_only/pick_windows.npy (483 k × 300 float32, ±1.5 s @ 100 Hz).
Per pick: rfft → |·|² → log1p → unit-area normalize → 151-D log power spectrum.
Per event: average across all valid picks.
Output: catalogs/event_spectra.npy (42,040 × 151 float32) + meta parquet.
Train classifier ( scripts/train_shot_classifier.py ): Labels (semi-supervised): SHOT = ±5 s temporal-flagged events in Jan 21 – Feb 4 (~8,900 events).
EQ = events outside Jan 21 – Feb 4 (~32,000 events). Pure because shotfiles cover exactly that window.
UNLABELED = unflagged events in Jan 21 – Feb 4 (gray zone).
Model: sklearn HistGradientBoostingClassifier on the 151-D spectra, class_weight="balanced" , 200 iter.
Held-out AUC: 0.9985. 98 % precision/recall on SHOT class. Confusion matrix on 7,872 held-out events: TN=6,040, FP=36, FN=32, TP=1,764.
In-window classifier verdict at p ≥ 0.5 added 1,542 more events beyond the temporal flag — these are the water-multiples and P/S conversions user predicted.
Out-of-window events default to flag_shot_v2 = False regardless of classifier output (avoids edge-effect false positives).
Mean-spectrum diagnostic ( notes/figures/event_spectra_v2_means.png ): EQ mean : broadband, peak 0-2 Hz, smooth decay.
SHOT mean : narrowband 5-7 Hz peak (airgun source), plus 11-12 Hz and 15-17 Hz bumps (water-column bubble reverberations). Clearly distinct shape.
Combined flag ( flag_shot_v2 ): True if (temporal ±5 s flag) OR (in-window AND classifier prob ≥ 0.5). Total v2 flagged: 10,524 events (25 % of catalog).

text:
Event 14341 (2.5 km below seafloor, on volcano summit, 17 pyocto picks).
At 3–10 Hz the seismologist picks matched pyocto to ~20 ms on the
overlapping picks. Added 11 picks pyocto missed (BRA13 P+S, BRA05 P+S,
BRA22 P, BRA23 P+S, BRA26 P+S, missed S on BRA16/BRA18/BRA24/BRA27).
Identified one pyocto error: BRA20 S at 0.79 s (only 0.3 s after its P) is
mislabeled; real S is at ~4 s. The BRA13 picks are also non-trivial:
the late arrival at 6.5 s pairs with a small earlier P at 3.65 s, giving
Vp/Vs=1.78 but implying BRA13 is recording an event ~20 km away — not 
the 0.6 km distance pyocto's location implies. Suggests the event 14341
"association" mixes signal from two physically distinct sources.
Event 26819 (5.6 km bsf, 16 pyocto picks). Cleaner geometry. Matched
pyocto to ~10 ms on overlaps. Added 4 missed picks. Several un-picked
stations (BRA19, BRA05, BRA15, BRA13, BRA09) showed continuous pre-event
activity — picking those would have mixed in arrivals from another event,
so they were correctly skipped.
Event 14115 (8.1 km bsf, 15 pyocto picks). At 3–10 Hz my first attempt
catastrophically failed: I picked the loud S arrival as P, and a later coda
as S. Implied Vp came out at 3.4 km/s — physically impossible. Median P
error vs pyocto: 0.86 s . Median S error: 1.63 s .
Diagnosis: emergent P first-motions on a deeper event get lost against the
later impulsive S; the eye is drawn to the wrong arrival.

noteTitle: Session 2026-05-19 — Hand-picking workflow, skill, Vp/Vs calibration
sectionPath: Session 2026-05-19 — Hand-picking workflow, skill, Vp/Vs calibration
text:
Documented the workflow as an agentic skill. Triggers on "look at picks",
"review picks", "hand-pick", "act as a seismologist", "can you do better
than pyocto", etc.
After the 14115 failure, the skill was upgraded with three concrete
safeguards:
Step 5a — moveout sanity check : compute Vp = hypo_dist / tP for each
candidate P. Reject any pick implying Vp outside 4–7 km/s (upper crust).
The 14115 wrong picks all gave Vp ≈ 3.4 km/s — would have been caught
immediately.
Step 5b — stretched-y pre-onset zoom : render the pre-arrival segment
with y-axis at ±6σ of pre-event noise. Forces the small first-motion
break to be visible (it gets washed out when normalized against the loud
later arrival).
Step 6a — anti-anchoring two-pass : pick blind first, reveal picker
picks second, write a justification for every disagreement. Stops the
"pyocto rubber-stamp" failure mode.
Multi-band probing : try 1–8, 2–10, 3–10, 5–15 Hz and pick the band
with cleanest pre-event flatlines and sharpest first motions. For
deeper Bransfield events (>5 km bsf), 5–15 Hz works much better than
3–10. For shallow Orca summit events (<3 km bsf), 3–10 stays preferred.
Re-running 14115 with the safeguards:
Median P error: 0.86 s → 0.01 s (sample-perfect)
Median S error: 1.63 s → 0.04 s on consensus picks
3 P picks added that pyocto had missed (BRA15, BRA18, BRA19)
3 pyocto S picks flagged as physically impossible (BRA15/BRA19/BRA21
implied Vs < 2.5 km/s — they were caught at later peaks, not S onsets)
The safeguards work.

 tS/tP ratios (assuming pyocto origin times). 106,841 P+S station-event
pairs in the physical range [1.3, 2.5].

|---|---|

sectionTitle: Manual P/S picks — cross-stage validation set
sectionPath: Manual P/S picks — cross-stage validation set
text:
User-provided manual P and S arrival times (with magnitudes) for a subset of stations in this region. Used as ground truth across multiple stages.
Originals: bransfield-eq/data/manual_picks/ (any format).
Normalized: bransfield-eq/catalogs/manual_picks.csv — written by src/bransfield_eq/manual_picks.py .
| column | notes |
|---|---|
| event_id | groups picks for the same event |
| origin_time | event origin (UTC) if known |
| magnitude | event magnitude if known |
| network, station, location, channel | SEED codes |
| phase | "P" or "S" |
| pick_time | UTC arrival |
| analyst | initials if known |
| source_file | original filename |
[!note] Polarities / hand-locations
Current set has P/S times + magnitudes. No polarities, no hand-located events. The schema reserves columns for them so they can be added later without a migration.
Validation: match each manual pick to the nearest PhaseNet pick on the same channel within ±0.5 s (P) / ±1.0 s (S). Compute precision/recall by station and overall.
Threshold tuning: sweep P_threshold / S_threshold over the validation set to find the operating point that matches your manual sensitivity.
Fine-tuning: if pick volume permits (≥ ~1000), fine-tune PhaseNet weights on Bransfield-specific data. Otherwise stick with stead / instance defaults.
Manual picks are assumed to be tectonic earthquakes — use them as the positive class for any ML discriminator. Need a separate negative set (T-phases, shots, ice signals).
Run associator on manual picks alone. Should cluster into the user's known events. If it doesn't, the associator config is the problem — not the picks.
If/when hand-located events arrive, compare to NLLoc / HypoDD locations as ground truth. Per-axis residual distributions (Δlat, Δlon, Δdepth, Δtime) measure absolute accuracy.
N/A unless polarities are added.
Files received (in data/manual_picks/ ):
nllmaleen_mag07_202210.out — NLLoc obs, 12,099 picks (events with M ≥ 0.7)
nllmaleen_magall_202210.out — NLLoc obs, 45,678 picks (all magnitudes)

Total: 58,630 picks across 6,970 events. Loader in src/bransfield_eq/manual_picks.py ; canonical CSV at catalogs/manual_picks.csv . Re-run with PYTHONPATH=src python -m bransfield_eq.manual_picks .
Nordic format has station code (cols 2-6) and component code (cols 7-8) packed with no whitespace, so naive whitespace tokenization produces nonsense like BRA26EZ . Parser uses fixed-column slicing.
Nordic magnitude regex is bounded to -2 < M < 10 and takes the last <float><L|b|B|w|s|S|c> match in the type-1 line — the first match would be the seconds field's location/agency code (e.g. "15.9BL").

noteTitle: Manual P/S picks — cross-stage validation set
sectionPath: Manual P/S picks — cross-stage validation set
text:
Manual picks are tectonic earthquakes only; PhaseNet will (correctly) also pick non-tectonic signals that have no manual entry:
Icequakes / cryo-signals — calving, basal slip, harmonic tremor; emergent onsets
Whale calls — fin and blue whales emit 15–30 Hz calls that look like seismic transients on OBS
Ship noise — hydrophone-dominant, broadband transients during shipping passes
T-phases — late, low-frequency, hydrophone-dominant
Volcanic tremor — sustained narrow-band signals near Orca submarine volcano
Active-source shots — once Wei's airguns deploy
Naive precision = TP / (TP + FP) over-penalises PhaseNet because all of the above land in FP. Two mitigations in scripts/05_validate_picks.py :
--event-window N (cheap, available now): only count PhaseNet picks within ±N seconds of any manual event origin time. Outside those windows, PhaseNet picks are ignored — neither TP nor FP. This isolates "did we recover known earthquakes" from "what fraction of all picks are tectonic". Trade-off: doesn't measure precision over the whole record, only inside known-event windows.
Class-aware FP attribution (deferred to [[02-discrimination]]): once we have a discriminator, split FPs into "tectonic-class but no manual match" (real model error) vs "non-tectonic class" (expected, not the picker's fault).
Use mode 1 for Stage 1 sign-off. Use mode 2 as the headline metric once Stage 2 lands.
[ ] Build scripts/05_validate_picks.py for Stage 1 precision/recall once waveform downloads + PhaseNet picks exist.

Meeting Notes data management and flow are centered on creating a streamlined, efficient pipeline for moving raw observational data into accessible public repositories like EarthScope. The discussion highlights a shift toward cloud-based processing and collaborative software development. The Data Pipeline: PI NAS to EarthScope The primary objective is to develop a protocol to move data from the PI NAS (Network Attached Storage) to EarthScope . Currently, the team views data sitting solely in the PI NAS as "functionally useless" and wants to ensure all project data, including that from "COSZO," eventually ends up in EarthScope. Test Case: The team plans to use data from Scripps SCPRs (Self-Contained Pressure Recorders) as a test case to develop these data streams. Frequency: Data transfer is intended to be daily rather than real-time. Raw vs. Calibrated Data: The strategy for EarthScope is to ingest raw data rather than derived products. The modern approach is for users to request data which is then processed into useful products "on the fly" in the cloud. Software and Technical Processing Because EarthScope will primarily host raw data, the project requires local tools to make that data useful for scientists. Python Packages: There is a plan to create a Python-based package—modeled after OBSpy —that allows users to import functions for pulling, cleaning, and applying calibrations to the data. Clock and Timing Corrections: A significant portion of the data management effort involves correcting timing jumps and data gaps. The team emphasizes the need for scripts that can handle clock jumps by setting boundaries rather than averaging data across the jump. Derived Products: Beyond pressure data, the team is looking at products for HYS4 and other short-period data requiring clock corrections. Infrastructure: GitHub and Website Migration The meeting participants expressed dissatisfaction with the current "COSZO" website, noting it "absolutely sucks" and remains "under construction". WordPress Migration: The plan is to migrate the project's public face to a WordPress site to meet disability requirements and simplify maintenance. GitHub Integration: GitHub is identified as the central hub for hosting software, Python scripts, and technical instrument documentation, such as README files explaining timing fixes. Collaborative Benefits: Using GitHub allows for collaborative development where multiple researchers can branch or fork repositories, though there were noted concerns regarding GitHub’s 100MB file size limit and the complexities of managing private versus public repositories. Key Configuration Details: The file specifies that the Ring server uses the "MiniSeed_scan" method, which: Scans the MiniSeed folder ( output/MiniSeed/ ) for new data files Loads the data into the "ring" (an in-memory buffer) Makes the data available for EarthScope's SeedLink client to retrieve How It Works: When data files are placed in the MiniSeed folder, the Ring server: Detects the new files through the scan method Loads them onto the ring buffer EarthScope's client reads from this ring and archives the data Important Note: The final line in ring.conf contains the MiniSeed_scan configuration that points to the MiniSeed folder path. This is what enables the automatic detection and transfer of pressure gauge data to EarthScope. Mika mentioned there's additional documentation about Ring server configuration in the COSZO Drive under "Non-Tier 1 Data Flow" if you need more detailed information about other settings in the file.

A new folder coszo-data-collection/testk/ was added with two standalone scripts. These are separate from the main pipeline — they don't use the shell wrappers or cron, and they write to their own output directory.
testk/pull_data.py 
Standalone script that replicates the core data request and conversion logic:
Loads OOI credentials from .ooi_env
Fetches most recent deployment info from the OOI M2M API
Submits an async 24-hour data request
Polls status.json until the job is ready (up to 10 tries, 30s apart)
Resolves the NetCDF file location via the NCML manifest
Opens the NetCDF via OPeNDAP (no download required)
Detects gaps using robust median Δt (same logic as main pipeline — [[gap detection]])
Splits time series at gaps and writes one MiniSEED file per channel per segment
Output goes to testk/output/mseed/
Reuses from main repo:
bin/read_param.py — parameter file parsing
bin/convert_utc.py — 1900-epoch timestamp conversion ( utcdata1900 )
To run:
cd coszo-data-collection
conda run -n ooi_env python testk/pull_data.py
To change the time window, edit START_TIME and END_TIME near the top of the script.
testk/verify_mseed.py 
Reads back all .mseed files in testk/output/mseed/ and:
Prints sample count, start/end times, duration, sampling rate, and data min/max/mean for each file
Generates a time-series plot saved to testk/output/verify_plot.png
To run:
conda run -n ooi_env python testk/verify_mseed.py
Both scripts pushed to dev/maleen branch on GitHub.

testk is a diagnostic tool — it confirms credentials work, the API responds, gap detection is sound, and MiniSEED files are correctly formed. It is not meant to replace the main pipeline.

sectionPath: Mode 1:  collect  — Build the Metrics Library
text: Replace the current Panel 1 (sample index vs timestamp) with a histogram of timing residuals . The timestamp-vs-index plot is useful for understanding overall shape but redundant once you have the Δt panel — the histogram gives the distributional information that's actually hard to read from the scatter. New 3-panel layout: | Panel | Content | What it shows | |-------|---------|---------------| | 1 | Histogram of residuals (ms, from best-fit line) | Shape of jitter distribution: Gaussian = random noise, bimodal = quantization artifact, long tail = occasional large timing errors | | 2 | Residuals scatter (sample index vs residual in ms) | Temporal structure — drift over the day, clusters, sudden jumps | | 3 | Δt between consecutive samples with adaptive gap threshold | Gap detection, whether threshold is well-placed | Histogram details: X axis: residual in ms, centred at 0 Bin width: auto (Freedman-Diaconis or fixed ~1ms bins) Vertical lines: ±1σ, ±p95 Annotate: σ, p95, skewness, n samples Overlay a Gaussian curve fit for easy comparison The residuals scatter (Panel 2) stays because it shows when during the day the jitter occurs — the histogram alone loses that temporal information. compute_stats() must be refactored to follow this order: Step 1 — Gap detection Compute all Δt ( np.diff(t_sec) ) across the full day Estimate day-level sp_calc from the full Δt array (robust median of lower 90th percentile — resistant to large gap intervals so this still works) Apply adaptive threshold, identify gap_idx Log: n_gaps , gap locations, gap durations, estimated missing samples per gap Step 2 — Per-segment sample rates Split t_sec into contiguous segments at gap_idx For each segment: compute its own sp_calc_seg (robust median Δt within that segment) Log: segment index, duration, sample count, sample rate Detects whether segments disagree — e.g. sensor slowed down after a dropout Step 3 — Jitter metrics (per segment, then concatenated) For each segment independently: fit a line, compute residuals Compute William's metric using the segment-level sp_calc_seg as the denominator: jitter_i = |dti / sp_calc_seg - round(dti / sp_calc_seg)| Using segment-level rate matters: if two segments run at slightly different rates, measuring jitter against a blended day-level average fits neither segment correctly Concatenate residuals and jitter values across all segments Compute summary stats of the combined jitter array: jitter_mean — mean jitter_median — median (robust central tendency) jitter_std — standard deviation jitter_p95 — 95th percentile (anomaly trigger candidate) jitter_max — maximum (catches worst single interval) Compute summary stats of the combined residuals array: res_std_ms — standard deviation in ms res_p95_ms — 95th percentile in ms skewness — asymmetry (negative/positive drift within segments) Important: residuals must be computed per segment, not across the whole day. If there is a gap mid-day and the best-fit line is fitted through all samples across the gap, the line slope is distorted by the gap. Samples before the gap appear systematically early and samples after appear systematically late — the histogram shows a smeared or bimodal distribution that looks like jitter or drift

sectionPath: Mode 1:  collect  — Build the Metrics Library
text: jitter_max — maximum (catches worst single interval) Compute summary stats of the combined residuals array: res_std_ms — standard deviation in ms res_p95_ms — 95th percentile in ms skewness — asymmetry (negative/positive drift within segments) Important: residuals must be computed per segment, not across the whole day. If there is a gap mid-day and the best-fit line is fitted through all samples across the gap, the line slope is distorted by the gap. Samples before the gap appear systematically early and samples after appear systematically late — the histogram shows a smeared or bimodal distribution that looks like jitter or drift but is purely a gap artifact. Correct approach: Detect gaps first ( gap_idx already available) Split t_sec into contiguous segments at gap boundaries For each segment independently: fit a line, compute residuals Concatenate all segment residuals into one array Histogram and scatter are built from this concatenated array This ensures residuals reflect only within-segment timing irregularity. For the residuals scatter (Panel 2): colour-code points by segment so it is visually clear which residuals belong to which contiguous block. Gaps appear as breaks between colour groups.

text:
For the first pass , only trigger on structural anomalies where no baseline is needed:
Any gap detected ( n_gaps > 0 )
Day is incomplete ( is_full = False )
Sample period deviation exceeds hybrid alert threshold ( sp_alert = True )
Jitter threshold is disabled on the first pass. The current code computes res_std , res_p95 , and William's jitter metric per day, but there is no meaningful threshold to compare against yet — every sensor has some baseline spread from network ingestion delays and timestamp rounding, and res_std > 0 is always true.
To establish a jitter threshold:
Run collect over a 30–60 day test window
Plot jitter p95 over time (summary Figure 3)
The distribution of values across clean days defines the normal baseline
Flag days where jitter p95 exceeds e.g. 3× the median baseline as anomalous
Set that value as jitter_p95_threshold in run_prest.txt and enable the trigger
Until Step 4 is done, jitter-based figure triggering is a guess. All jitter metrics are still stored in the CSV every day regardless — the threshold only controls whether a figure is generated.
If a row for this (station, date) already exists in the CSV, skip the API fetch — this lets the script be re-run incrementally without re-fetching data.
Reads the metrics CSVs and generates 4 figures saved to output/diagnostics/figures/summary/ .

X: date, Y: sp_calc (computed sample period in seconds)
Horizontal dashed line: nominal sp
Points coloured by sp_alert flag (red = alert triggered)
Gaps in the line where has_data = False
One subplot per station

Days with no data marked with a different colour

Gives a quick overview of which periods are problematic
Defined as:
jitter_i = |dti / mean_dt - round(dti / mean_dt)|
Where:
dti = inter-sample intervals ( np.diff(t_sec) )
mean_dt = sp_calc (robust median sample period, same as the pipeline uses)
Interpretation:
For a perfectly uniform signal: dti / mean_dt ≈ 1.0 for every interval → jitter ≈ 0
For a jittered signal: each interval deviates slightly from an integer multiple → jitter > 0
For a genuine gap: dti / mean_dt is a large integer (e.g. 5, 10, …) → round() cancels it → jitter ≈ 0 again
The metric is insensitive to gaps and specifically sensitive to sub-sample timing irregularity
Per-day summary statistics stored: jitter_mean , jitter_p95 , jitter_max
Note: William also suggested using the nominal sample rate instead of mean_dt as an alternative. We will compute both and compare during the first test run.

Pressure channel only. fetch_nc_timestamps reads only the time variable from the NetCDF — never pressure or temperature values. Temperature timestamps are identical to pressure. One API call per station per day is sufficient. No code change needed.
Why calls are slow. The OOI M2M API is async:
Submit request (~instant)
Poll status.json until job completes ( max_cycle=5 , delay=50s → up to 250s wait)
Open NetCDF via OPeNDAP and read timestamps
In practice a 24h window completes in 1–2 polls ≈ 50–100s per call.
Scale estimate. 3 stations × ~4000 days = ~12,000 calls × ~90s = ~12 days wall clock. Collect must run in chunks across multiple sessions. The CSV skip logic handles this — already-processed rows are skipped on resume.

Focus: Continued revisions to diagnose_timing.py per-day figure layout and understanding of timing metrics. Builds on [[04-10-26 Notes]].
| Metric | Definition | What it tells you |
|--------|-----------|-------------------|
| sp_nominal | Fixed from param file (e.g. 1.000000 s) | What the sensor should do — never changes |
| sp_calc | Robust median of inter-sample intervals (lower 90th percentile Δt) | What the sensor typically does that day — resistant to gaps and outliers |
| sp_fit | Least-squares slope through all timestamps | Average rate across the full day — sensitive to start/end position of data |
sp_calc ≠ sp_nominal → clock running fast or slow relative to design spec
sp_fit ≠ sp_calc → interval distribution is skewed; some very short or long intervals pull the mean away from the median. Strong skewness in residuals (Panel 1) is a symptom.
sp_fit ≠ sp_nominal → overall day-level drift from nominal when integrated across the whole day
Plot sp_calc − sp_nominal , sp_fit − sp_nominal , and sp_calc − sp_fit as time series across all days in the metrics CSV. This would reveal:
Long-term clock drift — is sp_calc consistently above/below nominal over weeks/months? Would show up as a persistent offset in sp_calc − sp_nominal .
Day-to-day variability — scatter in sp_calc from day to day may indicate instrument instability or environmental effects (pressure, temperature).
Skewness signature — large sp_calc − sp_fit on a given day means the interval distribution is asymmetric. Combined with residual skewness metric, this flags days with unusual timing behaviour that isn't just clock drift.
Deployment transitions — expect a step change in sp_calc at deployment boundaries (dep1 = 15 s, dep2 = 1 s). The series should be flat within each deployment.
sp_nominal = 1.000000 s
sp_calc = 1.000502 s (+0.502 ms above nominal — clock slightly slow)
sp_fit = 1.000000 s (+0.000 ms — mean rate equals nominal for this day)
sp_calc − sp_fit = +0.502 ms — skewed distribution; median > mean
The discrepancy between sp_calc and sp_fit is the skewness signature: most intervals are 1.000502 s but enough short intervals exist to bring the day-average back to 1.000000 s. Panel 1 residuals show skewness = −3.54, confirming this.
In plot_mode Figure 1 (sample rate over time), consider adding a third scatter series for sp_fit in addition to sp_calc , with the three reference lines. Over a long time series, divergence between sp_calc and sp_fit trends would indicate changing skewness character in the data.
| Panel | Content | Notes |
|-------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Histogram of residuals from best-fit line (ms, count) | Title shows sp_fit and offset from nominal |
| 2 | Histogram of residuals from nominal line (ms, count) | Span = drift error from nominal assignment |
| 3 | Residuals from best-fit scatter over time | Colour by segment |
| 4 | Residuals from nominal scatter over time | Slope = clock drift rate |
| 5 | Gap timeline — vertical red bands at gap locations | Annotated with duration and missing samples |
Panel 1 vs Panel 2: best-fit removes slope AND intercept (residuals centred at 0); nominal removes only slope (intercept fixed at origin). Even when sp_fit ≈ sp_nominal, Panel 2 is shifted by the intercept b_fit ≈ mean(t_sec) − sp_fit × mean(idx).
Panel 4 ramp slope = sp_calc − sp_nominal (clock drift rate from nominal).
Panel 5 replaces the old Δt scatter — vertical bands are easier to read for gap location and duration.

Replaced the old per-segment nominal residual computation with the round() approach in compute_stats() .
Old approach — anchored at each segment's first sample:
res_nominal[i] = (seg[i] - seg[0]) - i_within_seg * sp_nominal
Problem: after a gap, the next segment resets its anchor, but accumulated drift within a segment still grew without bound on long segments. Bins could blow up on gapped days.
New approach — gap-aware, anchored at first sample of the day:
t_rel = t_sec - t_sec[0]
nominal_slots = round(t_rel / sp_nominal)
res_nominal = t_rel - nominal_slots * sp_nominal
Properties:
Always bounded to ±sp_nominal/2 (e.g. ±500 ms for 1 s sampling) — no more millions-of-bins hang
Gap-aware: round() naturally skips missing nominal slots; after a gap, samples are assigned to the correct slot rather than the one immediately after the last pre-gap sample
No per-segment anchoring needed — the slot assignment is self-consistent across the full day
Panel 4 x-axis changed from sample index to nominal slot number. Because missing samples have no slot entry, gaps appear as empty horizontal regions in the scatter rather than being compressed into consecutive indices.

first sample 00:00:00.096 → last sample 23:59:59.117
wall-clock span ≈ 86399.02 s
at sp_nominal = 1.0 s , the ideal-grid slot count that physically fits
in that span is floor(86399.02 / 1.0) + 1 = 86400
we have 86400 samples → every slot is filled → no sample is
actually missing
So the n_gaps = 1, gap_total_missing = 1 is a false positive from
the rounding rule in Steps 3–4 of the plan.
dt_FG = median(Δt) = 1.000590 s for SLBS that day (larger than the true
1.0 s because of asymmetric jitter). One interval in the file is probably
≈ 1.5 s — a jitter event, not a dropout. Its normalised step count is
 Δi' = 1.5 / 1.000590 ≈ 1.499 . If that value tips just above 1.5 it
rounds to 2 (flagged as a gap); just below 1.5 it rounds to 1 (no gap).
The classifier is brittle at the Δi = 1.5 boundary.
The OLS fit confirms the grid has been stretched to absorb the fake extra
slot: Δt_true ≈ 0.999989 s (we only print 6 decimals, so it looks like
1.000000). That sub-1.0 slope lets 86401 slots fit into 86399 s.
So n_ideal = 86401 is arithmetically consistent with the reconstructed
grid but misleading as "samples the day should have held" — it
inherits the rounding artifact.

Wall-clock cross-check. Compute
 n_expected_wall = round((data_end − data_start) / sp_nominal) + 1 .
If n_points == n_expected_wall , suppress the spurious gap flag.
Tighter gap criterion. Only call it a gap when
 Δt > 1.5 × sp_nominal and Δi_int > 1 , using sp_nominal instead
of the noisy median dt_FG .
Decision pending — will pick one before re-running collect.
n_ideal = 86400 — same as n_points.
This is actually interesting and contradicts my earlier arithmetic. I was assuming n_ideal = n_points + gap_total_missing = 86401, but the actual reconstructed index length is 86400.
The explanation: somewhere in the day there's also at least one interval where Δi' rounds to 0 (two samples very close together, Δt < 0.5 × dt_FG). Those cancel the Δi = 2 event, so the net sum of Δi_j is 86399 → i_j[-1] = 86399 → n_ideal = 86400.
So the plan's rounding scheme is producing a paired artifact: one spurious "gap" (Δi=2) somewhere, paired with a spurious "overlap" (Δi=0) somewhere else. Net: no missing samples, which matches the wall-clock arithmetic. n_gaps = 1, gap_total_missing = 1 is misleading on its own — and n_ideal = 86400 is what actually tells you the day is whole.

Ran fresh collect across the full week for all stations. 14/15 succeeded;
AXBS 2025-01-25 hit the recurring OOI Cassandra 500 (LOCAL_QUORUM
unavailable) and needs a later retry.

| 01-22 | 86400, 0, 3.36 | 86400, 0, 3.50 | 5760, 0, 3.32 |
| 01-23 | 86400, 0, 3.14 | 86400, 1, 3.17 | 5760, 0, 3.11 |
| 01-24 | 85238, 3, 2.89 | 85308, 13, 2.98 | 5675, 3, 2.88 |

Observations:
01-22 and 01-23 are clean across all stations (0–1 gaps each, σ ≈ 3 ms).
01-24 and 01-25 show a clear dropout event visible on every station
simultaneously — gap counts jump an order of magnitude and sample
counts drop below the full-day expectation. The fact that all three
cabled stations degrade on the same days points to a shared
(network/ingest) cause, not a per-sensor failure.
01-26: counts recover to full day. SLBS retains one large jitter event
(σ = 26.74 ms, max|e| = 349 ms in Panel D near i_j ≈ 50000) even though
n_points = n_ideal = 86400, i.e. no actual missing sample.
SUM1 on 01-25 max|e| = 341.85 ms is likely the same class of
"catch-up" timestamp after a delay — not a dropout.
All figures regenerated with the new panel layout (A: 0–2, C: >2).

Added the wall-clock cross-check to compute_variability() :
n_expected_wall = round((data_end - data_start) / sp_nominal) + 1
if n_points >= n_expected_wall:
 n_gaps = 0; gap_total_missing = 0 # suppress rounding artifacts
Raw counts kept as n_gaps_raw / gap_total_missing_raw for traceability.
New CSV columns: n_expected_wall , n_gaps_raw , gap_total_missing_raw .
Re-ran collect 2025-01-22 → 2025-01-26, all 3 stations. 15/15 succeeded
(AXBS 01-25 returned data this time — OOI Cassandra was healthy).

| 01-22 | SLBS | 86400 | 86400 | 0 → 0 | 3.36 |
| 01-22 | SUM1 | 86400 | 86400 | 0 → 0 | 3.50 |
| 01-22 | AXBS | 5760 | 5760 | 0 → 0 | 3.32 |
| 01-23 | SLBS | 86400 | 86400 | 0 → 0 | 3.14 |
| 01-23 | SUM1 | 86400 | 86400 | 1 → 0 | 3.17 |
| 01-23 | AXBS | 5760 | 5760 | 0 → 0 | 3.11 |
| 01-24 | SLBS | 85238 | 86400 | 3 → 3 | 2.89 |
| 01-24 | SUM1 | 85308 | 86401 | 13 → 13 | 2.98 |

Two spurious gaps were suppressed: SLBS 01-26 and SUM1 01-23 — both had
 n_points == n_expected_wall , confirming no physical sample was missing.

dropout days (01-24, 01-25) retain their full gap counts.

Followed up on yesterday's SLBS 2025-01-26 anomaly (raw classifier flagged
1 gap / 1 missing sample, but wall-clock arithmetic said the day was
whole). Implemented the cross-check in compute_variability() :
n_expected_wall = round((data_end - data_start) / sp_nominal) + 1
if n_points >= n_expected_wall:
 n_gaps = 0
 gap_total_missing = 0
 gap_positions = [] # → no red markers in Panel D
Raw classifier output preserved as n_gaps_raw / gap_total_missing_raw 
so nothing is lost — just demoted from "gap" to "jitter artifact" when
the wall clock says no sample is physically missing.
New columns: n_expected_wall , n_gaps_raw , gap_total_missing_raw .
 n_gaps and gap_total_missing now carry the corrected (post-cross-check)
values. Wiped the three *_variability.csv files and re-collected the
full week to migrate.
Figure suptitle → uses corrected n_gaps
Panel D vertical red gap-markers → gated on corrected n_gaps > 0 ,
so a suppressed gap leaves no trace on the plot
variability_stats.txt → prints both lines for traceability: n_gaps (raw) : 1 total missing (raw): 1
n_gaps (corrected) : 0 total missing : 0 samples
15/15 succeeded (AXBS 01-25 came back this time — OOI Cassandra healthy).
| Date | Station | n | n_exp_wall | n_gaps (raw → corr) |

| 01-23 | SUM1 | 86400 | 86400 | 1 → 0 |
| 01-26 | SLBS | 86400 | 86400 | 1 → 0 |
Two spurious gaps suppressed. Both days had n_points == n_expected_wall ,
confirming no physical dropout — the raw 1 was a ±0.5 rounding
artifact around Δi = 1.5 (a single jittered interval paired with a
matching Δi = 0 elsewhere in the day, net zero missing samples).
Real dropout days (01-24, 01-25) retained their full gap counts on all
three stations, as expected — on those days n_points < n_expected_wall

Added two switches to bin/temporal_anomaly_investigator.py (and supporting change in bin/diagnose_timing.py ). Committed and pushed to dev/maleen — commit bc25ae1 .
New save_nc_dir kwarg on diagnose_timing.fetch_nc_timestamps .
When set, downloads the raw .nc via HTTPS (with M2M auth) right after NCML locates it — before the OPeNDAP Dataset open.
Files land in output/temporal_anomaly/netcdf/ as <station>_<YYYY-MM-DD>_deployment<NNNN>.nc . Overwrites on re-run.
Default off — existing callers in diagnose_timing.py unchanged.
Previously collect mode always wrote a 4-panel figure on every successfully processed day.
Now with --only-gaps , the figure is only written when the post-correction n_gaps > 0 .
CSV row is always written — figure_generated column reflects whether the figure was actually produced.
Skips both cases described by William: Day with no Δi>1 events at all ( n_gaps_raw = 0 ).
Day where Δi>1 events were reclassified as jitter by the wall-clock check ( wall_clock_clean = True → n_gaps = 0 ).
# collect a date range, download NetCDFs, only plot real-gap days
python bin/temporal_anomaly_investigator.py --mode collect \
 --start 2019-01-01 --end 2019-03-31 --save-nc --only-gaps
| flags | CSV row | per-day figure | NetCDF saved |
|---|---|---|---|
| (none) | always | always on successful fetch | no |
| --only-gaps | always | only if n_gaps > 0 | no |
| --save-nc | always | always | yes |
| --save-nc --only-gaps | always | only if n_gaps > 0 | yes |
The gap method in temporal_anomaly_investigator is not the same as the one in OOI_data_request_and_convert_mseed.py . Confirmed after reviewing both.
dt = np.diff(t) , strip top 10% → sp = median(dt_clean) .
Multiplier chosen by sample rate and whether segment is full: sp ≥ 10 s (15 s PREST): 3× or 4× → threshold ~45–60 s
sp ≥ 0.5 s: 2.5× or 3.5× → ~2.5–3.5 s
sp < 0.5 s: 2.0× or 2.5×
Gap = any Δt > multiplier × sp (absolute seconds).
Purpose: split MiniSEED files at gap boundaries.
Δt_FG = median(Δt') (plain median, no trim).
Δiⱼ = round(Δt'ⱼ / Δt_FG) — sample-step count.
Raw gap = any Δiⱼ > 1 .
Wall-clock correction: if n_points ≥ span/sp_nominal + 1 , reclassify all Δi>1 as jitter not gaps → n_gaps = 0 , wall_clock_clean = True .
Single missing sample ≈ 30 s. Below the pipeline's 45–60 s threshold → pipeline passes as continuous. Investigator flags n_gaps_raw = 1 , then wall-clock check decides whether real ( n_gaps = 1 ) or jitter ( n_gaps = 0 ).
Investigator is strictly more sensitive to single-sample gaps than the pipeline, with jitter discrimination on top.
n_gaps_raw , gap_total_missing_raw — pre-correction counts.
n_gaps , gap_total_missing — post-correction (the values the summary figures use and the ones --only-gaps gates on).
n_expected_wall — wall-clock threshold used for the correction.
max_abs_epsilon — rounding-stability sanity check (values near 0.5 mean Δi rounding is unstable; Δt_FG probably wrong).
Commit 6c5c5f4 on dev/maleen . Standalone tool to re-use locally saved NetCDFs without touching OOI.
Read .nc files saved by temporal_anomaly_investigator --save-nc (default output/temporal_anomaly/netcdf/ ).
Reproduce the investigator's 4-panel variability figure + variability_stats.txt without re-fetching.
Optional: convert the NetCDF to MiniSEED using the main pipeline's gap detection + per-segment split logic.
Does not read or modify the collect-mode metrics CSVs.
Figures: output/temporal_anomaly/figures_offline/<station>_<date>/ Separate from collect-mode figures/per_day/ on purpose — nothing from collect is overwritten.
MiniSEED: output/temporal_anomaly/mseed/<YEAR>/<NET>.<STA>.<LOC>.<CHA>.<start>-<end>.mseed
Imports compute_variability , make_per_day_figure , write_stats from temporal_anomaly_investigator.py , so the figure is byte-identical to what collect produces. The MiniSEED conversion mirrors the pipeline logic in OOI_data_request_and_convert_mseed.py (sample-period from trimmed-median Δt, adaptive multiplier by sp regime, split at dt > multiplier × sp , write one MiniSEED per channel × contiguous segment).
# single day, all 3 stations
python bin/plot_from_netcdf.py --date 2019-01-15
# range, one station, with MiniSEED conversion
python bin/plot_from_netcdf.py --start 2019-01-01 --end 2019-01-07 \
 --station RS01SLBS-MJ01A-06-PRESTA101 --convert-mseed
# skip figures, write mseed only
python bin/plot_from_netcdf.py --date 2019-01-15 --no-plot --convert-mseed
--date XOR ( --start + --end ) — required
--station — optional restriction (default: all 3 PREST)
--nc-dir , --plot-dir , --mseed-dir — path overrides
--no-plot — skip figures
--convert-mseed — also write MiniSEED
If we ever want the generated MiniSEED to be ingested by SeedLink or miniseed2dmc, override --mseed-dir to the main pipeline output ( output/mseed/ or output/mseed2dmc/<YEAR>/ ). Today's default keeps it isolated under output/temporal_anomaly/mseed/ so no pipeline state is affected by offline experiments.
New living doc at Obsidian Vault/COSZO/code migration.md . Captures the plan for replacing the legacy gap detection in OOI_data_request_and_convert_mseed.py with the integer-step + true_missing approach. Sections:
§1 / §1b — corrected mental model (both old and new use day-global sample rate; per-segment is not changing) + end-to-end pipeline walkthrough tagging every step as 🟥 affected / 🟨 indirectly affected / ⬜ unaffected.
§2 — refined algorithm: replace wall-clock check (param-file dependent) with true_missing = n_ideal − n_points (data-derived).
§3 — risks and edge cases.
§4 — phased plan: Phase 0 (investigator refactor) → Phase 0b (side-by-side comparison) → Phase 1 (extract detect_gaps_{legacy,anomaly} ) → Phase 2 (decisions) → Phase 3 (canary cutover, AXBS first) → Phase 4 (cleanup, includes removing pipeline's save_netcdf ).
§5 — open questions / decisions log with checkboxes.
✓ Splitting trigger : Option A — split only when true_missing > 0 . Jitter-only days produce one MiniSEED for the full day. (Pending William sign-off during Phase 3 canary.)
✓ Sample rate source : Δt_true (OLS slope) used as the day's sampling_rate .
✓ NetCDF saving : investigator-only (via --save-nc ); pipeline's save_netcdf to be removed in Phase 4. Investigator now adopts the server-provided filename convention.
✓ Instability flag : jitter_unstable = (frac_maxabs > 0.4) — sample-rate-agnostic (40 % of Δt_true ). CSV-only diagnostic, no email.
✓ Email policy : keep only sp_deviation as the algorithm-related email (redefined against Δt_true ). 6 upstream pipeline emails unchanged. Jitter instability does not trigger email.
Action on jitter_unstable days beyond the CSV flag (warn-and-write, refuse to write, or fall back to legacy median).
Whether true_missing > 0 should also trigger an email.
Threshold tuning (40 % is a starting guess).
Deployment-boundary policy when a 24 h window crosses one.
William sign-off on fragmented MiniSEED + canary station/duration.
Commit 7f961c0 on dev/maleen . Investigator refactor + NetCDF filename switch.
Removed n_expected_wall and wall_clock_clean (param-file-dependent wall-clock check).
Added true_missing = max(0, n_ideal − n) — direct, data-derived missing-sample count from the integer-step reconstruction.
Added jitter_unstable = (fmax > 0.4) — sample-rate-agnostic instability flag derived from Δt_true jitter fraction.
Gap classification now gates on true_missing == 0 instead of the old wall-clock flag.
gap_total_missing now reports the true count (= true_missing ) rather than Σ(Δi−1) over Δi>1 events. The two can differ when jitter compensates across the day — see SUM1 2025-01-24 below.
Dropped: n_expected_wall .
Added: true_missing , jitter_unstable .
Kept for auditing: n_gaps_raw , gap_total_missing_raw , frac_maxabs , max_abs_epsilon .
Switched from <station>_<date>_deployment<NNNN>.nc to the server-provided basename ( os.path.basename(netCDF) ). plot_from_netcdf.find_nc_file was updated to glob the new pattern first and fall back to the legacy form so older saved files keep working.
Stats text now surfaces true_missing and jitter_unstable .
Suptitle no longer shows sp_nominal ; Δt_true printed at full repr() precision (15–17 significant figures) going forward.
Ran the investigator on the same dates the pre-Phase-0 archive in commit f4196b4 covers, then ran the same range a year ahead (2026) for clean-week behaviour. Both runs without --save-nc ; 2026 with --only-gaps , 2025 without (so we kept all the figures).
| Date | n_points | n_ideal | gap_total_missing (old) | true_missing (new) | n_gaps_raw | jitter_unstable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-01-22 | 86400 | 86400 | 0 | 0 | 0 | False |
| 2025-01-23 | 86400 | 86400 | 0 | 0 | 0 | False |
| 2025-01-24 | 85238 | 86400 | 1162 | 1162 | 3 | False |
| 2025-01-25 | 84396 | 86400 | 2004 | 2004 | 37 | False |
| 2025-01-26 | 86400 | 86400 | 0 | 0 | 1 (jitter) | False — frac_maxabs = 0.349 , just under 0.4 |
Real-gap days match exactly. Jitter-only day (26) classified as no-gap by both, with the new instability flag False because a single 349 ms residual sat just below the 40 % threshold. Threshold validated.
| Metric | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| n_points | 85308 | |
| n_ideal | 86401 | |
| true_missing | 1093 | n_ideal − n_points |
| n_gaps_raw | 13 | Δi > 1 events |
| gap_total_missing_raw | 1103 | Σ(Δi − 1) over those 13 events |
Discrepancy of 10. The legacy algorithm reports 1103 missing (overcount); the new algorithm reports the actual 1093. The difference is jitter intervals that rounded down to Δi=0 elsewhere in the day, compensating for over-rounded gap events. Same pattern on SUM1 2025-01-25 (1809 raw vs 1807 actual — off by 2).
This is the substantive correctness improvement of the new algorithm: it counts samples that are actually missing, not the apparent count from gap events.
5 days × 3 stations = 15 day-stations, all true_missing = 0 .
0 figures generated ( --only-gaps correctly suppressed all of them on the clean week).
CSV rows still recorded with figure_generated = False .
One worth flagging: SUM1 2026-01-24 had 18 raw Δi>1 events but true_missing = 0 with 86401 points. Old absolute-threshold pipeline would split that day into 19 MiniSEEDs; new Option-A logic keeps it as one. Best validation case in the 2026 batch for the splitting decision.
CSVs: 10 rows per station (5 from 2025 + 5 from 2026).
Figures: 15 dirs from 2025 (full coverage); 0 from 2026 (clean week + --only-gaps ).
Estimate: ~12 000 day-stations × ~50 s per OOI fetch ≈ 150–170 hours of wall time (6–7 days continuous). collect_mode is idempotent — already-processed (station, date) pairs are skipped on resume — so chunking by year keeps progress safe across interruptions.
[ -n "$OOI_USERNAME" ] && [ -n "$OOI_TOKEN" ] && echo "creds set" || source .ooi_env
nohup bash -c '
for year in 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026; do
 echo "=== $year start: $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) ==="
 conda run -n ooi_env python bin/temporal_anomaly_investigator.py \
 --mode collect \
 --start ${year}-01-01 --end ${year}-12-31 \
 --only-gaps
 echo "=== $year end: $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) ==="
done
' > /tmp/collect_2016_2026.log 2>&1 &
echo "PID: $!"
disown
tail -f /tmp/collect_2016_2026.log
wc -l output/temporal_anomaly/metrics/*.csv
pgrep -af temporal_anomaly_investigator
ls output/temporal_anomaly/figures/per_day/ | wc -l
pkill -TERM -f 'temporal_anomaly_investigator.py' # graceful — finishes current day
# or:
pkill -TERM -f 'collect.*2016' # kill the year loop too
# resume — same command, skips everything already in the CSVs
nohup bash -c '...same loop...' > /tmp/collect_2016_2026.log 2>&1 &
Deployment-boundary day (SLBS / SUM1, 2018) may produce a garbage row because a single 24 h window can straddle 15 s → 1 s rates. Δt_FG lands between the two and the reconstruction breaks. Watch for one bad day around each transition; re-investigate manually after the bulk run.
OOI outages turn affected days into has_data=False rows. After the run, find them with awk -F, '$4=="False"' output/temporal_anomaly/metrics/*.csv and re-run that subset.
Disk projection : CSVs ~5 MB total; figures ~5 MB per real-gap day × ~600 days ≈ 3 GB. No NetCDFs unless --save-nc is added.
VM (Kozo) alternative: swap conda run -n ooi_env python for /home/coszo/miniconda3/envs/ooi_env/bin/python /home/coszo/coszo-data-collection/... . VM has ~10 GB free; figures would fit, NetCDFs might not.
Sanity check first : run a single noisy year before committing to the full span:
nohup conda run -n ooi_env python bin/temporal_anomaly_investigator.py \
 --mode collect --start 2019-01-01 --end 2019-12-31 --only-gaps \
 > /tmp/collect_2019.log 2>&1 &
disown
That's ~14 hours and gives a feel for OOI's actual response time before the full 11-year run.
Going forward, when running collect_mode :
Always use --save-nc so the local NetCDF archive grows alongside the CSVs (the investigator is the canonical place to save NetCDFs after migration; the pipeline will stop saving them).
Always use --only-gaps so figures are produced only when true_missing > 0 . Clean and jitter-only days get a CSV row with figure_generated=False and no figure directory.
Concretely: the standard collect invocation is
python bin/temporal_anomaly_investigator.py --mode collect \
 --start <YYYY-MM-DD> --end <YYYY-MM-DD> --save-nc --only-gaps
The big-run command above omits --save-nc only because of the disk hit (~12 000 NetCDFs). For smaller, targeted ranges always include --save-nc .
Phase 0 commit 7f961c0 .
code migration.md is the canonical place for migration decisions — refer to it rather than this note for ongoing planning.

Anonymous visitors keep browsing the notes site normally. Behind a shared password, /chat/ opens a conversational UI that retrieves the most relevant chunks of my notes and asks Gemini to answer using only those chunks, citing notes by title.
Obsidian vault
 | vaultnotes sync (or daily 5 PM launchd)
 v
pages-repo (notes/COSZO, notes/BransfieldEQ, notes/Earthnote)
 | git push to main
 v
GitHub Actions: Build RAG index
 - chunks markdown (~500 tokens, 100 overlap)
 - embeds chunks via gemini-embedding-001 (768d, L2-normalized)
 - writes public/{search-index.json, chunks.json, embeddings.bin}
 - commits public/ back to main
 v
GitHub Pages serves static site + index files + chat UI
 |
 | fetch (browser)
 v
Cloudflare Worker (notes-rag.quakehunt.workers.dev)
 - constant-time password check
 - holds GEMINI_API_KEY and CHAT_PASSWORD as Worker secrets
 - retries 429/503 with backoff
 - streams gemini-2.5-flash-lite via SSE
No database, no accounts, no per-user state.
Runs in GitHub Actions on every push that touches notes/** or the script itself. Walks the published project folders, strips markdown, splits into ~500-token chunks with ~100-token overlap, and embeds them with gemini-embedding-001 at 768 dimensions. Embeddings are L2-normalized so cosine similarity in the browser is just a dot product.
Outputs:
public/search-index.json — serialized MiniSearch index (BM25)
public/chunks.json — chunk metadata (id, noteId, title, url, text)
public/embeddings.bin — concatenated Float32Array , ordered by chunk id
[!note] The Action commits public/ back to main and Pages auto-redeploys. New notes are answerable within ~2–3 minutes of the daily sync push.
A tiny Cloudflare Worker that proxies Gemini. Two endpoints:
POST /embed — embeds a query string with taskType: RETRIEVAL_QUERY . The frontend calls this once per question, plus once on password entry as a verification ping.
POST /chat — takes the user query and pre-assembled context, streams gemini-2.5-flash-lite SSE back to the browser.
Other things the Worker does:
Constant-time password check so the password isn't string-equality-compared.
CORS locked to the Pages origin so the API key isn't trivially abusable from elsewhere.
Length caps (2000 chars for query, 20000 for context) to keep prompts well-bounded.
Retry with exponential backoff on 429 and 503, honoring Retry-After . This was needed because Gemini's free tier 503s under demand spikes, and the chat felt broken without the retry.
Three screens:
Password gate — single input. Password is held only in memory; refresh forgets it. Submitting calls /embed with a "ping" text; if the Worker returns 200, password is correct and we swap to chat.
Loading — fetches search-index.json , chunks.json , embeddings.bin in parallel.
Chat — message list with a streaming response panel and a pixel-fox avatar that walks through 4 frames.
Hybrid retrieval pipeline on every question:
async function ask(query) {
 const queryEmb = await fetchEmbedding(query); // via Worker
 const bm25 = miniSearch.search(query).slice(0, 10); // keyword
 const semantic = cosineTopK(queryEmb, embeddings, 10); // vector
 const fused = reciprocalRankFusion(bm25, semantic, 5); // merge
 const context = fused.map(c => `### ${c.noteTitle}\n${c.text}`).join('\n---\n');
 streamChat(query, context, onToken); // via Worker
}
Reciprocal Rank Fusion handles the BM25-vs-semantic blending without needing tuned weights. Top 5 fused chunks make up the context window passed to Gemini.
Citations are deduped by note and shown as clickable chips below each answer, linking to the raw .md URL.
Browser does MiniSearch.loadJSON(...) and wraps embeddings.bin as a Float32Array .
User types question → frontend calls Worker /embed to get the query vector.
Worker validates password, hits Gemini embedContent , returns 768 floats.
Frontend runs BM25 + cosine top-K locally, fuses with RRF, picks top 5.
Frontend posts {query, context} to Worker /chat .
Worker validates password, opens streaming Gemini call with system prompt + user content, pipes the SSE body straight back.
Frontend parses SSE events ( data: {...}\n\n ), appends each text token to the assistant bubble, renders citation chips.
Total wall-clock to first token on WiFi: ~1–2s when Gemini isn't throttling.
Adding notes — edit them in Obsidian. The launchd job at 5 PM rsyncs published folders into pages-repo and pushes. The Action sees notes/** changed, rebuilds the index, commits public/ , Pages redeploys. Done.
Adding a folder — vaultnotes add NewFolder . It edits config, syncs, and the indexer picks up the new folder via rag-config.json .
Worker code changes — git push does not update the Worker. Run vaultnotes rag deploy-worker (or npx wrangler deploy from worker/ ).
Rotating the password — npx wrangler secret put CHAT_PASSWORD from the worker dir, then npx wrangler deploy . Frontend doesn't need any change.
Once the chat worked for me, I lifted the whole thing into vaultnotes so other users get it for free. The new surface area:
vaultnotes rag enable — copies chat/ , worker/ , scripts/ , .github/workflows/build-index.yml , package.json , rag-config.json , chat/config.json into the user's pages repo. Worker name and CORS origin are derived from github.repo .
vaultnotes rag secret <NAME> — wraps wrangler secret put with the right cwd.
vaultnotes rag deploy-worker — runs npm install (one-time) + wrangler deploy from the worker dir.
vaultnotes rag set-worker-url <url> — stores the deployed URL in YAML config and chat/config.json .
vaultnotes where [--open] — prints (and optionally reveals in Finder) the local pages-repo path. Necessary because the default lives at ~/.local/share/vaultnotes/pages-repo which Finder hides.
vaultnotes upgrade — wraps pipx install --force git+https://github.com/MaleenKidiwela/vaultnotes.git .
The indexer in the package reads project folders from rag-config.json instead of hardcoded names. vaultnotes sync regenerates that file on every run, so each user's chat tracks their own published folders.
Embedding — runs once per chunk, only on changed pushes. ~140 chunks for my vault costs essentially nothing on free tier. Even at 10× the size, paid-tier embedding is a few cents per rebuild.
Chat — gemini-2.5-flash free tier is 20 requests/day. After hitting that limit on the first day of testing, I switched to gemini-2.5-flash-lite which gets ~1000 RPD free and is plenty for grounded RAG answers. The model gap matters less here because the answer is already grounded in retrieved text — the model is summarizing, not recalling.
gh repo create <name> --clone -- <path> is invalid; only one positional. Split into gh repo create <name> then gh repo clone <name> <path> .
display: flex overrides the browser default for [hidden] , so password screen stayed visible after success until I added [hidden] { display: none !important } .
Free-tier Gemini 503s during overload are common; Worker-side retry with Retry-After makes the chat feel reliable.
Pixel-art sprite frames need a single scale factor and baseline across all frames, otherwise the character visibly grows and shrinks between poses. Solution: take the union bbox across all frames, crop each frame to it, then scale everything by one factor.
When vaultnotes sync runs, only files you explicitly git add get pushed. Forgot to add the RAG files in the first version, so the chat folder existed locally but never reached the remote — easy to miss.

Replaced the legacy next_start = last_written + sp formula with next_start = UTCDateTime(end_time) (commit 57a703d ). Each cron run now advances endtime_*.txt by exactly 86400 s — completely independent of any per-day rate estimate (median Δt or OLS Δt_true).
Why: Δt_true varies day-to-day (sub-ms typically), so using today's value to predict tomorrow's first sample was a small extrapolation that could drift over time. Walking arithmetic across day boundaries also coupled the cron's continuity to the algorithm choice. Removing the dependency means the cron's day-stride is structurally fixed: 86400 s, every run, forever.
Tradeoff (consistent with "gaps are honest"): if a window only got partial data, the next cron jumps straight to the next calendar day instead of re-fetching from where partial data ended. Missing portions become permanent gaps in the archive rather than getting silently backfilled with a different timestamp.

We start with Chronos. which is the same as [[ChronFix — Implementation Plan]] with a new name.
The reason being, Chronfix would be reserved for fixing the timing errors that Chronos finds.
We will be writing it in a way that we could run it in realtime to detect any temporal anomalies in a given instrument. Chronos will produce a daily values of timing errors within seismometers. HYS14-Chronfix will realign time such that the timestamps represent accurate time. We are trying to do this with 8Hz data

Cross-correlation diagnosis of the HYS14 (OOI Hydrate Ridge OBS) clock issue.
Pairs HYS14 with two neighbouring stations and tracks the lag of the
ballistic-wave peak in the daily cross-correlation function over four years.
This document specifies the methods, presents the results, and states what
they imply for the Chronos timing-correction package.
For project context see [[ChronFix — Implementation Plan]]
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Network / stations | OO.HYS12 , OO.HYS14 , OO.HYSB1 |
| Channel | MHZ (mid-period vertical, 8 Hz native) |
| Time range | 2022-01-01 → 2026-05-01 (1582 days) |
| Source | EarthScope FDSN ( obspy.clients.fdsn.Client("EARTHSCOPE") ) |
| Local cache | /data/wsd02/maleen_data/OOI-Data/{sta}/{yr}/{doy:03d}/{sta}.OO.{yr}.{doy:03d}.MHZ |
| Coverage | HYS12: 1326/1582 days (84%); HYS14: 1326/1582 (84%); HYSB1: 1088/1582 (69%) |
Download script: scripts/download_hys.py . StationXML stored under
 /data/wsd02/maleen_data/OOI-Data/StationXML/OO.{sta}..MHZ.xml .
Adapted from the single-station preprocessing recipe used in Earthnote's
 phase13_pilot.py , generalized to inter-station pairs and parameterised over
the science band. No NoisePy dependency; bare ObsPy + NumPy + SciPy.
Implementation: diagnostics/hys_ccf.py .
For each station-day:
Read the daily MiniSEED, cast to float64 , merge(method=1, fill_value=0.0) .
Cosine-taper around zero-fill regions (100 s on each side of every gap).
detrend("demean") , detrend("linear") .
High-pass at HP_FREQ ; corner chosen below the science band.
remove_response(output="VEL", pre_filt=...) with corners clamped to
0.98 × Nyquist of the input trace (some channels have lower native rate).
Resample / interpolate to TARGET_FS = 8.0 Hz . Downsample uses ObsPy's
anti-aliased resample ; upsample uses interpolate(method="lanczos", a=20) .
Per pair (A, B), per day with both station traces present:
Cut 30-min windows with 7.5-min step (75 % overlap) → cc_len = 1800 s ,
 cc_step = 450 s .
Per window: demean / detrend / 20 s cosine edge taper / phase whiten
with raised-cosine band edges in the band (WHITEN_FMIN, WHITEN_FMAX) /
one-bit normalisation.
Frequency-domain cross-correlation: irfft(conj(FFT(a)) * FFT(b)) ,
truncated to ± MAXLAG = 60 s . Sign convention: positive lag = B lags A.
Per day: per-lag median across all windows (robust against transient
high-amplitude segments). Stored as one row of the daily-stack tensor.
Long-term reference: linear (mean) stack of all days with valid daily
stacks.
Outputs per pair under data/ccf/<pair_tag>/ :
cc_30min.npy (N_seg, n_lags) all 30-min CCs concatenated
cc_30min_times.npy (N_seg,) fractional day index
cc_daily.npy (N_days, n_lags) per-lag median per day
cc_dates.npy (N_days,) datetime64[D]
cc_ref.npy (n_lags,) reference stack
lags.npy (n_lags,) lag axis in seconds
The two pairs need different bands because of their different inter-station
SNR. Parameters used:
| Parameter | HYS12-HYS14 (highband) | HYS14-HYSB1 ( _lowband tag) |
| ------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Science band (FMIN, FMAX) | 1.0 – 3.0 Hz | 0.1 – 0.3 Hz |
| Whitening (WHITEN_FMIN, FMAX) | 0.5 – 3.8 Hz | 0.05 – 0.4 Hz |
| High-pass HP_FREQ | 0.4 Hz | 0.04 Hz |
| pre_filt | 0.05 / 0.1 / 3.6 / 3.95 Hz | 0.02 / 0.04 / 3.6 / 3.95 Hz |
| MAXLAG | 60 s | 60 s |
The lowband is the secondary microseism range. OBS pairs with longer
baselines have most of their coherent ambient noise energy at periods
3–10 s, so dropping the science band raised the reference RMS for
HYS14-HYSB1 from 1.46 → 50.4 (≈ 35× SNR gain) and recovered a clear
ballistic wave packet.
Implementation: diagnostics/peak_lag.py . For each daily CCF row $c(\tau)$,
compute the Hilbert envelope of $c^2$:
$$
e(\tau) = \left| \mathcal{H}\big(c(\tau)^2\big) \right|
$$
and report the lag at the global argmax of $e$. Squaring before
envelope-detection sharpens the peak; the location is the same as
$|\mathcal{H}(c)|$ would give.
Output per pair: data/peak_lag/<pair_tag>/peak_lag_global.npy , one
 float64 per day, NaN for missing days. --side {pos,neg} restricts the
search to one side of zero lag.
A separate diagnostic plotter diagnostics/ccf_plot.py writes a
two-panel overview ( ccf_overview.png ) showing the reference stack and
the daily-stack heatmap for any pair.
| | |
|---|---|
| Reference RMS | 12.8 |
| Ballistic anchor lag | ~0 s (stations near-co-located) |
| Plot | data/peak_lag/HYS12-HYS14/plot.png |
| Overview | data/peak_lag/HYS12-HYS14/ccf_overview.png |
The peak-lag time series shows multiple linear drift episodes punctuated
by resync events that snap the lag back near zero. Several episodes
drive the peak to ±60 s, where it walks off the analysis-window edge. From
roughly May 2025 onward the peak lag is stable at ~0 s with low scatter
— consistent with the clock issue having been resolved.
| | |
|---|---|
| Reference RMS | 50.4 |
| Ballistic anchor lag (post-fix) | ≈ −30 s (acausal side dominates) |
| Plot | data/peak_lag/HYS14-HYSB1_lowband/plot.png |
| Overview | data/peak_lag/HYS14-HYSB1_lowband/ccf_overview.png |
After 2025-05 the global peak settles tightly at ~−30 s, consistent with a
fixed inter-station travel time. The earlier history shows the same
drift-and-resync pattern as HYS12-HYS14 but with the lag walking around
the −30 s anchor. The most striking single event is the early-2023 ramp
from −30 s up through 0 to +20 s (a ~50 s drift over a few months) before
the next resync brings it back. There is a long unobserved stretch
mid-2023 → late-2024 where HYSB1 was off-air (487 missing days total).
Both pairs share HYS14, and both show the same temporal pattern of drift
episodes and the same stabilization date in May 2025. The other endpoints
(HYS12 and HYSB1) are different and the two pair plots use different
science bands, so the agreement is not artefactual. The conclusion that
 HYS14 is the source of the timing error is robust against the choice
of partner station.
The lag-vs-time pattern is:
Linear drift between events — peak walks at roughly steady rate
(order ~0.1–0.3 s/day, varies between episodes), suggesting a slow
oscillator drift rather than discrete jumps.
Periodic resync events — sharp resets back to the anchor lag, likely
tied to ship visits / power cycles / NTP-style sync events.
Stabilization from May 2025 — the drift turns off, consistent with
either a hardware fix or instrument replacement at that time.
This rules out the "constant offset" hypothesis from the implementation
plan and points to the drift + segments model as the right fit.
The Phase 1 priorities should be reordered around what the diagnostic
shows is actually needed:
Segment detection — find the resync boundaries automatically from
day-to-day jumps in the peak-lag time series. Defines the time
intervals over which a single drift fit is valid.
Per-segment linear drift fit and correction — within each segment,
fit t_apparent − t_true ≈ a + b·(t − t_segment_start) from the daily
peak-lag track and apply the inverse to the waveform timestamps.
Constant-offset correction kept as a building block but is no
longer the primary use case.
Clock-jump correction is a degenerate case of segment detection
(zero-length drift between two anchored values).
The peak-lag time series produced here is the empirical input to (1)–(2):
each segment's slope is the drift rate to invert. Correction validation
is straightforward — apply, recompute the CCF for that segment, and
verify the peak lag flattens.
MAXLAG = 60 s truncates several drift episodes; we cannot tell from
the present data how much further the lag walked before the next
resync. Re-running with --maxlag 200 (or larger) would resolve the
full drift profile.
The peak-lag plot reports only the lag of the envelope maximum; it
does not yet quantify SNR or peak prominence. Days with weak ambient
noise will have peaks at lag values driven by noise, not the
ballistic, and currently appear in the plot indistinguishably from
good days.
Sub-sample lag accuracy is at the 8 Hz native rate (0.125 s);
parabolic refinement around the envelope max would push that to
~10 ms if needed.
The lowband HYS14-HYSB1 picks were tested with --side global . The
causal-side --side pos picks were bimodal (jumping between two
arrivals at ~+15 s and ~+37 s) which is why we use the global picker,
whose argmax falls reliably on the dominant acausal packet at −30 s.

sectionTitle: one initial issue related to timing corrections
sectionPath: one initial issue related to timing corrections
text:
Symptom: corrected hourly peak-lag still showed drift ramps after correction.
Root cause: load_day_z returned just the data array, dropping the trace's UTC starttime. The original pipeline implicitly assumed sample 0 of every daily file = midnight UTC, which was true for original input files but not for chronfix-corrected ones (whose starttime is offset by −Δt
Net effect: re-introducing the same Δt misalignment we'd just removed, so the corrected CCF output looked unchanged.
Fix: trim/pad each loaded trace to span exactly the canonical UTC day with tr.trim(..., pad=True, fill_value=0.0) before returning the data array. Forces sample 0 of every trace to correspond to the same UTC second, regardless of where the input file actually begins or ends. After the fix the validation passes and the closed-loop table reflects the post-fix behaviour.
Full method of correcting the timing errors in the trace files is outlined in [[HYS14 — Correction Method V1]]

Vaultnotes is a lightweight AI-powered notes assistant that turns a personal Markdown vault into a searchable knowledge interface. It uses a static hybrid RAG pipeline, where notes are preprocessed into chunks, embedded with Gemini embeddings, and stored as a browser-accessible index. At query time, Vaultnotes combines BM25 keyword search, lexical matching, and semantic vector search, then fuses the results to retrieve the most relevant note chunks before sending them to a language model for response generation. The system is designed to run efficiently on static hosting, with a Cloudflare Worker handling secure model calls and API access, while the frontend performs local retrieval over prebuilt index files. To reduce cost and rebuild time, Vaultnotes also uses a content-hash embedding cache, so unchanged notes do not need to be re-embedded.
RAG workflow was implemented in [[RAG implementation]] in maleenkidiwela.github.io/chat

But the final workflow was updated using [[05-01-26 Notes]] for Chronos which detects the timing errors.
