sectionTitle: Agent E: Ontology, agents, and model extension
sectionPath: Agent E: Ontology, agents, and model extension
text:
Owns: packages/sim , the ontology in packages/contracts , the Gemini agent in workers/api .
[ ] Formalize the Cousin entities and edges into the ontology. Preserve every coefficient and citation. Mark uncalibrated edges calibrated: false . Widen geography to the PNW.
[ ] Extend the model downward and outward with first-class state nodes: seismicity rate, dv/v, H/V f0, receiver-function conversion timing, deep-tremor rate, GNSS strain, a fused slow-slip index, plus the weather and hydromet couplings below. Define the Cascadia ETS index as a CompositeMonitor over tremor rate, GNSS reversal, and dv/v.
[ ] Wire the compound-hazard couplings (see below) as edges so atmosphere and hydrology drive ecology, ports, and people.
[ ] Scenario and what-if API on the Worker, reusing the baseline-versus-scenario engine across all three modes.
[ ] Gemini agent behind the Worker proxy, reusing the notes-RAG pattern. It reads the ontology and the observability API and commands the view. It obeys the two-contract prediction principle: it may relay weather forecasts with their stated skill, and it must never phrase a solid-earth signal as a forecast.
Done when: the ontology round-trips the existing model with no behavior change, a solid-earth and a weather state node each participate in a causal chain, and the agent answers a grounded why-question that spans both.

All of these are geocompute modules under services/geocompute/methods . They differ only in cadence and output shape, and they all reduce to the shared contracts: continuous outputs become Sample , heavy outputs become GeoProduct , threshold crossings become HazardEvent , derived state nodes live in the ontology.
| Method | Cadence | Inputs | Emits | Detects |
|--------|---------|--------|-------|---------|
| dv/v | continuous, daily | ambient noise, pairs and autocorr | dv/v Sample , dvvMatrix | stress, fluids, thermal, hydrology, co-seismic and ETS-related change |
| H/V (HVSR) | continuous, rolling | 3-component noise, single station | f0 and A0 Sample , hvsrCurve | near-surface velocity, water table, damage |
| Receiver functions | per teleseism, accumulate | teleseismic events, broadband | conversion time and amplitude Sample , rfStack | crustal and slab structure, Vp/Vs, deep fluid change |
| Deep tremor | continuous | network waveforms | tremor rate Sample , episode HazardEvent , tremorCatalog | slow slip on the deep interface |
| GNSS | daily and high-rate | EarthScope NOTA positions | displacement and strain Sample , gnssSeries | crustal deformation, slow-slip surface reversal |
EarthScope is the source layer beneath this table, not a row in it. PNSN and ONC supply regional and offshore stations.
Deep tremor, a GNSS surface-displacement reversal, and a dv/v change are three views of one Episodic Tremor and Slip event on the deep Cascadia interface. The plan fuses them in one CompositeMonitor emitting cascadia.slowSlipIndex , and adds offshore seafloor geodesy (bottom pressure and GNSS-Acoustic) so the index sees the offshore updip portion of the megathrust where the tsunamigenic slip sits, not just the onshore downdip edge that land GNSS resolves. ETS in northern Cascadia recurs near a 14-month interval, so this index is genuinely trackable and is a real leading indicator of slow slip. Integrity boundary: slow slip is observable and quasi-periodic and loads the locked megathrust, but it is not a deterministic predictor of a great earthquake. The contract carries isPrediction: false , and the UI and agent describe it as ongoing slow slip, never a countdown.

This is the one domain that is allowed to predict, because numerical weather prediction is calibrated and skillful. The discipline is the contract split: observations and issued warnings are HazardEvent records, model output is a Forecast . They never mix.
| Product | Contract | Source | Role |
|---------|----------|--------|------|
| Station observations | Sample | NWS | current conditions |
| Issued warnings | HazardEvent (officialSource) | NWS alerts API | official, mirror only |
| Model forecasts | Forecast | HRRR, GFS, ECMWF | predictive, with stated skill |
| Radar | GeoProduct (radarSweep) | NEXRAD | precipitation field on the globe |
| Marine wind and waves | Sample , Forecast | WaveWatch III | vessel and ocean-mixing forcing |
| Storm surge and tides | Sample , Forecast | NOAA surge, Tides | coastal-flood forcing |
| Atmospheric river | metric and Forecast | model IVT | the region's signature winter hazard |
| Streamflow | Sample on riverGauge | USGS NWIS, Environment Canada | flood state |
| Snow water equivalent | Sample | SNOTEL | rain-on-snow setup |

The Cascadia megathrust and the tsunami source are offshore, so a twin that stops sensing at the coastline is blind to where its defining hazard originates. This tier extends the solid earth and ocean state past the shelf. Like the others, everything reduces to the shared contracts.
| Product | Cadence | Source | Emits | Role |
|---------|---------|--------|-------|------|
| Seafloor pressure (vertical) | continuous | ONC, OOI bottom pressure | Sample | offshore vertical deformation, Axial inflation |
| GNSS-Acoustic (horizontal) | campaign | seafloor sites | gnssAcoustic | offshore strain into the slow-slip composite |
| DART tsunami | continuous | NDBC buoys | Sample , tsunami HazardEvent | the offshore tsunami sensor |
| Offshore OBS | continuous and archived | ONC, OOI, Cascadia Initiative via EarthScope | folds into FDSN | rebalances dv/v and tremor offshore |
| Axial inflation | continuous | OOI Cabled Array | Sample , labeled threshold readout | the one skillful volcanic forecast, scoped |
| Satellite ocean state | daily | PODAAC, Coral Reef Watch, Copernicus | sstField , MHW metric | marine heatwaves, upwelling |
| Shelf hypoxia and OA | continuous | OOI Oregon shelf, NANOOS | Sample | the Oregon dead zone into the calcifier nodes |
| Fishing effort and SAR | daily to weekly | Global Fishing Watch 4Wings | fishingEffort , sarDetections | offshore human pulse, fishing pressure |
Two honest limits. Seafloor geodesy is sparse and partly campaign-based, not a dense real-time network like land GNSS, so the offshore deformation signal is thinner and slower than the onshore one. And terrestrial AIS thins past the shelf, which is exactly why Global Fishing Watch matters here: its satellite AIS and SAR detections see the vessels, including the dark ones, that AISStream misses offshore.
The Axial nuance, restated because it is the one place the prediction line bends. Axial Seamount inflates to a fairly repeatable threshold before it erupts, and that has produced genuinely skillful eruption windows. The plan treats this as an explicitly labeled, evidence-based threshold readout with a window, never a precise date, never generalized to other volcanoes or to earthquakes. It is a Sample and a labeled state, not a Forecast .
This is why the twin exists rather than a set of separate dashboards. The region's signature risks are couplings, and the Cousin already models couplings, so the work is to make them spatial, live, and multi-physics by wiring atmosphere and hydrology into the existing graph as edges:
Atmospheric river onto a burn scar drives the debris-flow and sediment term the Cousin already has.
Rain on snow, the SNOTEL layer against an AR, drives a flood through the river-gauge nodes.
Storm surge stacked on a king tide on rising sea level drives coastal flooding.
Vessel noise from the AIS layer against orca foraging efficiency, an edge the Cousin already encodes.
Fishing effort from Global Fishing Watch against salmon and groundfish, a fishing-mortality edge onto the prey base the resident orca depend on.
Cascadia under all of it, where a great-earthquake scenario cascades into tsunami, liquefaction, and port and population exposure.
Each coupling is a CausalEdge with a mechanism and, where possible, a citation. Uncalibrated couplings are marked calibrated: false .
Roughly half the data is United States and half Canadian, under two regimes, and Coast Salish sovereignty crosses the border. Tag every source and entity with jurisdiction. Reconcile units, datums, and cadences at ingest, not in the UI. Treaty and Usual and Accustomed data and sensitive ecological locations are flagged and handled with consent. The border is a data-engineering and ethics constraint, not a visual one. The twin renders one continuous region.
M0, scaffold: Phase 0 complete. Monorepo, contracts including region and forecast, CI, three modes green, globe shell with one WorldView layer.
M1, flagship vertical slice: one story wired end to end through every plane. This is the open decision (see below).
M2, integration: all three modes work with the globe and live feeds. Weather forecasts render distinctly from events. The agent answers grounded questions spanning solid earth and weather. Compound-hazard couplings online.
M3, hardening: calibrated baselines on real station noise, uncertainty everywhere, cost controls on 3D Tiles, jurisdiction and sovereignty enforcement, post-event records, forecast-skill display.
Pick one to wire first. Both touch every plane.
Cascadia slow-slip and tremor: shows off the seismic depth. Tremor plus GNSS plus dv/v fuse into the slow-slip index, render on the globe, and the agent explains the ongoing ETS without forecasting a quake.
Atmospheric river to flood: shows off weather and compound hazards. An AR forecast plus radar plus SNOTEL plus river gauges cascade into a flood setup through the Cousin couplings, with the forecast band rendered as forward-looking and skill-stated.
Axial Seamount: shows off the offshore and marine-geophysics depth. Bottom-pressure inflation, seismicity, and the OOI Cabled Array on one offshore volcanic node, with the inflation threshold rendered as a labeled, windowed readout. It is the one place a solid-earth forecast is defensible, and it is a system you know firsthand.
Explorer, Research, and Policy all work, now able to open into the globe.
The globe renders land and bathymetry, goes below the waterline, and shows at least one WorldView human-pulse layer and one geophysical layer on the shared clock.
The chosen flagship slice runs end to end on real PNW data.
A weather Forecast renders as forward-looking with a lead time and stated skill, visibly distinct from observed events.
One compound-hazard coupling is live, driving a downstream ecology, port, or population node.
At least one offshore layer is live below or beyond the shelf: seafloor pressure or GNSS-Acoustic feeding the slow-slip composite, a DART buoy, Axial inflation, or Global Fishing Watch SAR detections.
One real inversion update flows from a fired event to a versioned, uncertainty-tagged volume on the globe.
The agent answers a grounded question spanning solid earth and weather, relaying forecasts with skill and never phrasing a solid-earth signal as a forecast.
No real secret committed. No commit carries Claude attribution. No em dashes in shipped copy.

The two-contract prediction line is the central integrity risk. Weather may forecast, the solid earth may not, and the contracts keep them apart. A polished command center invites over-reading, so this is load-bearing.
This is the Pacific Northwest only. It is not a global system, and scope creep beyond OR, WA, BC is a v1 failure.
It does not replace official warnings. It mirrors and contextualizes ShakeAlert, the NWS, and the tsunami centers, with officialSource set, and never presents itself as the authority.
Transboundary data is two regimes and two sets of units and licenses. Reconcile at ingest. Sovereignty is consent, not a flag toggled after the fact.
Cost: Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles is an Enterprise SKU. Cache aggressively, consider NASA GIBS or self-hosted tiles for heavy public traffic.
The geocompute service is the one non-edge piece. Keep it small so it runs on modest hardware.
Offshore data is thinner than onshore. Seafloor geodesy is sparse and partly campaign-based, not a dense real-time network, so offshore deformation is slower and less certain. Terrestrial AIS thins past the shelf, which is why Global Fishing Watch satellite AIS and SAR are the offshore vessel picture. State these limits in the UI rather than implying uniform coverage.
Axial is the only solid-earth forecast the plan allows, scoped and labeled. Do not let it soften the no-forecast rule for earthquakes or other volcanoes.
The line between an impressive demo and a real instrument is calibrated baselines, real inversions, and stated forecast skill, not a prettier overlay.
APPENDIX
The Salish Sea Digital Cousin: An Open-Source Prototype of Coupled Socio-Ecological Modeling for an Urban Sea System
M. Ryan Delaney, Haas School of Business, University of California, Berkeley

The Salish Sea Digital Cousin is a browser-based simulation of the Salish Sea region. Twenty-four compute modules organized into eight coupling domains share a quarterly time step over a fifty-year horizon, draw on 76 live public-sector data endpoints, and surface through four audience-specific user interfaces. It runs in any modern web browser, requires no installation, and is freely accessible. This Appendix describes that artifact and the claim its existence supports: that the integration challenge the main paper develops conceptually is now tractable at single-developer scale. Five years ago it was not. The Cousin is one empirical data point for that change. The close of Section 4.2 introduces the artifact as an “initial prototype of [the Urban Sea System Digital Twin] architecture, developed as an independent open-source project and deliberately designated a ‘Digital Cousin’ rather than a Digital Twin to reflect its status as a teaching and scenario tool rather than a physics-accurate replica.” Digital Twin literature converges on three features: a virtual computational representation, bi-directional data flow with the physical system, and decision support through scenario exploration. The Cousin satisfies the first and third constraint. Its data flow is one-way: observations feed in, but the simulation does not write back to any physical system. It is also not built to operate persistently over decadal timescales. Against the three-aspect extension this paper proposes for Urban Sea System Digital Twins specifically (multi-module by necessity, governance-facing by design, persistent rather than project-bounded), the Cousin satisfies the first two and does not satisfy the third. It is a teaching and scenario tool that demonstrates what a Twin’s coupling architecture might look like at operational scale, not a Twin itself. The empirical claim is bounded but specific. A combined architecture covering ocean physics, marine ecology, port economics, contaminant transport, climate forcing, infrastructure resilience, and tribal governance was assembled, united through explicit shared state, visible through four audience-specific interfaces, and validated against fifteen years of historical observations. The Cousin does not approach the operational Salish Sea Model (PNNL), LiveOcean (UW), or SalishSeaCast, and is not intended to. Its contribution lies in showing that integration architecture itself is now within reach. The Cousin was developed in the San Francisco Bay Area, where AI-assisted software development has become a dominant working tool for technical projects. The artifact reflects what is now achievable by a single developer with access to current AI tools and a focused domain target, working on a timescale of weeks rather than years. This regional and methodological context is part of the empirical claim. Section A.2 describes the architecture, what it demonstrates, and supporting module and coupling taxonomy. Section A.3 walks through the Cascadia M9 earthquake recovery scenario as a worked example, exercising the cascading-failure dynamics that conventional sector-by-sector planning treats incompletely (§6). Section A.4 provides an accounting of validation, parameterization, structural limitations, and known gaps. Section A.5 closes with reflection on the Cousin’s development, where it sits in the lineage of related simulation work, and how it might inform Digital Twin development that the main paper proposes. Section A.6 contains a competing-interests disclaimer. The Cousin is independent of any institutional Digital Twin development effort. Its purpose is to make a complex coupled system inspectable and teachable: to a knowledgeable audience of practitioners, scientists, and policy actors who already understand the Salish Sea, and through them to the broader community that may engage with the Workshop and the Digital Twin development effort the main paper sets out.
The architecture demonstrates three integration patterns the main paper argues are load-bearing for Urban Sea System Digital Twin development. First, combined modules with shared state and orchestrated convergence. Second, one-way data ingestion at scale across public-sector sources. Third, audience-specific interfaces consuming a single computational substrate rather than parallel platform implementations. Each is described below with the supporting module and coupling detail.
The Cousin runs entirely client-side in JavaScript with no server-side computation. The choice eliminates infrastructure dependencies, makes the artifact freely accessible to anyone with a web browser, and removes the institutional commitments that operating a server-backed system over time would require. The trade-off is computational scale: the Cousin operates at quarterly time steps over a fifty-year horizon (200 simulation steps total). That resolution is appropriate to a teaching and scenario tool but would be insufficient for operational forecasting.

sectionTitle: A.2.1  Combined modules with explicit coupling
sectionPath: A.2.1  Combined modules with explicit coupling
text:
The main paper’s discussion of Figure 4 states: “the critical intellectual and engineering challenge is not the development of individual modules, most of which already exist in mature form, but the construction of the couplings among them — the exchanges of state, flux, and boundary conditions that allow system-level feedbacks and emergent behavior to be represented.” The Cousin’s design follows this principle directly. Individual modules are simpler than their domain-specific operational counterparts. What the Cousin demonstrates is that the couplings among them can be made explicit and computationally tractable at the scale of a full system. The simulation engine consists of twenty-four compute modules organized into eight coupling domains: (1) ocean physics, including tidal exchange, stratification, and dissolved-oxygen dynamics across marine basins; (2) marine ecology, including 42 species from primary producers to orcas with explicit predator-prey and habitat coupling; (3) carbonate chemistry, implementing CO2SYS for full speciation across the dissolved-inorganic-carbon system; (4) climate forcing, including atmospheric and oceanic boundary conditions and propagating them through downstream modules; (5) port economics and supply chain, covering Vancouver, Seattle, Tacoma, and Olympia terminal operations and regional employment; (6) infrastructure resilience, including I-5 corridor, ferry network, and grid reliability; (7) tribal governance, highlighting the 34 sovereign Indigenous nations whose treaty rights and co-management responsibilities span the basin; and (8) hazards, including the Cascadia M9 earthquake scenario, atmospheric-river risks, and marine heatwave dynamics. Figure 5 of the main paper identifies sixteen SubMod domains that an operational Urban Sea Digital Twin would need to represent. The Cousin’s twenty-four compute modules constitute one particular implementation that covers most of those domains and adds several that emerged from the prototype’s scope: an individual-based Southern Resident orca model with 73 named whales drawn from the Center for Whale Research 2024 census; a Cascadia M9 earthquake scenario module; speciated contaminant transport with biomagnification through the food web. The mismatch between sixteen and twenty-four reflects different decompositions for different purposes. Figure 5 enumerates the domains that must be represented; the Cousin enumerates the compute modules that implement a representation. Three coupling examples illustrate how state flows across the combined module set. In the first, what the project calls the Cascadia hero cascade, Federal Reserve housing-and-rates data drives a regional development-pressure index, which drives shoreline armoring, which drives eelgrass habitat loss, which drives Pacific herring forage availability, which drives Chinook salmon condition, which drives Southern Resident orca prey base. Each link is engine-backed, with explicit state-contract exchanges between modules. The carbonate chemistry chain follows a similar pattern: atmospheric CO₂ forcing drives ocean uptake, then speciated DIC and pH and aragonite-saturation calculations, then shellfish larvae viability and Bigg’s orca contaminant burden. The M9 disaster coupling propagates an instantaneous event through infrastructure damage, port-throughput collapse, supply-chain disruption, and multi-year recovery dynamics across marine, economic, infrastructure, and community-health domains. Section A.3 walks the M9 scenario in detail. The simulation step orchestrates these couplings via a three-iteration convergence on the watershed-port-urban coupling, where feedback loops are tightest. sectionTitle: A.2.2  One-way data ingestion at scale
sectionPath: A.2.2  One-way data ingestion at scale
text:
The Cousin connects to 76 live data endpoints across federal, state, provincial, tribal, and academic sources. These include NOAA tide and meteorological stations, Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) economic indicators, Washington State Department of Transportation traffic and ferry feeds, AirNow air quality monitoring, USGS stream gauges, and Ocean Networks Canada cabled-array streams. The data ingestion layer is one-directional. Real-time observations feed the simulation’s initial conditions and certain ongoing forcing terms; the simulation does not write back to any physical system. This is one of the principal ways the Cousin differs from the bi-directional data flow that defines a Digital Twin per the main paper’s §4 criteria. An operational Twin would close this loop, with simulation outputs informing the operation or configuration of the physical system.
Of the 76 endpoints, approximately 31 are currently live and continuously polled. The remainder are wired but operate against cached or scheduled-pull data sources rather than streaming feeds. The asymmetry is operational, not architectural: the wiring is in place, and full streaming would require either lightweight server infrastructure or unification with existing observing-system APIs that operate behind authentication. Both are feasible extensions, neither necessary for the Cousin’s purpose as a teaching and scenario tool. The unification challenge across the heterogeneous public-sector observational landscape (different agencies, different access regimes, different update cadences, different schemas) is computationally tractable at the scale at which Urban Sea System Digital Twins would need to operate. The Cousin’s data layer is evidence of that.

sectionTitle: A.2.3  Audience-specific interfaces from a common substrate
sectionPath: A.2.3  Audience-specific interfaces from a common substrate
text:
The Cousin presents the simulation through four primary user-facing experiences, with a fifth governance-lab module in development, each tuned to a distinct audience. The Explorer interface is built for general public and educational users, presenting the simulation as a narrative-scaffolded “what if” experience with scenario cards, story beats, and a map. The Policy interface is built for policymakers and regulators, presenting the same simulation as a decision-support environment with policy bundles, parameter sliders, and expected-outcome projections. The Research interface is built for scientists and analysts, presenting the simulation as a dense information environment with multi-panel gauges, time-series charts, and direct access to model state. The Briefing interface is built for executive and funder audiences, presenting an executive summary with risk taxonomy, KPI grid, and policy recommendations.
Each user experience runs on the same simulation engine, data feeds, and module state, however each visual interfeace is tuned to what each audience needs to see. A user who activates a scenario from the Explorer interface (for example, “What if the big earthquake hits?”) sees that scenario’s state propagate to the Policy Dashboard’s recovery panels, the Research Dashboard’s sub-basin grid, and the Briefing’s executive summary, each rendered in its surface’s own register. Scenario activation can also happen from Policy’s Scenarios listing. Engine state is the single observable shared across all surfaces. An in-app mode-switcher allows direct navigation among the four interfaces, with simulation state and active scenario preserved across transitions. A user can activate a scenario in Explorer, navigate to Policy to see policy implications, navigate to Research to inspect the underlying engine state, and navigate to Briefing for the executive summary, without losing simulation context at any step.
The main paper observes that “real value emerges when the system allows different users — scientists, planners, emergency managers, port authorities, regulators, communities — to explore conditions, test assumptions, and compare scenarios.” The Cousin demonstrates that a single underlying model can support multiple audience-specific interfaces from the same computational substrate. Audience differentiation is otherwise addressed through parallel platforms; this is a pattern worth carrying forward into Digital Twin development.
Caption draft: Architecture of the Salish Sea Digital Cousin. Twenty-four compute modules organized into eight coupling domains share a quarterly-time-step state object orchestrated by a three-iteration convergence on watershed-port-urban coupling. Seventy-six live data endpoints feed the simulation one-way (the Cousin does not write back to any physical system). Four audience-specific user interfaces (Explorer / Policy / Research / Briefing, plus Governance Lab in development) surface the same underlying simulation through distinct visual vocabularies, with engine state as the single shared observable across all four; an in-app mode-switcher allows direct navigation among interfaces with state preserved. To be illustrated; possible candidates include commission from Hunter Hadaway per the main paper’s graphics workflow, or an SVG built directly from the codebase’s module registry.

sectionTitle: A.3  Worked Example: Cascadia M9 Recovery Scenario
sectionPath: A.3  Worked Example: Cascadia M9 Recovery Scenario
text: Section 6 of the main paper develops the Cascadia M9 scenario as the strongest practical argument for the Digital Twin framework. The initial seismic shock cannot be predicted. The secondary cascading failures can be explored with greater rigor than is commonly done. The recovery dynamics extend across years rather than weeks. Seasonal context matters: a major rupture during atmospheric-river season, with saturated soils, elevated river systems, vulnerable transportation corridors, and grid stress already present, produces compound failure modes that conventional sector-by-sector planning treats incompletely. This section walks through what the Cousin simulates when the M9 scenario is activated. The scenario activates an instantaneous event at simulation time t₀ and propagates its consequences across the coupled module set over subsequent quarterly steps. Shock distribution is sub-basin-resolved across eighteen basins in the Salish Sea. Peak Ground Acceleration values are drawn from the USGS M9 ShakeMap scenario (Atkinson and Adams 2003). Liquefaction susceptibility is drawn from the Washington Department of Natural Resources Liquefaction Susceptibility Map and the USGS Seattle Urban Hazard Map. Tsunami arrival times and wave heights are drawn from PMEL tsunami modeling (Walsh et al. 2000) for the Cascadia Subduction Zone shelf-rupture tsunami, augmented by a Fraser Delta submarine landslide tsunami envelope (Rabinovich et al. 2003). The magnitude range of [8.7, 9.2] is calibrated to Satake et al. (2003), using the moment-magnitude derivation from Japanese tsunami-height records of the January 1700 Cascadia event. Macro-economic shock magnitudes and casualty range estimates are calibrated against FEMA Cascadia Rising exercise scenarios (2016, 2022) and CREW reports. Combined sub-basin damage compounds shaking, liquefaction, and tsunami damage multiplicatively, modulated by a preparedness factor that maps regional infrastructure investment to a damage-reduction modifier. Civilian recovery dynamics unfold over a five-phase progression that the Cousin tracks across simulation quarters. In phase one (immediate response, weeks 0–4), port throughput is near zero, the ferry network is offline, the I-5 corridor is severed at multiple points, and emergency supply distribution is constrained by transportation collapse. In phase two (stabilization, months 1–6), partial port reopening occurs through alternative terminals, the ferry network restores on routes whose terminal damage permits it, and I-5 detour reconstruction begins. In phase three (reconstruction, months 6–18), infrastructure investment ramps up, supply chains reroute through Canadian and southern alternatives, and the first significant ecological signals emerge as marine sediment disturbance and coastal contamination work through the food web. In phase four (ecological response, years 1–3), contaminant releases, habitat damage, and disrupted fisheries propagate through marine ecology modules, with explicit visibility into Southern Resident orca prey-base impacts via the salmon-herring-eelgrass coupling chain. In phase five (structural transformation, years 3–5 and beyond), the long-tail dynamics become visible: regional economic restructuring as supply chains permanently shift, demographic redistribution, and the slow trajectory of marine ecosystem recovery. Recovery trajectories are computed as exponential decay curves with category-specific time constants: infrastructure takes approximately four years to achieve 63% recovery, environmental ten years, economic three years, and population two years. These constants are framed against Tohoku-oki and Cascadia Rising but are not directly

This Appendix endeavors to report what the Cousin can do, what it cannot, and which limitations are inherent versus addressable. Three subsections follow: what has been validated, what is bounded by structural choices, and what is deferred.

The Cousin’s primary validation metric is hindcast skill against the 2010–2025 historical period. The simulation is initialized at the start of 2010, run forward over 60 quarterly steps, and its trajectory compared against observational data for the same period across ten validation variables. Core hindcast skill (Pearson R, computed across the ten-variable set) is currently 0.71. This represents substantive improvement from an earlier baseline of 0.68, achieved through carbonate chemistry refinements (CO2SYS implementation) and sediment phase-coupling work.
Per-variable skill varies considerably. Port-TEU throughput tracks at R ≈ 0.999, reflecting that the Cousin’s economic and supply-chain modules are well-validated against published port statistics. Puget Sound Chinook salmon tracks at R ≈ 0.88. Sea-surface temperature tracks at R ≈ 0.76, comparable to Hood Canal dissolved oxygen at R ≈ 0.76. Puget Sound pink salmon tracks at R ≈ 0.74. The Southern Resident orca population tracks at R ≈ 0.70, a skill level that on inspection contains a structural error component rather than purely random noise (discussed below in A.4.2). Fraser River sockeye tracks at R ≈ 0.70. Other variables fall in the 0.5–0.7 range.
The Cousin’s parameterization is heterogeneous. When possible, inputs are grounded in published primary sources and are directly citable. Others are hand-tuned for plausible behavior consistent with the broader literature but are not derived from a specific paper. Parameters with mechanistic grounding in primary sources include: the Cascadia magnitude range [8.7, 9.2] from Satake, Wang, and Atwater (2003); Peak Ground Acceleration distribution from the USGS M9 ShakeMap scenario (Atkinson and Adams 2003); liquefaction susceptibility from the Washington Department of Natural Resources and USGS Seattle Urban Hazard maps; tsunami arrival times and wave heights from PMEL tsunami modeling (Walsh et al. 2000), augmented by a Fraser Delta submarine landslide tsunami envelope (Rabinovich et al. 2003); casualty range estimates and economic-loss bands calibrated against FEMA Cascadia Rising exercise scenarios (2016, 2022) and CREW reports; spawning-beach recovery time constants from Penttila (2007); and aquaculture and farmed-salmon escape parameters from Naylor et al. (2005). Parameters that are hand-tuned for plausible behavior, framed against literature context but not citation-grounded, include: the four recovery time constants used to compute exponential recovery curves (infrastructure τ = 16 quarters, environmental τ = 40 quarters, economic τ = 12 quarters, population τ = 8 quarters); the shaking-damage nonlinearity exponent (1.5 in the PGA-to-damage mapping); the 15-meter tsunami-to-90%-damage calibration; the per-terminal vulnerability fractions for the 26 named port and refinery terminals; the per-system infrastructure damage weights; and the contamination transport graph between sub-basins.

sectionTitle: A.4.2  What is bounded by structural choices
sectionPath: A.4.2  What is bounded by structural choices
text:
The orca skill of R ≈ 0.70 contains a structural error component identified through validation investigation. The error pre-dates the carbonate chemistry refinements and reflects limitations in the individual-based orca model’s coupling to prey availability rather than randomness. The structural error is documented in the project’s known-issues record and represents a bounded, investigable limitation rather than a general failure of the orca module.
The ocean acidification (OA) chain through carbonate chemistry into shellfish viability and orca contaminant burden is currently latent. The chain is computed but its outputs are not yet fully surfaced to user-facing interfaces. This is an implementation gap, not a modeling gap; the underlying physics is in place. Surfacing the chain end-to-end is a near-term development priority.
The Cousin’s pH validation is bounded by an observational ceiling. High-resolution pH observational data for the Salish Sea is comparatively limited relative to the temperature and dissolved-oxygen observational records, which means the Cousin’s pH skill cannot be validated to the same precision as other variables. The operational Salish Sea Model and SalishSeaCast navigate the same constraint. It reflects a regional observational gap that several investigators are working to address.
There are several limitations specific to the M9 scenario implementation. The recovery window terminates structurally at twenty years post-event, after which the M9 scenario state releases and baseline dynamics resume; this twenty-year horizon is a structural choice rather than a literature-grounded recovery boundary. The marine contamination and sediment-mobilization pathway in the M9 module is currently dormant under the orchestrator’s wiring (the function is invoked with a null marine-state argument); marine M9 effects flow through an independent, simpler shock pathway that models co-seismic subsidence and liquefaction intensity at coarser sub-basin grouping. The preparedness modifier in the M9 dynamics is a parameter: only the I-5 maintenance investment slider feeds it. The other infrastructure investment sliders affect recovery initial conditions but do not modulate the shock magnitude. Casualty estimates are presented as prose-only output and do not feed back into engine state; population displacement does not propagate to the urban module. Fraser Delta submarine landslide collapse is modeled as binary and certain on every M9 event, with no probabilistic slope-stability model.
Several aspects are bounded by deliberate scope rather than implementation gap. The Cousin does not attempt to deliver physics-accurate forecasting. It does not attempt to substitute for operational modeling efforts that have decades of investment and domain-specific validation behind them; Section A.4.3 below names the appropriate federated dependencies. It does not attempt to represent the institutional, governance, and stakeholder coordination that the main paper argues constitutes the binding constraint on Twin development; that work remains genuinely human and no software artifact can replace it. And it does not attempt persistence: the Cousin is a teaching and scenario tool that may be developed further, but it is not built to operate over the decadal timescales an operational Twin requires. Each of these is a positive scoping choice, not an unaddressed limitation.

Several gaps in the Cousin remain unaddressed. Outer-coast upwelling boundary forcing is currently parameterized rather than coupled to a regional ocean model; an operational Twin would couple to LiveOcean or a comparable source for this. Sediment diagenesis is implemented at advisory level: the mechanistic sediment-oxygen-demand module is dimensionally honest but provides advisory rather than authoritative deep-DO output. Uncertainty quantification is not yet implemented; the Cousin produces deterministic single-trajectory outputs rather than ensemble distributions, which limits its utility for risk assessment and is a substantial development priority. Satellite-data integration is not yet implemented; ocean-color, sea-surface-temperature, and altimetry products would substantially strengthen the Cousin’s representation of the marine layer. Validation against post-event recovery data from analog M9 events, particularly Tohoku-oki 2011, would shift the M9 recovery time-constant parameterization from prose-justified to literature-fitted; this is a tractable extension that has not yet been undertaken.
These gaps are documented in the project’s comparative analysis against PNNL Salish Sea Model, UW LiveOcean, CSIRO Atlantis, and EU Digital Twin Ocean. None blocking the Cousin’s purpose as a teaching and scenario tool, and all are on the path to implementation as the project continues to develop.
The Cousin is not a competitor to PNNL’s Salish Sea Model (Khangaonkar et al. 2012, 2018), UW’s LiveOcean (MacCready et al. 2009, 2010, 2025), or SalishSeaCast. Those operational models are the appropriate federated dependencies that an operational Salish Digital Twin would coordinate among, each providing physics-accurate domain modeling at spatial and temporal resolutions directly relevant to management. The Cousin operates at quarterly timesteps with deliberately simplified domain modules; its purpose is to demonstrate the integration architecture, not to provide operational forecasts. Comparison against the operational models on per-variable skill is not the right metric. The right metric is whether the Cousin demonstrates that the integration architecture is computationally tractable, governance-facing, and audience-tunable.
Looking outward to the international Digital Twin Ocean (DTO) effort, the Cousin sits in a comparable role to the EU Digital Twin Ocean prototypes and the CSIRO Atlantis end-to-end ecosystem model. It is a coupled socio-ecological simulation tool that demonstrates integration patterns rather than serving as an operational forecasting system. The architectural patterns it demonstrates (federated modules, explicit shared state, and audience-specific interfaces from a common substrate) are directly portable to operational Twin development. The Cousin is a teaching tool that may inform the architectural choices of operational efforts.

sectionTitle: A.5  What the Cousin Demonstrates and Where It Sits
sectionPath: A.5  What the Cousin Demonstrates and Where It Sits
text: The integration architecture the main paper develops conceptually is now computationally tractable at single-developer scale. Five years ago, the cost, complexity, and team-size required for the kind of multi-module coupled simulation the Cousin demonstrates would have placed it firmly in major-institutional-commitment territory. Section 10 of the main paper makes the abstract claim that AI-enabled productivity has changed what is possible and at what cost. The Cousin is a concrete data point in support of that claim. The scenario-exploration approach extends an intellectual lineage exemplified by the Chesapeake Bay Game (Learmonth et al. 2011), in which participants take stakeholder roles and explore the consequences of decisions within a simulated watershed-management context. The Bay Game demonstrated, at the resolution its era permitted, what immersive participatory simulation could do for systems-thinking education and for stakeholder engagement with complex environmental decisions. The scale of what is possible has shifted since then. Modern computing, real-time data ingestion, AI-assisted development workflows, and interactive visualization make it feasible to ground simulation environments in the actual coupled behavior of specific Urban Sea Systems rather than stylized abstraction. The Cousin extends the Bay Game’s approach to a higher-resolution, multi-audience, system-of-systems target. The gap between simulation-as-concept and simulation-as-deployed-reality has not changed. The governance, institutional, and adoption challenges the Bay Game navigated remain the same challenges any Urban Sea System Digital Twin will encounter. The Workshop the main paper proposes is the venue where those challenges will be addressed; the Cousin is a working substrate to inform those conversations, not a substitute for them. Several development directions are anticipated as the project continues toward the Workshop and Twin development the main paper proposes. Integration with reinsurance and parametric-insurance risk-modeling frameworks is a near-term priority. Section 7 of the main paper identifies insurance and reinsurance firms as one of the principal private-sector participants whose engagement with Urban Sea System Digital Twin infrastructure has structural rather than incidental motivation; the compound-risk assessment described in Section 6 is precisely the analytical surface where reinsurance-grade risk modeling intersects with integrated system simulation. The Cousin’s existing M9 worked example surfaces the cascading-failure dynamics that reinsurance modeling would integrate with. What remains is to wire those dynamics into return-period exposure and capital-adequacy frameworks that industry actors can engage with directly. This work is appropriately scoped for post-paper development with industry consultation rather than asserted as current capability. Other anticipated extensions include uncertainty quantification (ensemble-trajectory rather than single-trajectory outputs), satellite-data integration for the marine layer, federation with operational forecasting models for boundary forcing, and validation against analog M9 recovery data. In its current form, the Cousin offers the Workshop and Twin development the main paper proposes a working substrate. Architectural choices can be evaluated against it. Audience-specific interface patterns can be inspected. Cascading-failure dynamics that conventional planning treats incompletely can be made visible. The integration challenge can be engaged concretely rather than abstractly. The Cousin’s open-source status, independent of any institutional Digital Twin development, means it can be inspected, modified, or extended by anyone who finds its patterns

Production pipeline src/phase3p1_pipeline.py extends Phase 3 with:
Denoise gate (band-agnostic) : compute K=full per-pair stretching, |cc|-weighted combine, then take mean(|cc_combined|) . If > 0.8 → keep K=full; if ≤ 0.8 → apply Wiener soft-thresholding with effective rank K=2.5 ( Σw_i = 2.5 , weights w_i = σ_i² / (σ_i² + λ²) with λ chosen by bisection) per pair, re-stretch against the pristine reference, recombine.
MAXLAG cut from 60 s to 30 s (noise window moved from [40, 60] s to [22, 30] s). Saves ~2× disk and memory; adaptive coda is bounded at 20 s so 30 s of lag is plenty.
Vectorized stretching — inner loop swapped so the bulk numpy work is (n_hours × n_coda) per trial-ε. ~5× faster on the stretching step.
Resume support via per-station done.npy markers; CSV writes incrementally.
38 ProcessPoolExecutor workers on cascadia (48 cores), single-thread numpy per worker.
Station selection rule (locked 2026-05-23): one instrument per unique site, priority broadband > short-period > accelerometer. The 304-site list lives at data/inventory/phase3_priority_2020.csv .

K-sweep on UW.CBS.HH + UW.CBS.EN hourly tensors with K ∈ [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 35, 70, 139, 209, 278, 348, 558, 592, 627, 662, 690]. Found a clean inflection at K ≲ 10: |cc| starts rising and dv/v std starts dropping. Higher K values (139–690) are completely flat — the trailing modes carry no signal AND no noise that the PWS step hasn't already concentrated. See data/phase13/svd_sweeps/svd_sweep.png (log–log).
K=2 vs Wiener eff_K=2.0 vs K=full overlay — K=2 over-truncates the broadband (preserves dv/v shape but amplitude clipped to ~60 % of true), Wiener eff_K=2.0 even more aggressive. Hard K=2 and Wiener at eff_K=2 are nearly identical on the accelerometer.
K=3 dv/v vs K=full time series — UW.CBS.HH dv/v amplitudes preserved at K=3, ZN collapses (std crashes to 0.015 %); UW.CBS.EN dv/v recovered a coherent ~±0.05 % signal from K=full's ±2 % noise.
Wiener eff_K=2.5 vs hard K=3 vs K=full ( data/phase13/svd_sweeps/wiener_vs_hard3.png ) — Wiener 2.5 over-shrinks broadband amplitude, but on accelerometer it gives a smooth, coherent dv/v series with |cc| roughly doubled.
Net decision: Wiener eff_K=2.5 with pristine reference is the denoise rule when |cc|_full ≤ 0.8. See ~/.claude/projects/-home-seismic/memory/earthnote_phase3_svd_denoise.md .
UW.MDW Jan 2020 , single worker, --max-doys 31 : 50 min wall (vs 67–69 min for previous Phase 3 smoke tests on CBS.HH/CBS.EN — confirms ~25 % speedup from MAXLAG=30 + vectorize). K=full combined |cc|=0.963 → gate passed, no denoise. Adaptive coda fired: [1.50, 4.60] s. First time the intersect-three-pairs adaptive rule succeeded in Phase 3 (CBS.HH and CBS.EN both fell back to default).
Launched 110 broadband full year 2020 at 08:25, 38 workers. Status as of evening: 67–86 of 110 done (61–78 %), 0 errors, mean per-station elapsed ~9.9 h.
| Metric | K=full | Post-Wiener |
|---|---|---|
| Median combined |cc| | 0.54 | 0.85 |
| Min combined |cc| | 0.38 | 0.60 |
| Max combined |cc| | 0.80 | 0.96 |
| denoise_applied = True | — | 64 / 67 (95 %) |
UW.MDW Jan-only was |cc|=0.96 well above the 0.8 gate. Same station on full year drops because the year-long PWS reference averages real dv/v drift — no individual hour matches the year-averaged shape perfectly, so |cc| against the year ref is necessarily lower than against a 1-month ref. Conclusion: the 0.8 gate is operating correctly; Wiener denoise is the dominant path for year-scale production , not the exception.
Three stations passed the gate (|cc|_full > 0.8). Need to look at them once the run finishes to see what makes them special.
src/phase3p1_plot.py generates per-station 4×2 diagnostic plots from stacks_3p1/{tag}/ . Iterated through three improvements today:
y-axis of hourly dv/v fixed to ±1 % (was auto-scaled — combined series got dwarfed by per-pair outliers).
Per-pair lines at 40 % transparency so the combined dv/v line dominates.
CC sections row-normalized to absmax — each hour scales to its own peak amplitude, making faint and loud hours equally readable. Coda banding is now clearly visible across the year.
One-off override: --dvv-ylim 0.1 for stations with very low std (e.g. CC.SHRK).

Installed PyTorch CPU + scikit-learn + UMAP into the noisepy2 env. Wrote src/cc_shrk_fingerprint.py :
Loaded CC_SHRK_X_BH hourly tensors (8737 hours × 3 pairs × 1201 lag samples after zoom to ±15 s).
Per-hour normalized each row to absmax.
1-D conv autoencoder: 3 channels → Conv1D(32, 64, 128) with strided convs → AdaptiveAvgPool to 8 → Linear bottleneck of dim 32 → ConvTranspose1d mirror. 179,619 params.
Trained 80 epochs on CPU (4 threads, so it didn't compete with the pipeline). 436 s wall. Loss converged 0.0034 → 0.00186.
Extracted 32-D fingerprint per hour → UMAP to 2-D → KMeans k=6.
UMAP scatter shows long curve-like trails — adjacent-in-time hours are nearby in fingerprint space, confirming temporal continuity. Cluster mean CCs look very similar (because absmax normalization clamps the zero-lag peak to ±1; real differences are subtler coda variations not visible at the y-scale).
Per-month top cluster ( cc_shrk_monthly_cluster.py , monthly_top_cluster.png ):

sectionTitle: Tremormetry: LFE coda wave interferometry dv/v workflow
sectionPath: Tremormetry: LFE coda wave interferometry dv/v workflow
text:
End-to-end, reusable per-station workflow for NLLB-style LFE-coda dv/v, as run this
session on UW.HDW (worked example) and UW.GNW . Built for the 32-CPU + 1× L40S pod.
All scripts are generic (pass --station ); this is the runbook for adding any station.
Pipeline: backfill → PNSN catalog → station box → discover (stage1+GPU stage2) →
coverage-select → densify (GPU MF) → daily stacks → coda dv/v → metadata QC.
scripts/download_hdw.py — FDSN bulk pull of one station's vertical channel, daily files
into data/waveforms/<NET>.<STA>/<year>/<jday>.mseed . Threaded (8 workers), resumable,
picks preferred vertical channel (EHZ>HHZ>BHZ>SHZ). HDW: 1995–2026, 11,281 files, 73 GB.
Generic: copy/parametrize for any NET.STA. Keep ALL data (not just tremor days) — the
matched filter runs on every day.
The catalog drives candidate detection. catalogs/pnsn_tremor_2014-2026.csv
 is
download-cut at lat 47.5°N (fetched with 00b_fetch_pnsn_tremor.py --bbox 47.5 ... ) →
zero tremor south of 47.5, which starves stations near/south of that line.
USE THE MASTER: catalogs/pnsn_tremor_cascadia_full.csv — 748k rows, lat 39.5–50.9,
2010–2026 (full Cascadia). Source: tremorapi.pnsn.org ( scripts/00b_fetch_pnsn_tremor.py ).
Tremor catalog only starts ~2010 → families are 2010+ LFEs (still matched-filtered across
the full waveform record in densify).
Center the discovery bbox on the station, choose ±km (don't use arbitrary geographic boxes).
HDW (47.649, -123.053), ±100 km N/S+E/W → bbox 46.748 48.550 -124.390 -121.716 .
Preview: scripts/plot_station_box.py --station HDW --station-lat .. --station-lon .. --ns-km 100 --ew-km 100
The tremor band has a downdip (eastern) edge — families terminate where the slab drops
below the ETS depth window ( scripts/plot_downdip_edge.py ). That eastern blank is real, not missing data.
scripts/discover_nllb_pnsn_driven.py --candidates-only — envelope-peak detections at the
station inside every PNSN tremor window. Now uses _load_day_poly (resample_poly) + a
 --candidates-only flag.
python scripts/discover_nllb_pnsn_driven.py --station HDW \
 --pnsn catalogs/pnsn_tremor_cascadia_full.csv \
 --bbox 46.748 48.550 -124.390 -121.716 \
 --candidates-out data/hdw_pnsn_candidates_100km.parquet --candidates-only --workers 16
⚠ MEMORY: at 24 workers with obspy FFT-resample this hit anon 99 G (near-OOM). The
 resample_poly loader + 16 workers → anon 4 G , 1543 days in ~95 s. HDW: 1.72 M candidates.
scripts/discover_gpu.py — replaces the slow/OOM CPU clustering. Three wins, validated
bit-equivalent (zero cluster-flips at cc≥0.8):
load-each-day-once (group cuts by calendar day; ~11k loads not ~100k)
resample_poly not obspy FFT-resample
GPU all-pairs max-shifted CC ( src/tremorferometry/repeater_gpu.py ): 11.6 s → 0.06 s
per 2000-window bin, 197×, max|Δ|=1.8e-7 vs CPU.
Single GPU process; CPU workers only cut waveforms (KB) → no N²-per-worker blowup → full
2000-cap, no OOM.
python scripts/discover_gpu.py --station HDW \
 --candidates data/hdw_pnsn_candidates_100km.parquet \
 --out data/hdw_pnsn_families_100km.npz --max-bin-candidates 2000 --workers 24
HDW: 29,721 families in 89 s at anon 2 G (CPU path was ~100 min / 54 G / 50-cap).
⚠ It writes the snr
 column (template env-peak / pre-pulse-RMS, pre=T[:34]) that the
committed discover script silently stopped writing — coverage selection / map need it.
Output: *.npz (templates) + .summary.csv (family_id,n_members,n_years,first/last_year,lat,lon,snr) + .members.parquet .
scripts/select_coverage_families.py — bin by (azimuth sector × distance ring) from the
station, keep top-K per cell by SNR with an SNR floor. Avoids 100s of redundant clustered
patches; fills azimuth/distance evenly; loosens to the floor only where a cell is empty.
python scripts/select_coverage_families.py --summary data/hdw_pnsn_families_100km.summary.csv \
 --station-lat 47.649 --station-lon -123.053 --min-snr 10 \
 --az-sectors 12 --dist-rings "0,20,40,65,100" --k 2 \
 --out data/hdw_coverage_selection_100km.summary.csv --out-fig <fig>
HDW: 96 SNR≥10 → 37 selected (+5 southern-tail by hand) = 42; 10/12 az sectors, all rings.
Maps: scripts/plot_family_map.py (SNR≥X family map), scripts/plot_candidate_map.py 
(raw candidate density; --extent to show the full box).
scripts/densify_gnw_gpu.py — runs the selected templates across the full waveform record.
GPU rfft template×data + GPU sliding-norm + cc>1 fix + threshold + sparse extraction; CPU pool
preprocesses (resample_poly). ~180× CPU. Per-year chunks, resumes by skipping existing
 <prefix>YYYY.csv . QC: drops a day if median count>2000 or median cc>0.96; top-N=100 cap 
per (family,day); --max-raw-det 3000000
 glitch-day guard (skip pathological days BEFORE
the O(N) dedup — speeds glitchy analog-era years ~5×).
python scripts/densify_gnw_gpu.py --templates-npz data/hdw_pnsn_families_100km.npz \
 --summary-csv data/hdw_densify_set.summary.csv --min-snr 0 \
 --network UW --station HDW --out-prefix mf_hdw_ --workers 20 --top-n 100 --max-raw-det 3000000
Selection = summary∩npz filtered by --min-snr . HDW (42 fam, 2010–2026): ~24 days/s, GPU 84%,
anon ~15 G. (For a long Nisqually baseline, run from 1995 — glitch guard handles the old data.)
scripts/build_long_window_resp.py --no-deconv — for each (family, day), cut a 13 s long
window (−3..+10 s, 520 samp @ 40 Hz) around each detection and stack (average). spawn workers
(no COW; the old fork stacker ballooned to ~135 G). --no-deconv = resample_poly + bandpass
(the resample_poly fix kills the obspy dv/v drift; deconv only matters cross-era).
python scripts/build_long_window_resp.py --mf-csv data/mf_hdw_all.csv --network UW --station HDW \
 --no-deconv --workers 16 --out data/long_window_daily_HDW.npz
Output npz keys: stacks (n,520) patches(n) dates(n) n_det(n) t(520) fs . (concat year CSVs → mf_*_all.csv first.)
REUSE, don't re-stack: stacks are mergeable across runs (same 520-sample format).
 scripts/merge_stacks.py concatenates several npz and dedupes (patch,date), keeping max-n_det.
GNW: merged 53+22+28 family stacks (767k → 714k rows after dedup) without re-stacking the 75.
scripts/dvv_coda_parallel.py (all-time-mean ref) and scripts/dvv_coda_perera.py (per-era ref).
Stretch each day's coda (default 1–4 s here) against the family reference; cross-patch 60-d median.
python scripts/dvv_coda_perera.py --npz data/long_window_daily_GNW_merged.npz --window 1.0 4.0 \
 --station GNW --era-bounds "2010-12-01,2019-05-07" \
 --out-csv <csv> --out-fig <fig> --workers 24
Sensor/sample-rate changes inject apparent dv/v steps. Two safeguards:
Per-era referencing at the rate/sensor-change dates (each instrument epoch referenced
to its own mean). Get the dates from FDSN, NOT guesses.
Overlay all metadata changes on the dv/v: scripts/plot_dvv_metadata.py --station <STA> 
(fetches FDSN channel epochs, flags sensor/rate changes red, response epochs grey).
Rule of thumb: distrust dv/v jumps that coincide with a red line; trust the rest.
Verifying "real": (1) not coincident with a metadata change (survives per-era), (2) coherent
across many patches (e.g. 90% of patches), (3) ideally appears at neighbouring stations.

text:
HDW (Olympic Pen., 47.649/-123.053): new tooling debut. Discovery on the ±100 km box with the
master catalog → 29,721 families (96 at SNR≥10, 23 south — the 47.5 cut had hidden the south).
42-family coverage set densified 1995–2026 → daily stacks → dv/v.
2017 rise = REAL (stable EHZ era, per-era invariant +0.043%, 90% of patches rose).
2023 jump = instrument artifact of the EHZ→HHZ swap (Sept 2022); per-era shrinks it to +0.015%,
no coherent within-HHZ-era trend. (Real regional 2023 rise exists — GNW sees it — but HDW's swap masks it.)
HDW is not a Nisqually recorder: only 1 pre-EQ date in 2001 (13 in 1999, 0 in 2000); no usable baseline.
GNW (47.564/-122.825): already had southern coverage (families to lat 46.51 — discovered with a
south-covering catalog). Coverage check vs the 75 done (53 main + 22 circle): of the coverage-optimal
50, only 22 were done, 28 were gaps. Densified the 28 gaps → merged all three stacks (no re-stacking)
→ 96-family coverage-complete per-era dv/v (692k meas, eras split at 2010-12 & 2019-05). 
GNW metadata: BHZ 50 Hz (→2010-12) → BHZ 40 Hz (→2019-05) → HHZ 100 Hz.
PNSN catalog 47.5°N cut → use pnsn_tremor_cascadia_full.csv ; center box on station.
obspy FFT-resample = recurring OOM + dv/v drift → resample_poly everywhere .
Sensor/rate swaps fake dv/v steps → per-era + metadata overlay (HDW EHZ→HHZ, GNW 50→40→100).
discover_gpu.py must write the snr column (committed discover script dropped it).
Reuse daily stacks (merge_stacks.py); don't re-stack already-done families.
Glitch-day guard ( --max-raw-det ) for slow analog-era densify.
Monitor loops: grep with the bracket trick ( [d]ensify… ) or they self-match and hang.
Pod cap 32 CPU; keep total workers ≤30. Always run a memory watchdog (anon > ~120 G = kill).

Paper: Marwitz et al. (2026), Predicting new research directions in materials science using large language models and concept graphs . Nature Machine Intelligence 8, 535-544.
Core pipeline (their version):
Concept extraction -- Fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13B extracts key concepts from ~221K materials science abstracts. Superior to RAKE (rule-based keyword extraction) because the LLM can nominalize, remove filler words, normalize plurals, and extract concepts not verbatim in the text.
Concept graph -- Nodes = concepts (filtered: ≥3 occurrences, ≥2 words). Edges = co-occurrence in the same abstract. The graph is temporal : each edge carries the publication date. Result: ~137K nodes, ~13M edges.
Concept embeddings -- MatSciBERT encodes each concept in-context (averaged across all abstract occurrences) to produce 768-dim semantic vectors per concept node.
Link prediction -- Binary classification: will two currently-unconnected concepts co-occur in a future paper? Four model variants: Baseline : Graph topology features only (node degree + 2-path count at 5 historical time slices → 20-dim feature vector per node pair)
Concept embeddings only : Concatenated 768-dim vectors per pair (1,536-dim)
Combination of features : Concatenate both (1,556-dim)
Combination of models : Weighted average of independent model outputs (best: 60/40 baseline/embeddings, AUC 0.9372)
Report generation -- For a specific researcher, compute their "own concepts" (C_own) from their publications, then rank predicted links involving C_own. Filter by heuristics (avoid generic concepts, avoid too-similar or too-unrelated pairs via embedding distance). An LLM curates the top suggestions with explanatory paragraphs.
Expert interviews -- 10 materials scientists evaluated the suggestions. 29% rated "interesting/inspiring" (51% precision when LLM pre-curated).
Key insight for us: The paper's power is in the temporal concept graph + link prediction. Concepts that haven't co-occurred yet but are predicted to form links represent potential new research directions. The semantic embeddings improve prediction especially at distance dprev=3, i.e., the more surprising, non-obvious connections.

| Component | Status | Details |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Concept extraction | ✅ Built | index-notes.mjs extracts methods, instruments, datasets, quantities per chunk via Gemini 2.5 Flash. 1,054 unique concepts across 236 chunks. Cached by sha1(text). |
| Concept taxonomy | ✅ Built | Four kinds: method (414), quantity (354), dataset (175), instrument (111). Each concept has chunkIds, noteIds, projects. |
| Concept co-occurrence | ⚠️ Implicit | byChunk records which concepts appear in which chunk. Co-occurrence within a chunk (or note) can be derived but isn't stored as an explicit graph. |
| Concept embeddings | ✅ Available | Each chunk already has a Gemini embedding (768-dim). Concept-level embeddings don't exist yet, but we have the per-chunk vectors in embeddings.bin. |
| Temporal data | ✅ Partial | dateFromFilename on each chunk gives us publication dates for most notes. The concept graph can be sliced by time. |
| Concepts UI | ✅ Built | The Concepts tab in notes.html shows an interactive force-directed graph (constellation canvas). |
| Cross-project overlap | ✅ Exists | Some concepts (cross-correlation, histogram, hydrophone, sampling rate) span multiple projects (COSZO, BransfieldEQ, Earthnote). |
| RAG chat | ✅ Built | Hybrid BM25 + semantic retrieval, Cloudflare Worker proxy, streaming Gemini/Claude answers. |
Their system: ~221K abstracts, ~137K concept nodes, ~13M edges.
Our system: ~40 markdown notes, ~1,054 concepts, ~236 chunks.
This is a personal knowledge base , not a public literature corpus. The approach adapts: instead of predicting what the field will do next, we're predicting what Maleen should investigate next -- connections between concepts across projects and notes that haven't been explored together yet.

sectionTitle: Phase 1: Build the Temporal Concept Co-occurrence Graph
sectionPath: Phase 1: Build the Temporal Concept Co-occurrence Graph

sectionTitle: Phase 3: Link Prediction -- Finding Missing Connections
sectionPath: Phase 3: Link Prediction -- Finding Missing Connections
text:
Goal: Score all non-existing concept pairs and rank them by likelihood of being a productive research connection.
The paper's approach uses a neural network trained on historical data. We don't have enough historical data for that (40 notes vs. 221K abstracts). We need a simpler scoring function.
Proposed scoring function (adapted for small corpus):
For a pair of currently-unconnected concepts (u, v):
score(u, v) = α * semantic_similarity(u, v)
 + β * shared_neighbor_score(u, v)
 + γ * cross_project_bonus(u, v)
 + δ * temporal_recency(u, v)
Where:
semantic_similarity(u, v) = cosine similarity of concept embeddings. High similarity suggests related ideas that haven't been combined yet.
shared_neighbor_score(u, v) = Jaccard index of their graph neighborhoods (analogous to the paper's "common neighbors" / 2-path features). Concepts that share many neighbors but aren't directly connected are strong candidates.
cross_project_bonus(u, v) = bonus when u and v come from different projects. Cross-pollination between COSZO, BransfieldEQ, and Earthnote is exactly the kind of "novel combination" the paper targets.
temporal_recency(u, v) = concepts appearing in recent notes are more likely to be actively relevant.
Filtering heuristics (from the paper):
Exclude pairs where both concepts are very generic (high degree, like "histogram" or "sampling rate").
Exclude pairs where semantic similarity is too high (>0.95 -- they're basically synonyms) or too low (<0.3 -- no plausible connection).
The paper calls this the "Goldilocks zone" for novelty.
Output: A ranked list of concept pairs with scores, stored as predictions.json :
{
 "generatedAt": "...",
 "predictions": [
 {
 "source": { "id": "methods:beamforming", "display": "beamforming", "kind": "method", "projects": ["BransfieldEQ"] },
 "target": { "id": "quantities:dv/v", "display": "dv/v", "kind": "quantity", "projects": ["Earthnote"] },
 "score": 0.847,
 "semanticSim": 0.61,
 "sharedNeighbors": 3,
 "crossProject": true,
 "rationale": null
 }
 ]
}
Goal: For the top-N predicted links, use Gemini to generate a paragraph explaining why these concepts could be productively combined, following the paper's "LLM Curation" step.
Prompt template:
You are a research advisor for a marine geophysicist.
Two concepts from different research projects have been identified as a
potentially productive but unexplored connection:
Concept A: "{display_a}" ({kind_a})
 - Appears in: {projects_a}
 - Context: {sample_chunk_text_a}
Concept B: "{display_b}" ({kind_b})
 - Appears in: {projects_b}
 - Context: {sample_chunk_text_b}
These concepts share {shared_neighbors} neighbors in the concept graph
but have never appeared together in the same note.
Write 2-3 sentences explaining:
1. Why combining these concepts could lead to a new research direction
2. What specific experiment, analysis, or investigation this combination suggests
3. How this could build on existing work in both projects
This runs at build time (during npm run index ) and the rationales are baked into predictions.json . Cost: ~20 Gemini 2.5 Flash calls for top-20 predictions. Cheap.
Goal: Add a new tab (or section within the existing Concepts tab) that surfaces the predicted research directions.
Design:
Two possible approaches:
Option A: "Suggestions" panel in the Concepts tab
Bottom drawer or side panel in the existing constellation view
When you click a concept node, the panel shows "Unexplored connections" -- concept pairs involving that node, ranked by prediction score
Each suggestion shows the LLM-generated rationale
Option B: Dedicated "Directions" tab alongside Dashboard/COSZO/BransfieldEQ/Earthnote
Card-based layout showing top-20 predicted research directions
Each card shows the two concepts, their projects (color-coded), the score, and the LLM rationale
Filterable by project, kind, or score threshold
Clicking a card highlights the relevant nodes and path in the constellation graph
I lean toward Option A because it integrates naturally with the existing concept graph visualization. The constellation already has the nodes and edges. Predicted links could be rendered as dashed lines in a different color (e.g., the accent color with lower opacity) overlaid on the existing graph.
Goal: Make the predictions queryable through the chat.
Changes to 
chat.js
:
Load predictions.json alongside the other assets
Detect intent queries like "what should I work on next?", "suggest research directions", "what connections am I missing?"
Instead of doing normal RAG retrieval, inject the top predictions + rationales as context
The system prompt gains a new mode: "The user is asking for research direction suggestions. Use the following predicted concept connections..."
Changes to the worker (optional):

Or keep it all client-side since the predictions are precomputed
