noteTitle: Coda-Wave Sensitivity Kernel for a Deep Repeating Source and a Surface Receiver
sectionPath: Coda-Wave Sensitivity Kernel for a Deep Repeating Source and a Surface Receiver
text:
Classical coda-wave interferometry (CWI) and passive image interferometry build their travel-time sensitivity kernels for a surface source / surface receiver geometry, and they treat the coda as a composite of a 2-D surface-wave field (early coda) and a 3-D body-wave field (late coda) (Obermann et al., 2013b, 2016; Margerin et al., 2016). That composite is why the standard kernel has two strong lobes beneath each station and weak-but-nonzero sensitivity in between, decaying with depth.
Your geometry breaks three of those assumptions, and each break simplifies or relocates the kernel:
The source is deep ($z_s = d \approx 30$ km), inside the fault zone, and is a repeating LFE family — i.e. an effectively fixed point source you can re-record indefinitely.
A deep source does not radiate surface waves. At $d \gg \lambda$ the source-side field is pure 3-D body-wave (S) intensity . There is no 2-D component on the source leg. This is the analytical content of your statement "we clearly have only S in the coda": the source leg is single-mode 3-D, and the only place a 2-D (surface-wave) channel can enter is the free surface near the receiver.
The receiver is at the free surface , so the receiver leg carries the free-surface energy amplification and is the only leg where body↔surface coupling can occur.
The consequence is a kernel with one lobe pinned in the fault zone (at the source) and one lobe at the surface station, joined by a sensitivity tube. Because every surface station shares the same deep source, the deep lobe is common-mode across the whole network — which, as shown in §6 and §9, is exactly what lets you separate a fault-zone change from a shallow site change.
Nobody has written the kernel for this geometry. Below I derive it from radiative-transfer / diffusion first principles, give the explicit half-space closed form, and then formulate both the forward map ($\delta\beta/\beta \to$ coda observables) and the regularized inverse problem (coda observables $\to$ fault-zone $\delta\beta/\beta$ and source-location change).

noteTitle: Coda-Wave Sensitivity Kernel for a Deep Repeating Source and a Surface Receiver
sectionPath: Coda-Wave Sensitivity Kernel for a Deep Repeating Source and a Surface Receiver
text:
| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| $\mathbf{s}=(0,0,d)$ | source position (LFE family centroid), depth $d$ |
| $\mathbf{r}=(\mathbf{r}_h,0)$ | receiver position, on the free surface $z=0$ |
| $\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{x}_h,z)$ | scatterer / model point, $z\ge 0$ downward |
| $\beta$ | shear-wave (S) speed; single propagating mode |
| $\ell$ | scattering mean free path; $\tau=\ell/\beta$ scattering mean free time |
| $\ell^*$ | transport mean free path, $\ell^*=\ell/(1-\langle\cos\theta\rangle)$ |
| $D$ | energy diffusivity, $D=\beta\ell^*/3$ (3-D) |
| $\sigma_a=1/\tau_i$ | intrinsic absorption rate ($\tau_i=Q_i/\omega$) |
| $t$ | lapse time in the coda (measured from the LFE origin time) |
| $P(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,t)$ | mean intensity (energy-density) propagator |
| $K(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)$ | travel-time sensitivity kernel |
| $\delta\beta/\beta$ | relative shear-velocity perturbation field (the target) |
| $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ | source-location displacement vector between two LFE realizations |
Working assumptions (each flagged where it matters):
Single mode (S body waves), isotropic background, statistically homogeneous scattering — so radiative transfer (RTE) applies and, at lapse times $t\gg\tau$, the diffusion approximation holds.
Free surface treated as a perfectly reflecting boundary for S energy → zero net energy flux through $z=0$ (Neumann condition). This is the leading approximation; a radiation/extrapolation-length boundary condition is the refinement (§5).
Weak, localized perturbations → first-order (Born / linear) sensitivity.
Coda windows long compared to the dominant period but short compared to the timescale of medium change.
The mean intensity (specific energy density integrated over propagation directions) obeys the scalar radiative transfer equation. For $t\gg\tau$ this reduces to a diffusion equation with absorption (Paasschens, 1997; Margerin et al., 2016):
$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial t} = D,\nabla^2 P ;-; \sigma_a,P ;+; \delta(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0),\delta(t),
\qquad D=\frac{\beta,\ell^*}{3}.
\tag{1}
$$
The infinite-medium Green's function of (1) is
$$
P_\infty(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_0,t)=\frac{1}{(4\pi D t)^{3/2}},
\exp!\left[-\frac{|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0|^2}{4Dt}\right]e^{-\sigma_a t},
\qquad t>0 .
\tag{2}
$$
Dimensional check: $[D]=\mathrm{m^2/s}$, so $[P_\infty]=\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ (energy density per unit source energy), and $\int P_\infty,d^3x=e^{-\sigma_a t}$ — energy is conserved up to absorption. ✓
The diffusion form (2) is only the multiple-scattering limit. The full RTE intensity carries a coherent ballistic term plus a scattered halo (Paasschens, 1997, 3-D scalar, isotropic scattering):
$$
P_{\mathrm{RTE}}(R,t)=\underbrace{\frac{e^{-\beta t/\ell}}{4\pi R^2},\delta!\left(t-\frac{R}{\beta}\right)} {\text{ballistic}}
;+;\underbrace{P {\mathrm{sc}}(R,t),\Theta!\left(t-\frac{R}{\beta}\right)}_{\text{scattered halo}},\qquad R=|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0|,
\tag{3}
$$
where the halo $P_{\mathrm{sc}}$ smoothly interpolates from single scattering to the Gaussian (2) at large $t$, and $\Theta$ is the Heaviside causality factor. The factor $e^{-\beta t/\ell}$ is the exponential decay you referred to: it attenuates intensity along ballistic/low-order paths by the number of mean free paths traversed. Equation (3) is the object to use in the early S-coda; equation (2) is its long-lapse limit. (I keep $P$ generic below; substitute (2) for the closed form and (3) — or a Monte-Carlo RTE solution — for accuracy in the early coda.)
With the reflecting free surface, build the half-space propagator by the method of images. Let $\mathbf{x} 0=(\mathbf{x} {0h},z_0)$ and its mirror $\mathbf{x} 0'=(\mathbf{x} {0h},-z_0)$. Using $g(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_0,t)=(4\pi Dt)^{-3/2}\exp[-|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0|^2/4Dt]$ (absorption stripped for clarity, restored by an overall $e^{-\sigma_a t}$):
$$
P_{!\frac12}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_0,t)=
g(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_0,t)+g(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_0',t).
\tag{4}
$$
Two important specializations:
Source leg ($\mathbf{x}_0=\mathbf{s}=(0,0,d)$): a genuine two-term propagator — real source at depth $d$ plus image at $-d$. Crucially there is no surface-wave term : a source at $d\approx 30,\mathrm{km}\gg\lambda$ does not excite the 2-D channel. The source leg is strictly 3-D body-wave.
Receiver leg ($\mathbf{x}_0=\mathbf{r}$, $z_0=0$): the two image terms coincide, giving the well-known factor-2 free-surface amplification of a diffuse field:
$$
P_{!\frac12}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{r},t)=\frac{2}{(4\pi D t)^{3/2}}\exp!\left[-\frac{|\mathbf{x}_h-\mathbf{r}_h|^2+z^2}{4Dt}\right].
\tag{5}
$$
The direct source→receiver propagator is then ($|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{s}|^2=|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{s}'|^2=r_h^2+d^2$, because the receiver is at $z=0$):
$$
P_{!\frac12}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)=\frac{2}{(4\pi D t)^{3/2}}\exp!\left[-\frac{r_h^2+d^2}{4Dt}\right]e^{-\sigma_a t},
\qquad r_h=|\mathbf{r}_h|.
\tag{6}
$$
Decompose the coda as a sum over multiply-scattered S trajectories from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{r}$ (Snieder, 2006). A trajectory of geometric length $L$ has travel time $T=\int_{\text{path}}\beta^{-1},d\ell$. A relative velocity perturbation $\delta\beta/\beta$ localized near $\mathbf{x}$ changes the travel time by
$$
\delta T=\int_{\text{path}}\delta!\left(\frac1\beta\right)d\ell=-\int_{\text{path}}\frac{\delta\beta}{\beta},\frac{d\ell}{\beta}.
\tag{7}
$$
So each unit of time the path spends near $\mathbf{x}$ contributes $-(\delta\beta/\beta)$ to the fractional travel-time change. We therefore need the expected time a $\mathbf{s}!\to!\mathbf{r}$ trajectory of total duration $t$ spends in a volume element around $\mathbf{x}$. By the Markov (bridge) property of the scattered intensity, the probability density of visiting $\mathbf{x}$ at intermediate time $u$ is $P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},u),P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{r},t-u)/P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)$. Integrating the occupation time over $u$:
$$
\rho(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)}\int_0^{t}P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},u),P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{r},t-u),du .
\tag{8}
$$
The mean relative travel-time change of the coda recorded at lapse time $t$ is the occupation-time-weighted velocity perturbation:
$$
\boxed{;\frac{\delta\tau(t)}{t}=-\int_{V}K(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t),\frac{\delta\beta(\mathbf{x})}{\beta(\mathbf{x})},d^3x;}
\tag{9}
$$
$$
\boxed{;K(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)=
\frac{\displaystyle\int_0^{t}P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},u),P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{r},t-u),du}
{\displaystyle\int_V d^3x'\int_0^{t}P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x}',u),P(\mathbf{x}',\mathbf{r},t-u),du};}
\tag{10}
$$
This is the Pacheco & Snieder (2005) kernel, here written for arbitrary source/receiver positions and for whatever $P$ you choose (diffusion (2), or RTE (3)). The minus sign encodes that a velocity drop lengthens travel times ($\delta\beta<0\Rightarrow\delta\tau>0$).
Normalization. The Chapman–Kolmogorov identity for the (half-space) propagator,
$\int_V P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},u)P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{r},t-u),d^3x = P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)$,
collapses the denominator of (10) to $t,P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)$:
$$
K(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)=\frac{1}{t,P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)}\int_0^{t}P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},u),P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{r},t-u),du,
\qquad \int_V K,d^3x=1 .
\tag{11}
$$
Two consequences: (i) for a homogeneous perturbation, (9) gives $\delta\tau/t=-\delta\beta/\beta$ (the familiar stretch); (ii) intrinsic absorption contributes $e^{-\sigma_a u}e^{-\sigma_a(t-u)}=e^{-\sigma_a t}$ to both numerator and denominator and therefore cancels — the kernel shape is independent of $Q_i$ (Pacheco & Snieder, 2005). $Q_i$ only controls how far in lapse time you can push before the coda drops below noise.
Insert (4)–(6) into (11). Let $a\equiv 4D$. Define the horizontal distances $\rho_s=|\mathbf{x}_h|$ (to the epicentre) and $\rho_r=|\mathbf{x}_h-\mathbf{r}_h|$. The source-leg and receiver-leg propagators are
$$
P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},u)=\frac{1}{(\pi a u)^{3/2}}
\Big[e^{-\frac{\rho_s^2+(z-d)^2}{a u}}+e^{-\frac{\rho_s^2+(z+d)^2}{a u}}\Big],\qquad
P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{r},t-u)=\frac{2}{(\pi a (t-u))^{3/2}},e^{-\frac{\rho_r^2+z^2}{a (t-u)}} .
\tag{12}
$$
Hence the kernel is the single quadrature
$$
\boxed{;
K(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)=
\frac{1}{\mathcal{N}(t)}\int_0^{t}\frac{du}{[u(t-u)]^{3/2}}
\Big[e^{-\frac{\rho_s^2+(z-d)^2}{a u}}+e^{-\frac{\rho_s^2+(z+d)^2}{a u}}\Big]
e^{-\frac{\rho_r^2+z^2}{a (t-u)}};}
\tag{13}
$$
with the normalizer fixed analytically by (6)/(11):
$$
\mathcal{N}(t)=t,(\pi a)^{3/2},P_{!\frac12}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)\Big/2
= t,\frac{(\pi a)^{3/2}}{(\pi a t)^{3/2}},e^{-\frac{r_h^2+d^2}{a t}}
= \frac{e^{-(r_h^2+d^2)/(a t)}}{\sqrt{t}} .
\tag{14}
$$
Equation (13) is evaluated by one 1-D numerical integral per model point — no full wavefield simulation needed. (The $u$-integral has the form of a product of two heat kernels and can also be written via modified Bessel functions, but numerical quadrature is the practical route.)
For the early S-coda, where only a few scattering events have occurred, use the single-scattering (Born) kernel (Pacheco & Snieder, 2006) instead of (13). Substituting the ballistic term of (3) into (10) gives sensitivity concentrated on the locus of constant total path length:
$$
K_{\mathrm{ss}}(\mathbf{x});\propto;
\frac{e^{-(R_s+R_r)/\ell}}{R_s^2,R_r^2};
\delta!\left(t-\frac{R_s+R_r}{\beta}\right),\qquad
R_s=|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{s}|,;; R_r=|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{r}| .
\tag{15}
$$
The $\delta$-function is the surface $R_s+R_r=\beta t$: a prolate ellipsoid with foci at the source and the receiver , plus a mirror ellipsoid with focus at the image source $\mathbf{s}'$. The factor $e^{-(R_s+R_r)/\ell}$ is again the exponential mean-free-path decay you mentioned. So the kernel evolves with lapse time from a thin ellipsoidal shell (early coda, eq. 15) to the two-lobe diffusive cloud (late coda, eq. 13). For a deep source the early-coda ellipsoid is tilted and elongated along the $\mathbf{s}$–$\mathbf{r}$ line, threading the full crustal column including the fault zone.

noteTitle: Coda-Wave Sensitivity Kernel for a Deep Repeating Source and a Surface Receiver
sectionTitle: 5. Validity, and the one caveat that matters for your geometry
sectionPath: Coda-Wave Sensitivity Kernel for a Deep Repeating Source and a Surface Receiver
5. Validity, and the one caveat that matters for your geometry
text:
The diffusion kernel (13) is exact only where the perturbation sits in a near-isotropic diffuse field — i.e. beyond about one transport mean free path $\ell^*$ from both source and receiver , in the diffusive regime (Margerin et al., 2016; Barajas et al., 2022). Within $\ell^*$ of a sensor the energy flux is directional and one needs the specific-intensity kernel built from the full RTE angular field, not just the energy density.
For your problem this caveat lands favorably and unfavorably in different places:
Deep lobe (fault zone, your target): at $d\approx 30$ km the source region is far from the surface receiver and, for crustal $\ell^*$ of order tens of km, plausibly near or beyond $\ell^*$ — so the diffusion kernel is most trustworthy exactly where you want the answer . Good.
Near the source itself and near the surface station: within $\ell^*$ the diffusion form degrades; use the Margerin et al. (2016) specific-intensity kernel or a Monte-Carlo RTE solution there. This is also the only region where receiver-side body↔surface-wave coupling enters (Barajas et al., 2022; Margerin et al., 2019).
Recommended practice: use (13) for the bulk/deep sensitivity, splice in an RTE/specific-intensity kernel within $\ell^*$ of the surface station, and use Monte-Carlo RTE (Paasschens, 1997; Margerin et al., 2016) as the reference solution to calibrate the partition. This is the deep-source analogue of the Obermann et al. (2013b, 2016) surface-wave (2-D) + body-wave (3-D) splicing — except your source leg has no 2-D term , so the only splice is at the receiver.

noteTitle: Coda-Wave Sensitivity Kernel for a Deep Repeating Source and a Surface Receiver
sectionTitle: 6. Geometry of the kernel, and why the deep lobe is special
sectionPath: Coda-Wave Sensitivity Kernel for a Deep Repeating Source and a Surface Receiver
6. Geometry of the kernel, and why the deep lobe is special
text:
Reading (13): $K$ is large where both legs are large. $P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},u)$ peaks near the source; $P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{r},t-u)$ peaks near the receiver. So:
Deep lobe at the source $\mathbf{s}$ — inside the LFE fault zone . This lobe does not exist in the surface–surface geometry; it is the entire point of using deep repeaters.
Surface lobe at the station $\mathbf{r}$, carrying the factor-2 free-surface enhancement (5).
Connecting tube along $\mathbf{s}$–$\mathbf{r}$, with the early-coda ellipsoid (15) as its sharp limit.
Lapse-time depth migration. Early lapse times weight the least-scattered (most direct) paths → sensitivity concentrated along the deep tube and the fault zone. As $t$ grows, the field diffuses, the surface lobe broadens laterally, and shallow near-receiver sensitivity gains relative weight. Scanning coda windows $t_1<t_2<\dots$ therefore gives you a depth-resolving family of kernels — the lever that lets you attribute a change to the fault zone rather than the shallow crust.
Common-mode deep lobe (the network trick). Every surface station shares the same source $\mathbf{s}$, so every station's kernel has its deep lobe in the same place. A real fault-zone velocity change therefore produces a coherent $\delta v/v$ across all station pairs and all lapse times , weighted by the shared deep-lobe sensitivity $\int_{\text{fault}}K,d^3x$. A shallow change near one station shows up only in that station's pairs. This common-mode-vs-station-specific contrast is a strong, model-light discriminant and should be built directly into the inversion (§9).
For each station $\mathbf{r}_a$ and lapse-time window centered at $t_i$ you measure two things from the coda of repeating LFEs:
(a) Stretch / mean travel-time change (velocity-change channel):
$$
\left(\frac{\delta\tau}{\tau}\right)_{a,i}=-\int_V K(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r}_a,t_i),\frac{\delta\beta(\mathbf{x})}{\beta(\mathbf{x})},d^3x .
\tag{16}
$$
(b) Waveform decorrelation (structural-change / scatterer-change channel). A localized change in scattering strength $\delta\Sigma$ (new cracks, fluid fronts) decorrelates the coda with a kernel of the same convolutional form but built from the single-visit intensity product (Rossetto et al., 2011; Planès et al., 2014; Obermann et al., 2013b):
$$
1-\mathrm{CC}_{a,i};\approx;\int_V K^{\mathrm{dec}}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r}_a,t_i),\delta\Sigma(\mathbf{x}),d^3x,
\qquad
K^{\mathrm{dec}}\propto\frac{\int_0^t P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},u)P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{r},t-u),du}{P(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)} .
\tag{17}
$$
Use (16) for shear-velocity changes in the fault zone; use (17) when the change is a scattering change (e.g. fault-zone damage/healing) rather than a smooth velocity change.

noteTitle: Coda-Wave Sensitivity Kernel for a Deep Repeating Source and a Surface Receiver
sectionPath: Coda-Wave Sensitivity Kernel for a Deep Repeating Source and a Surface Receiver
text:
Your LFEs repeat, so the source can also move between realizations — and that is itself a target ("changes in the deep source location"). CWI separates the two cleanly because they leave different fingerprints in the coda (Snieder, 2006; Snieder & Vrijlandt, 2005).
Velocity change → a coherent mean shift: $\langle\delta\tau\rangle/t=$ const $\neq 0$, so $\delta\tau$ grows linearly with lapse time $t$, with the same sign across the window. This is the "stretch."
Source displacement $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ → a path-length change only on the source leg, $\delta\tau = -\boldsymbol{\delta}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}/\beta$, where $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the take-off direction. For an isotropic diffuse take-off distribution the mean vanishes but the variance is nonzero and lapse-time-independent :
$$
\langle\delta\tau\rangle=0,\qquad
\sigma_\tau^2=\langle\delta\tau^2\rangle=\frac{\delta^2}{3,\beta^2}\quad(\text{single S mode}),
\tag{18}
$$
generalizing to an energy-weighted combination of $\alpha^{-2}$ and $\beta^{-2}$ when P is present (Snieder & Vrijlandt, 2005; Robinson et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2019).
The discriminant: fit each coda window for a stretch (coherent, $\propto t$) and a residual scatter (incoherent, flat in $t$).
A nonzero, lapse-time-growing stretch that is common-mode across the network → a fault-zone velocity change (§6).
A flat-in-$t$ decorrelation/variance with $\langle\delta\tau\rangle\approx0$ → a source relocation of magnitude $\delta=\sqrt{3},\beta,\sigma_\tau$.
So the same coda gives you both the fault-zone $\delta\beta/\beta$ and the LFE migration distance, and they do not alias onto each other.
Partition the half-space into cells $V_j$, $j=1,\dots,M$, centered at $\mathbf{x} j$. Stack observations over stations $a$ and lapse-time windows $i$ into a data vector $\mathbf{d}$ with entries $d {ai}=(\delta\tau/\tau)_{a,i}$. The forward map (16) linearizes to
$$
\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{G},\mathbf{m}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},\qquad
G_{(ai),,j}=-,K(\mathbf{x}_j;\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r}_a,t_i),V_j,\qquad
m_j=\frac{\delta\beta}{\beta}(\mathbf{x}_j) .
\tag{19}
$$
Each row of $\mathbf{G}$ is one kernel (13) sampled on the grid; it has the deep lobe (shared by all rows with the same source) and a station-specific surface lobe.
The problem is ill-posed (smooth, overlapping kernels), so regularize. Tikhonov form:
$$
\hat{\mathbf{m}}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{m}};
\big|\mathbf{G}\mathbf{m}-\mathbf{d}\big|_{\mathbf{C}_d^{-1}}^2
+\lambda^2\big|\mathbf{L}\mathbf{m}\big|^2 ,
\tag{20}
$$
with $\mathbf{L}$ a smoothing (Laplacian) or damping operator and $\mathbf{C}_d$ the data covariance. Equivalently, the Bayesian/Gaussian solution and its resolution:
$$
\hat{\mathbf{m}}=\big(\mathbf{G}^{!\top}\mathbf{C}_d^{-1}\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{C}_m^{-1}\big)^{-1}\mathbf{G}^{!\top}\mathbf{C}_d^{-1}\mathbf{d},
\qquad
\mathbf{R}=\big(\mathbf{G}^{!\top}\mathbf{C}_d^{-1}\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{C}_m^{-1}\big)^{-1}\mathbf{G}^{!\top}\mathbf{C}_d^{-1}\mathbf{G}.
\tag{21}
$$
Solve with LSQR/CGLS for large $M$. Inspect $\mathbf{R}$ (and checkerboard/point-spread tests) to see where the deep lobe + surface-lobe geometry actually resolves structure — the deep-lobe resolution is set by how many stations view the common source from different azimuths.
Append the source displacement to the model vector and linearize (18) about the current source estimate. Two practical routes:
Decoupled (recommended first pass): estimate the network-common stretch → velocity field via (19)–(21); separately estimate $\delta=\sqrt{3},\beta,\sigma_\tau$ from the incoherent variance (§8). The orthogonality of the two fingerprints (coherent-$\propto t$ vs. incoherent-flat) keeps them from trading off.
Fully joint: extended model $\tilde{\mathbf{m}}=[,\mathbf{m};,\boldsymbol{\delta},]$ with an extended operator $[\mathbf{G},|,\mathbf{H}]$, where $\mathbf{H}$ holds the linearized source-displacement partials $\partial(\delta\tau)/\partial\boldsymbol{\delta}=-\hat{\mathbf{n}}/\beta$ averaged over the take-off distribution per (station, lapse) pair. Solve (20)–(21) on $\tilde{\mathbf{m}}$.
Multiple lapse-time windows per pair → depth resolution (§6). Use them.
Azimuthal coverage of surface stations → resolves the deep lobe (different surface lobes, shared deep lobe). A single station cannot separate "fault-zone change" from "change anywhere on my tube"; an azimuthal ring can.
Multiple LFE families at different points along the slab interface → multiple source positions → along-strike and depth coverage of the fault zone, turning the monitoring into a sparse 4-D tomography of the source region.
$Q_i$ sets the usable lapse-time range , not the kernel shape (§3, Step 5) — pick the latest windows for which the coda stays above noise to reach maximum diffusive (and hence deep) coverage.
Estimate $\beta$, $\ell^*$ (hence $D=\beta\ell^*/3$), and $Q_i$ for the Cascadia source-receiver volume from the LFE coda envelope decay.
For each (station $a$, lapse window $t_i$): evaluate the half-space kernel (13)–(14) on the 3-D grid by 1-D quadrature; for cells within $\ell^*$ of a sensor, substitute the RTE/specific-intensity kernel (Margerin et al., 2016) or a Monte-Carlo RTE solution; switch to the ellipsoidal single-scattering kernel (15) for the earliest windows.
Measure, per pair and window, the stretch $(\delta\tau/\tau)_{a,i}$ and the residual decorrelation/variance.
Build $\mathbf{G}$ (19), invert (20)–(21) for the fault-zone $\delta\beta/\beta$ field; estimate the source displacement $\delta=\sqrt3,\beta,\sigma_\tau$ from the incoherent channel; optionally do the fully joint inversion (§9, route 2).
Validate against full-wavefield simulations with a planted thin-layer velocity perturbation at depth (the Obermann-style calibration, adapted to a buried source).

noteTitle: Mapping $\delta\beta(x_0,y_0)$ on the Fault Plane from Many LFE-Family / Station Coda Pairs
sectionTitle: Mapping $\delta\beta(x_0,y_0)$ on the Fault Plane from Many LFE-Family / Station Coda Pairs
sectionPath: Mapping $\delta\beta(x_0,y_0)$ on the Fault Plane from Many LFE-Family / Station Coda Pairs
text:
Companion to "Coda-Wave Sensitivity Kernel for a Deep Repeating Source and a Surface Receiver." That document gives the volumetric kernel $K(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t)$; this one assembles all $(\text{LFE family}, \text{station}, \text{lapse window})$ observations into a single inverse problem whose model is the relative shear-velocity change as a function of position on the fault plane , $m(\xi)=\delta\beta/\beta,(x_0,y_0)$.
Each LFE family is a fixed repeating source sitting on the fault , at fault coordinate $\xi_a=(x_{0a},y_{0a})$. The travel-time kernel for that family recorded at any surface station has its deep lobe pinned at $\xi_a$ — i.e. its strongest sensitivity is to the velocity change of the family's own fault patch. So family $a$ "self-images" patch $\xi_a$, with weaker leakage to neighboring patches set by the deep-lobe width, plus off-fault sensitivity along the up-going tube and under the station. Tile the fault with the families you have, add every station and lapse window as a redundant look, and the result is a fault-plane tomography with a near-diagonal core (each family ↔ its patch) plus a controllable off-fault nuisance space that the network redundancy lets you suppress.

noteTitle: Mapping $\delta\beta(x_0,y_0)$ on the Fault Plane from Many LFE-Family / Station Coda Pairs
sectionTitle: 1. Indices, model, and the one modeling choice
sectionPath: Mapping $\delta\beta(x_0,y_0)$ on the Fault Plane from Many LFE-Family / Station Coda Pairs
1. Indices, model, and the one modeling choice
text:
| Index / symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $a=1,\dots,A$ | LFE family; source on the fault at 3-D position $\mathbf{X} a=\mathbf{X}(\xi_a)$, fault coord $\xi_a=(x {0a},y_{0a})$ |
| $b=1,\dots,B$ | surface station at $\mathbf{R}_b$ |
| $i=1,\dots,I$ | lapse-time window centre $t_i$ |
| $\xi=(x_0,y_0)$ | intrinsic coordinate on the (dipping, possibly curved) fault surface $\Sigma$; embedding $\mathbf{X}(\xi)$ |
| $k=1,\dots,K$ | fault-mesh node; the family locations ${\xi_a}$ are a subset of the nodes ${\xi_k}$ |
| $h(\xi)$ | fault-zone thickness (across-fault extent over which $\delta\beta/\beta$ is coherent) |
| $A_k$ | area of fault patch $k$ |
| $m_k=\dfrac{\delta\beta}{\beta}(\xi_k)$ | target model : relative shear-velocity change on fault patch $k$ |
The modeling choice (state it, defend it, price it). We assume the velocity changes we are imaging are localized to the fault zone , so the volumetric field collapses onto the surface $\Sigma$. This is justified physically — fault zones concentrate the fluids, pore-pressure transients, and damage/healing that move $\beta$ — and geometrically — the deep lobe is pinned to $\Sigma$ by the on-fault source. Its cost is quantified in §2: anything that changes off the fault (shallow site hydrology, bulk crustal change) projects onto the data through the tube and surface lobe and must be carried as nuisance (§4) or it biases $\hat{m}$.

noteTitle: Mapping $\delta\beta(x_0,y_0)$ on the Fault Plane from Many LFE-Family / Station Coda Pairs
sectionTitle: 2. From the 3-D kernel to a fault-plane kernel
sectionPath: Mapping $\delta\beta(x_0,y_0)$ on the Fault Plane from Many LFE-Family / Station Coda Pairs
2. From the 3-D kernel to a fault-plane kernel
text:
Start from the forward relation in the companion document,
$\delta\tau/t=-\int_V K(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{s},\mathbf{r},t),(\delta\beta/\beta),d^3x$, with $\int_V K,d^3x=1$.
Step 1 — Thin-zone collapse. If $\delta\beta/\beta$ is confined to a thin zone of thickness $h(\xi)$ about $\Sigma$ and varies slowly across it, the volume integral reduces to a surface integral:
$$
\frac{\delta\tau}{t}\Big| {a,b,i}
=-\int \Sigma \underbrace{K\big(\mathbf{X}(\xi);\mathbf{X} a,\mathbf{R}
b,t_i\big),h(\xi)}
{\displaystyle \kappa {abi}(\xi)\ \ [\text{area}^{-1}]};\frac{\delta\beta}{\beta}(\xi),dA(\xi);+;e^{\text{off}}_{abi}.
\tag{1}
$$
$\kappa_{abi}(\xi)$ is the effective 2-D (fault-plane) kernel . The term $e^{\text{off}} {abi}=-\int {V\setminus\Sigma}K,(\delta\beta/\beta),d^3x$ is the off-fault contribution (§4).
Step 2 — Captured-sensitivity fraction. Because $\int_V K,d^3x=1$ but only the fault slice is kept,
$$
\eta_{abi}\equiv\int_\Sigma \kappa_{abi}(\xi),dA(\xi);\le;1
\tag{2}
$$
is the fraction of the coda's sensitivity that actually lies on the fault for that pair. $\eta$ is largest for short lapse times (tight deep lobe on $\Sigma$) and shrinks as the field diffuses into the off-fault bulk and toward the station. Reporting $\eta_{abi}$ is the honest measure of how fault-confined each datum is — low-$\eta$ pairs are dominated by off-fault paths and should be down-weighted.
Physical note: the deep lobe sits on the fault by construction (on-fault source), so $\kappa_{abi}(\xi)$ peaks sharply at $\xi=\xi_a$. The peak width is the deep-lobe radius $\sim\sqrt{2D,t_i}$ in the diffusive regime (or $\sim\ell^*$), which sets the fault-plane resolution length (§6).
Discretize (1) on the fault mesh. A single datum is
$$
d_{abi}\equiv\left(\frac{\delta\tau}{\tau}\right) {abi}
=\sum {k=1}^{K} G_{(abi),k},m_k+e^{\text{off}} {abi}+\varepsilon {abi},
\qquad
\boxed{,G_{(abi),k}=-,\kappa_{abi}(\xi_k),A_k=-,K(\mathbf{X}_k;\mathbf{X}_a,\mathbf{R}_b,t_i),h_k A_k,}.
\tag{3}
$$
Stack all valid triples $(a,b,i)$ into the data vector $\mathbf{d}\in\mathbb{R}^N$ ($N=\sum_a B_a I_a$, missing pairs simply omitted), the fault model $\mathbf{m}\in\mathbb{R}^K$, and the design matrix $\mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times K}$:
$$
\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{G},\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{e}^{\text{off}}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
\tag{4}
$$
Structure of $\mathbf{G}$ — the near-diagonal core. Because $\kappa_{abi}$ peaks at $\xi_a$, the rows belonging to family $a$ load most heavily onto the model node $k(a)$ co-located with the source. Ordering nodes so that family nodes come first, $\mathbf{G}$ is dominated by a (block-)diagonal "self-imaging" part plus off-diagonal leakage to neighboring patches:
$$
d_{abi}\approx \underbrace{-,\kappa^{\text{self}} {abi}A {k(a)},m_{k(a)}} {\text{own patch}}
;\underbrace{-\sum {k\in\mathcal{N}(a)}\kappa_{abi}(\xi_k)A_k,m_k} {\text{neighbour leakage}}
;+;e^{\text{off}} {abi}+\varepsilon_{abi}.
\tag{5}
$$
This is what makes the problem well-conditioned where families are dense: every patch hosting a family is directly illuminated by its own source.

noteTitle: Mapping $\delta\beta(x_0,y_0)$ on the Fault Plane from Many LFE-Family / Station Coda Pairs
sectionTitle: 4. Off-fault nuisance and the bipartite (two-way) structure
sectionPath: Mapping $\delta\beta(x_0,y_0)$ on the Fault Plane from Many LFE-Family / Station Coda Pairs
4. Off-fault nuisance and the bipartite (two-way) structure
text:
The off-fault term $e^{\text{off}}_{abi}$ has two physically distinct, separable parts that the all-pairs design lets you remove:
a site term $c_b$: a shallow velocity change near station $b$ (e.g. groundwater), sampled by the surface lobe — depends on $b$, not on the source;
a path/bulk term $p_{abi}$: a smooth change in the off-fault crust along the $a!\to!b$ tube.
Write the augmented forward model
$$
\boxed{;\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{G}_f,\mathbf{m}_f+\mathbf{G}_s,\mathbf{m}_s+\mathbf{G}_p,\mathbf{m}_p+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon};}
\tag{6}
$$
where $\mathbf{m}_f$ is the fault map (target), $\mathbf{m}_s={c_b}$ the per-station site terms ($\mathbf{G}_s$ built from the surface-lobe weights), and $\mathbf{m}_p$ a coarse 3-D off-fault field ($\mathbf{G}_p$ from the tube weights).
Why the network makes this identifiable. Index the data by the pair $(a,b)$. To leading order the datum is additive in a source-side (fault) effect that is a function of $a$ and a receiver-side (site) effect that is a function of $b$:
$$
d_{abi};\approx;\alpha_{abi},m_{k(a)};+;\beta_{abi},c_b;+;(\text{path}).
\tag{7}
$$
This is a two-way / bipartite structure (a row effect per fault patch, a column effect per station). Two consequences you can use directly:
Common-mode over stations isolates the fault. Averaging a family's data over all its stations and lapse windows,
$$
\langle d\rangle_a=\frac{1}{B_aI_a}\sum_{b,i}d_{abi};\approx;\langle\alpha\rangle_a,m_{k(a)}+\langle\beta,c\rangle_a,
$$
and if site changes are zero-mean across the network the second term averages out, giving a quick robust estimate $\hat m_{k(a)}\approx-\langle d\rangle_a/(\langle\kappa^{\text{self}}\rangle_a A_{k(a)})$. A true fault change is the part of family $a$'s signal that is coherent across all stations recording it .
Common-mode over families isolates the site. Averaging over all families recorded at station $b$ isolates $c_b$. These two marginals are the practical first pass; the joint inversion (§5) refines them and handles the non-zero-mean case.
If site changes are not zero-mean (a regional shallow transient), the marginal estimate is biased — that is exactly when you must keep $\mathbf{m}_s$ explicit in (6) rather than relying on the marginal.
Solve (6) as a single regularized least-squares (or Bayesian) problem:
$$
\boxed{;
[\hat{\mathbf{m}}_f,\hat{\mathbf{m}}_s,\hat{\mathbf{m}}_p]
=\arg\min;
\big|\mathbf{W}^{1/2}!\left(\mathbf{G}_f\mathbf{m}_f+\mathbf{G}_s\mathbf{m}_s+\mathbf{G}_p\mathbf{m} p-\mathbf{d}\right)\big|^2
+\lambda_f\big|\mathbf{L} \Sigma\mathbf{m}_f\big|^2
+\lambda_s|\mathbf{m}_s|^2
+\lambda_p\big|\mathbf{L}_3\mathbf{m}_p\big|^2
;}
\tag{8}
$$
$\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{C} d^{-1}$ data weights; set entry $(abi)$ from the CWI measurement uncertainty and **scale by $\eta {abi}$** (eq. 2) so low-fault-sensitivity pairs count less.
$\mathbf{L}_\Sigma$ is the surface Laplacian on the fault mesh , optionally anisotropic (smoother along strike than dip) to encode fault fabric. This couples patches with no family of their own to their neighbours, so the fault map is defined on the full mesh, not just at family nodes.
$\lambda_s$ damps the site terms; $\mathbf{L}_3$ smooths the coarse path field.
Bayesian/Gaussian form with model covariance $\mathbf{C}_m=\mathrm{blkdiag}(\mathbf{C}_f,\mathbf{C}_s,\mathbf{C}_p)$ and full design $\mathbf{G}=[\mathbf{G}_f,\mathbf{G}_s,\mathbf{G}_p]$:
$$
\hat{\mathbf{m}}=\big(\mathbf{G}^{!\top}\mathbf{C}_d^{-1}\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{C}_m^{-1}\big)^{-1}\mathbf{G}^{!\top}\mathbf{C} d^{-1}\mathbf{d},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf{C}} {\hat m}=\big(\mathbf{G}^{!\top}\mathbf{C}_d^{-1}\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{C} m^{-1}\big)^{-1},
\qquad
\mathbf{R}=\widehat{\mathbf{C}} {\hat m},\mathbf{G}^{!\top}\mathbf{C}_d^{-1}\mathbf{G}.
\tag{9}
$$
Solve with LSQR/CGLS for large $K$. The fault-block of $\mathbf{R}$ gives the spatial resolution of $\hat{\mathbf{m}} f$ (§6); the cross-blocks of $\widehat{\mathbf{C}} {\hat m}$ tell you how much fault↔site↔path trade-off remains given your station geometry (Aster et al., 2018; Tarantola, 2005).
Fault-plane resolution length: 
$$
L_{\text{res}}(\xi)\approx\max!\big(\underbrace{\sqrt{2D,t_{\min}}} {\text{deep-lobe radius}},;\underbrace{\Delta {\text{LFE}}(\xi)} {\text{family spacing}}\big).
\tag{10}
$$
Two levers: denser LFE families tighten $\Delta {\text{LFE}}$; earlier lapse windows tighten the deep lobe. Note this is the opposite of surface–surface monitoring, where you push to late coda to reach depth: here the source is already at depth, so the earliest usable S-coda gives the sharpest fault image. Use $Q_i$ only to set how early-to-late you can go before the coda drops into noise — it does not change kernel shape (companion doc, §3).
Azimuthal station coverage per family decides whether the on-fault patch separates from the up-going tube. A single station cannot tell "change at $\xi_a$" from "change anywhere along my tube"; an azimuthal ring of stations sharing family $a$ pins the change to the common deep lobe.
Run point-spread / checkerboard tests with synthetic fault patterns through the real $\mathbf{G}$ to map where the family+station layout actually resolves the fault and where the null space (off-fault leakage) dominates.
4-D map. Each family repeats, so every observable is a time series. Replace the scalar measurement by epochs $T$ (reference vs current, or a sliding stack):
$$
d_{abi}(T)=\sum_k G_{(abi),k},m_k(T)+\dots,\qquad m_k(T)=\frac{\delta\beta}{\beta}(\xi_k,T).
$$
Invert each epoch (or jointly with temporal smoothing $|\partial_T \mathbf{m}_f|^2$) to get $\delta\beta/\beta(x_0,y_0,T)$ across the slab — e.g. through an ETS cycle. This is the deliverable: a movie of shear-velocity change on the plate interface.
Source migration as a second-moment channel. From the companion document (§8), a source displacement $\boldsymbol{\delta} a$ of family $a$ produces 
no
 coherent stretch but a lapse-time-independent variance $\sigma {\tau,a}^2=\delta_a^2/(3\beta^2)$, common across all stations recording $a$. Add a per-family migration parameter estimated from the incoherent (variance) channel rather than the stretch channel; it is orthogonal to $\mathbf{m}_f$ (first moment, coherent, $\propto t$ vs. second moment, incoherent, flat in $t$) so it does not alias onto the fault velocity map. This gives you, alongside $\delta\beta/\beta(x_0,y_0,T)$, a map of where the LFE sources themselves are moving — a second fault-process observable for free.
Geometry & medium. Place each family on the fault mesh $\mathbf{X}(\xi_a)$; estimate $\beta,\ell^*$ (so $D=\beta\ell^*/3$), $Q_i$, and a fault-zone thickness prior $h(\xi)$.
Kernels. For every valid $(a,b,i)$ compute the volumetric kernel (companion eq. 13), restrict to $\Sigma$, multiply by $h_k$ → effective 2-D kernel $\kappa_{abi}(\xi_k)$; record the captured-sensitivity fraction $\eta_{abi}$ (eq. 2). Use the single-scattering ellipsoid / RTE kernel for the earliest windows and within $\ell^*$ of stations.
Data. Per $(a,b,i,T)$ measure the coherent stretch $(\delta\tau/\tau)$ (→ $\mathbf{d}$) and the residual variance $\sigma_\tau$ (→ migration channel).
Assemble $\mathbf{G}=[\mathbf{G}_f,\mathbf{G}_s,\mathbf{G}_p]$ (eq. 3, 6); weight by $\mathbf{C} d^{-1}$ scaled by $\eta {abi}$.
Quick look: network-common marginals (eq. of §4) for a regularization-free first map and a fault-vs-site sanity check.
Invert (8)/(9) with the fault-surface Laplacian; tune $\lambda_f,\lambda_s,\lambda_p$ by L-curve / cross-validation.
Resolve & validate: resolution matrix, point-spread tests, and a full-wavefield synthetic with a planted on-fault patch to confirm $\hat{\mathbf{m}}_f$ recovers it without off-fault smearing.
Iterate over epochs $T$ for the 4-D fault map; co-estimate per-family migration $\delta_a$ from the variance channel.

Tremormetry Methodology had some issues that was first discovered by Fable 5
We were able to fix it. But to start, lets double check the methodology and fix where we need to fix more
The whole analysis is based on the Tremor catalog of PNSN where it has a continuous catalog of Pacific northwest tremor.
Tremor is a collection of Low Frequency earthquakes. So what we did was to use these windows of tremor to first pick LFEs.
Pick a station.
Draw a box  (~100 km) around it.
Pull all PNSN tremor  epicenters in that box, 2010→now. Each tremor entry becomes a short  time window  to inspect.
Run a detector inside those tremor windows  to pick impulsive arrivals. Specifically it's  envelope-peak detection : bandpass 2–8 Hz → take the Hilbert envelope → find peaks exceeding  3× the local background (SNR ≥ 3) , with a minimum peak separation. Each surviving peak = one  candidate  arrival.
Cut a waveform snippet at each candidate, cross-correlate all of them, and cluster by shape  (complete-linkage, cc ≥ 0.8). Each cluster = a set of identically-shaped arrivals = one repeating source = a family.
Keep clusters that repeat ≥3 times across ≥3 different years , average their snippets into a clean  template , and  densify  = slide that template as a matched filter over the station's  entire continuous record  to log every time it fired.
Two small precisions on your last line:
The keep-rule is  ≥3 members AND ≥3 distinct years  (not just ≥3 repeats) — the years part is what enforces  persistent  repeaters over transient bursts.
"Densify" runs over the  full archive , not just 2010–now. The tremor catalog only located the family; the template then gets matched against everything the station ever recorded (so B018 reaches back to 2006).
Envelope-peak picking is  fine as a band-limited energy-burst triage that bootstraps templates  — but calling it "picking LFEs" overstates it. It has an impulsive bias, a real discovery-completeness hole, and  no interface/depth or network constraint , and several of the project's hardest downstream headaches (the spiky-contaminant class, the wrong-depth site-carriers) trace straight back to it. The clustering + matched-filter + trust-battery stack mostly  rescues  the result after the fact, but the cleaner fix is to push network coincidence and spectral discrimination  upstream into discovery , not just into the Phase-C densify rebuild.

sectionTitle: Phase 1 — Set up ground truth and data
sectionPath: Phase 1 — Set up ground truth and data
text:
Reframed the problem.  The original discovery (envelope-peak picks in tremor windows → cluster → densify) is single-component, 2-s, cc≥0.8, and admits noise. Goal: identify genuine LFEs by  waveform features  and reject noise/earthquakes/blasts/cultural — toward an EQTransformer-style picker and cleaner discovery seeds.
Chose ground truth + stations.  Used the  Lin (2023) LFE catalog  as labeled positives; worked at the Lin-region stations  PGC  (broadband) and  B011 / B926  (boreholes), with  B011  primary (it's a borehole like the deployment targets, in the dense part of Lin's catalog). Downloaded 3-component data for these.
Defined 23 hand-crafted features  ( feature_defs.py ) on 40-s windows: spectral shape (slope, centroid, band fractions, HF ratio), envelope/onset (kurtosis, crest, rise-time), and  3-component polarization  (H/V, rectilinearity, planarity).
Positives:  curated Lin LFEs (N≥6 stations, residual<1.2 s, ≤35 km) → windows ( extract_lin_positives.py ).
Negatives, in stages:  random-noise windows (RAND),  ANSS earthquakes  ( extract_eq_negatives.py ),  ANSS explosions/blasts  (same script,  --eventtype explosion ), and  in-tremor ambient/cultural  windows ( extract_tremor_noise.py ).
LFE vs noise  ( analyze_lfe_features.py ): CV-AUC  0.95–0.98  at both PGC and B011, and — key control —  unchanged when all amplitude/SNR features are removed  → it's waveform  character , not loudness. Top features: spectral slope, S-polarization, HF depletion, band concentration.
LFE vs earthquakes vs blasts  ( analyze_multiclass.py ):  0.97  each — it rejects the impulsive confusers. The one hard residual is  in-tremor ambient noise (0.81) , which shares the LFE low-frequency band.
Cross-checked against the project's existing families  ( family_stack_test.py ): coherently-stacked B011 families are spectrally LFE-consistent (this is where I caught and corrected 3 of my own method artifacts).
Per-window picker v0  ( build_picker_v0.py ): calibrated 3-class LFE/EQ/NOISE classifier,  LFE AUC 0.975 , saved model. Dominant feature:  hv_ratio  (S-polarization).
Transfer test  ( build_picker_v0.py --sta PGC ): holds on the broadband instrument (0.97) → not a single-instrument artifact.
Unsupervised autoencoder  ( extract_spectrograms.py  +  train_autoencoder.py ): a conv-AE on spectrograms rediscovers the LFE cluster with  no labels  (latent AUC 0.965) — independent confirmation.
Per-sample U-Net picker  ( build_picker_dataset.py  +  train_phasenet.py ): the actual EQTransformer-style continuous P(LFE) stream — works (per-sample AUC 0.85) but is  single-station-capped  (precise-label refinement failed because LFEs are patch-specific + emergent).
Continuous scanner  ( scan_continuous.py ): deployed picker v0 over whole days → strong  LFE-activity detector  (ETS day P=0.94 vs quiet day 0.05).
Tremor-window picker  ( build_tremor_picker.py ): trained LFE vs {EQ, blast, in-tremor noise}; rejects EQ/blast at 0.97, enriches LFEs ~3×.
Wired into real GPU discovery  ( score_candidates.py  →  discover_gpu  →  compare_discovery.py ): scored 415k B011 candidates, ran clustering on the full vs P(LFE)-filtered pool. Learned to  filter at the family level, not per-candidate ; and that  B011's contamination is in-tremor noise, not EQ/blast  (so the picker bites harder at EQ/blast-contaminated stations).
Template-length test  ( discovery_filter_demo.py  /  discover_gpu  runs): tested 2 s vs 4 s vs 6 s templates —  longer does 
not
 help clustering  (LFE coda decorrelates; ~2 s ≈ the coherent duration). Surfaced that the whole discovery/clustering backbone is  vertical-only , and the strongest discriminator (S-polarization) is invisible to it — making  3-component clustering  the most promising untested next lever.
A  credible, physical, validated LFE fingerprint  (separates LFEs from noise  and  earthquakes/blasts at ~0.97–0.98, SNR-independent, instrument-transferable, autoencoder-confirmed); a  deployable per-window/family-level LFE detector ; an  EQTransformer-style per-sample picker  whose single-station ceiling is characterized; and the honest conclusion that the next real gains are  3-component clustering  and  multi-station (network)  input.

The picker uses 23 hand-crafted features per window (defined in lfe_features/feature_defs.py ), in three groups. LFEs are low-frequency, S-polarized, and emergent — so each feature points a known direction for a real LFE. Continues [[06-15-26 Notes]].
| feature | what it is | LFE signature |
|---|---|---|
| sp_slope | log-log spectral slope (2–40 Hz) | steep negative ← top discriminator |
| sp_centroid | spectral centroid (Hz) | low (~3–4 Hz) |
| sp_spread | spectral bandwidth | narrow |
| sp_peakfreq | peak frequency | low |
| sp_rolloff85 | 85%-energy rolloff freq | low |
| sp_flatness | spectral flatness | — |
| sp_entropy | spectral entropy | — |
| bf_1_2 , bf_2_4 , bf_4_8 | energy fraction in 1–2 / 2–4 / 4–8 Hz | high (energy in 2–8 Hz) |
| bf_8_16 , bf_16up | fraction in 8–16 / 16–Nyquist Hz | low |
| hf_ratio | E(>8 Hz) / E(2–8 Hz) | low (HF-depleted) |
env_crest (peak/RMS), env_kurt , env_skew , rise_time (10→90%), duration (>half-max), zcr (zero-crossing rate), snr (signal vs pre-event noise).
→ LFEs are emergent (low crest/kurtosis, slow rise), unlike impulsive earthquakes/blasts.
hv_ratio (horizontal/vertical energy), rectilinearity , planarity .
→ LFEs are S-dominant → high H/V. hv_ratio is the single strongest discriminator in the picker.
Across the validations, the features that actually carry the separation: hv_ratio (polarization), sp_slope , the 2–8 Hz band fractions, hf_ratio , sp_centroid , and the envelope shape ( env_skew / env_crest / env_kurt ). Two important properties we verified:
SNR-independent — dropping all amplitude features ( snr , env_crest ) left the AUC unchanged, so it's waveform character, not loudness.
Polarization is in here — so the vertical-dominance flag ( hv_ratio ) is already part of the categorizer, not a separate filter.
(That's the hand-crafted set. Separately, R6 showed an unsupervised spectrogram autoencoder rediscovers the same LFE structure — latent AUC 0.965 — confirming these aren't arbitrary.)

A real LFE is:
steep negative spectral slope (sp_slope) — energy falls off fast with frequency
low-frequency, concentrated in 2–8 Hz (low sp_centroid/sp_rolloff85, high bf_2_4/bf_4_8)
HF-depleted (low hf_ratio, low bf_16up) — the opposite of an earthquake
strongly S-polarized (high hv_ratio, planarity, rectilinearity) — LFE energy lives on the horizontals
emergent, not impulsive (low env_kurt/env_crest, longer rise_time) — the classic LFE gradual onset vs an EQ's sharp spike
The class means make it concrete: LFE hv_ratio 3.69 (highest of all classes) vs EQ 2.70 vs noise 1.43; LFE centroid 7.3 Hz vs EQ 10.2 Hz

Build a  4-D movie of shear-velocity change (δβ/β) on the Cascadia plate interface  — the megathrust fault, ~30–50 km deep. If the fault's velocity changes over time, that's a proxy for stress/fluid changes on the part of the fault that produces great earthquakes. The novel axis is  depth  — most velocity-monitoring works on shallow structure; we're trying to see the deep fault.
LFEs (low-frequency earthquakes) are tiny, endlessly-repeating quakes on the deep fault. Because a given family repeats with near-identical waveforms, we can measure how its  coda  (the scattered tail of the waveform) slightly  stretches or compresses  over months/years. That stretch =  dv/v , the fractional velocity change along the wave's path. We measured this for  12,703 certified LFE families across 187 stations  — the raw material.

Each dv/v measurement is a  path-averaged 
velocity change — sensitive to a smear of the crust along its wave path, weighted by a physics  kernel . The inversion is the step that turns thousands of these path averaged measurements into an actual  map :
data = G · model  → solve for the model. data  = all the (station, family) dv/v values over time
G  = the sensitivity kernels (which map cells each measurement "sees")
model  = δβ/β in each cell of the fault interface, per time window
Plus  site terms  — one nuisance number per station that soaks up the shallow, near-station common signal (seasonal, weather, site response) so it doesn't masquerade as a deep-fault change. It's a regularized least-squares solve, done per time window → the 4-D result.
Resolution first (before trusting any map):  checkerboard tests to ask " if  there were a pattern on the fault, how finely could this network even see it?" Answer:  ~70–140 km scale , sharpening as the fleet grew; the geometry could resolve finer but  noise is the limit .
The inversion:  produced deep δβ/β  anomaly maps per year , a  margin-wide index  (the network-mean deep change over time), and an  ETS composite  (does the fault change during tremor episodes?).

A single measurement is d_p(t) = K_pᵀ m(·, t) + c_p + ε_p(t) The constant c_p appears because dv/v is measured against a reference stack over some window R_p: d_p(t) = K_pᵀ m(·, t) − (1/|R_p|) Σ_{s∈R_p} K_pᵀ m(·, s) So c_p = −K_pᵀ m̄_{R_p}. If every pair used the same reference window, c_p would be fully determined by m and there would be nothing to estimate. It becomes a free parameter precisely when pairs have different usable spans, or when there are per-pair processing offsets — response changes, a switch between stretching and MWCS, changing station availability inside the stack. The augmented system. Stack m over all cells and epochs into a vector of length MT, and the offsets into c of length P. Then d = G m + S c + ε where G places K_p into the block for epoch t, and S is the pair-indicator matrix, S[(p,t), q] = δ_pq. Since c enters additively and linearly, this is the original system with P extra columns. Nothing about the inversion changes structurally. The null space, and why your reference choice is the fix. Take any time-independent field f(x) and set m(·, t) = f for all t, c_p = −K_pᵀ f. Then G m + S c = 0 exactly. A static velocity anomaly is indistinguishable from a set of per-pair offsets, so the augmented system has a null space of dimension M. Imposing (1/|R|) Σ_{t∈R} m(x, t) = 0 for all x supplies exactly M constraints and removes it. That condition is the statement "the reference is the last year of the stack" — the reference window is the gauge that makes c estimable, rather than an extra assumption layered on top. Solving for c costs almost nothing. The normal equations are [[GᵀWG + Λ GᵀWS]] [m] [GᵀWd] [ SᵀWG SᵀWS ] [c] = [SᵀWd] SᵀWS is diagonal and P×P — entry p is just the summed weight of pair p — so eliminating c is a rank-P update: ĉ = (SᵀWS)⁻¹ Sᵀ W (d − G m̂) Substituting back gives (Gᵀ W̃ G + Λ) m̂ = Gᵀ W̃ d, W̃ = W − W S (SᵀWS)⁻¹ SᵀW W̃ is the projector that removes the weighted mean of each pair's time series. Solving for the offsets is algebraically identical to demeaning every pair before inverting — the same "within" transformation as a fixed-effects panel regression. Which route you code is a matter

= [SᵀWd] SᵀWS is diagonal and P×P — entry p is just the summed weight of pair p — so eliminating c is a rank-P update: ĉ = (SᵀWS)⁻¹ Sᵀ W (d − G m̂) Substituting back gives (Gᵀ W̃ G + Λ) m̂ = Gᵀ W̃ d, W̃ = W − W S (SᵀWS)⁻¹ SᵀW W̃ is the projector that removes the weighted mean of each pair's time series. Solving for the offsets is algebraically identical to demeaning every pair before inverting — the same "within" transformation as a fixed-effects panel regression. Which route you code is a matter of convenience; keeping c explicit has the advantage that you get its posterior covariance, and pairs with few epochs get correspondingly loose offsets instead of being demeaned by a noisy sample mean. Three consequences. The time-average of m is not recoverable, by construction. Only temporal variations are constrained, which is all dv/v means anyway. You consume P degrees of freedom. With daily samples under a 31-day average carrying roughly 160 independent epochs per pair, that matters for any pair with a short span. Regularisation on m must not fight the gauge. If Λ includes a temporal-smoothness or damping term that penalises m toward zero, it partially determines the mean and quietly reintroduces the trade-off with c. Damp toward the reference-window mean instead, or apply the constraint as a hard projection.

Advanced Digital Technologies as cross-cut. Nominee stream: postdoctoral researcher. Host institution: University of Saskatchewan, Centre for Hydrology. What Canada actually has (geometry constraints, Clean Tech framing)
text:
The methodology is national in scope. The natural centrepiece is the Saskatchewan and Alberta co-located test bed (DEEP geothermal and Aquistore CCS in the same Deadwood Formation, with overlapping monitoring), but every region of Canada hosts clean-energy infrastructure where the same single-station ambient-noise approach applies.
Saskatchewan (centrepiece). DEEP Earth Energy Production (Canada's first deep geothermal plant, horizontal wells in the Deadwood Formation, southeast SK), Aquistore CO2 storage at SaskPower's Boundary Dam (CO2 injected into the same Deadwood Formation since 2015, permanent geophone array plus DAS fibre in the observation well), pervasive produced-water reinjection across the southeast SK oil and gas play, and emerging lithium-from-brine operations in the Williston Basin.
Alberta. Quest CCS (Shell, Scotford), the CaMI Field Research Station (Carbon Management Canada's dedicated CCS monitoring testbed near Newell County), the Alberta Carbon Trunk Line, and emerging hubs (Pathways, Polaris). RAVEN (network code RV) and ATSN provide open FDSN seismic coverage focused on induced-seismicity hotspots (Fox Creek, Crooked Lake).
British Columbia. Site C and Peace River hydro reservoirs (induced seismicity and reservoir-loading dv/v), Garibaldi-belt geothermal exploration (Mount Meager, South Meager), and run-of-river hydro along the south coast. The 400-sensor BC Earthquake Early Warning network (QW, since 2024) provides ambient-noise coverage across the southwest.
Manitoba. Manitoba Hydro's Nelson River system (Limestone, Kettle, Long Spruce) is one of the world's largest hydroelectric complexes; Tanco lithium and cesium mine; permafrost-fringe pipelines and grid.
Ontario. Nuclear sites (Bruce, Darlington, Pickering) require continuous geotechnical and groundwater monitoring; Marmora pumped-hydro proposal; Ring of Fire critical minerals; Lambton-area CCS hub emerging at Sarnia. Salt caverns in southwestern ON are leading hydrogen-storage candidates.
Quebec. Hydro-Québec's La Grande, Manicouagan, and Romaine complexes are global benchmarks for reservoir-induced seismicity and reservoir-loading effects. Quebec Lithium (Whabouchi, North American Lithium) and northern nickel and rare-earth deposits add critical-mineral monitoring. The 200-sensor QW Eastern network (since 2025) provides ambient-noise coverage along the populated St. Lawrence corridor.
Atlantic Canada. Bay of Fundy tidal energy installations (NS), proposed Goldboro and Bear Head green-hydrogen and ammonia projects (NS), Churchill Falls and Bull Arm hydrogen projects (NL), New Brunswick potash and salt-cavern hydrogen storage potential.
Yukon, NWT, Nunavut. Emerging geothermal prospects, the Nechalacho rare-earth project (NWT), and the Northern grid and Trans-Northern pipelines exposed to permafrost change. Long-running CN stations provide multi-decade baselines.

text:
(1,800 character max in English, including spaces)
Canada has a large, untapped deep-geothermal resource. Southern Saskatchewan is its most promising frontier: kilometres of insulating sediment trap heat in the Cambrian Deadwood Formation, where Canada's first deep geothermal plant (DEEP Earth Energy Production) draws 120 °C brine from horizontal wells at 3.5 km. Comparable plays sit in Alberta, BC (Garibaldi belt, Mount Meager), and Yukon (Whitehorse trough). The same basin also hosts active helium production and emerging native-hydrogen exploration in similar reservoirs.
What is unknown is how each reservoir evolves under production and injection: where the cooling front advances, how pore pressure moves between wells, and what triggers induced seismicity. Existing methods, downhole tools and episodic 3D surveys, see only one well or arrive years late.
The Canadian data needed for continuous answers already exist. The Aquistore CO2 storage facility, 50 km from DEEP in the same Deadwood Formation, has run a permanent geophone array and downhole DAS fibre since 2015. The CaMI Field Research Station https://www.fdsn.org/networks/detail/8O_2019/ in Alberta hosts a fully instrumented testbed with surface and borehole DAS. DEEP has completed a 56 km² 3D seismic baseline, and CN, RAVEN, and ATSN seismic networks cover the regional background.
The project will apply ambient-noise interferometry to these data to produce time-lapse maps of seismic velocity change across each reservoir, at hourly to monthly resolution, tracking pore pressure, the advance of cooling fronts between injection and production wells, and stress changes that precede induced seismicity. Cross-checked against operator pressure logs and microseismic catalogues, the outputs form a continuously updated monitoring framework for safe scale-up of Canadian geothermal, hydrogen, and helium production.

text:
(1,800 character max in English, including spaces)
This research aligns directly with Clean Technology and Resource Value Chains, broadly defined.
Canada's clean-energy transition depends on the sedimentary subsurface. Deep geothermal promises baseload renewable power; helium from the same basins underpins quantum and critical technology; and native-hydrogen exploration in similar traps could open a domestic clean fuel. Each depends on how rocks and fluids behave kilometres below the surface as wells produce and inject for years. Today this knowledge comes only from single-well downhole tools or from periodic 3D surveys that arrive too late to inform operations.
This project closes the gap by extracting reservoir-scale information from data already being collected: continuous background vibration recorded by nearby seismometers and distributed acoustic sensing fibres. Single-station ambient noise interferometry converts that vibration into velocity-change time series tracking temperature, pore pressure, and stress. The method is mature internationally; this project operationalises it for Canadian deep geothermal and the adjacent helium and hydrogen plays.
Beyond science, the project delivers outputs useful to communities, operators, and regulators. It requires no new installations or site access, making it non-invasive across agricultural, Crown, and Indigenous lands overlying the reservoirs. Data will be deposited in open-access repositories and plain-language summaries shared through regional outlets. The work supports the National Strategy for an Electrified Canadian Economy (2026), which targets doubling the grid by 2050 with geothermal in the required low-emitting mix. The result is a unified, low-cost monitoring layer supporting safer scale-up of Canadian geothermal, hydrogen, and helium production.

I operate the only permanent broadband seismic station in Saskatchewan which is located at the UofS geophysics test site about 12 km NE of Saskatoon. It is a good installation with a vault, proper seismic pier, a broadband ("HH") Trillium Compact sensor and Taurus seismometer but now getting noisier with acreage development and a cell tower constructed nearby. However, it records earthquakes well including those from Esterhazy cluster (potash salt belt), and of course lots of noise records. Within 20 m from the sensor, there is also a GPS site of the permanent Canadian national geodetic network. So, fully within the topic of your current proposal, a strong and natural approach would be to analyze records from this station, including coda and noise: receiver functions, coda attenuation, H/V ("transfer function"), deconvolved and/or cross-correlated H/V components ("dv/v"), maybe noise polarizations, and anything else. I had been always wanting to do this but never got a student to work on it. Comments from Igor thank you for the interesting meeting today. I've attached a zip file with several papers about topics I mentioned. Most of the papers are about "coda Q", but please note that dv/v is closely related to it. As stated on page 3 in Clements-Denolle paper, quantity dv/v is only inferred from variations of time intervals between the different arrivals within coda: "With the assumption that there is a homogeneous velocity change in the sampling medium, the relative time delay in the coda, dt/t, is related to the relative change in seismic velocity, dv/v, by dt/t = −dv/v." The above assumption is the Aki coda model in which a uniform crust without basin or Moho and collocated source and receiver are also assumed. This is shown in Figure 4 of Yuan's et al paper which I also include in the zip file. This model is completely unrealistic and it cannot be trusted with ~1% accuracy required in the dv/v or Q interpretations. The key paper directly revisiting Aki's (1980) paper (among a few other things) is "Critique_of_Aki_coda_model/Morozov_Q_PAGEOPH2010.pdf" (Fig 4 there).

Building a large-scale seismic velocity change (dv/v) monitoring system covering ALL PNSN and PNW seismic stations. We start with single-station cross-component (SC) dv/v — auto-correlations and cross-component correlations (EN, EZ, NZ) at individual stations — before scaling to inter-station pairs. This approach lets us validate the pipeline on a simpler problem first and identify which stations produce reliable measurements.

Pipeline constants below (e.g. coda window [2, 30] ) were revised during execution; the final pipeline used [2, 10] and added hourly-resolution dv/v — see the results doc for the final form. The stretching-grid quantization seen in the results motivated the move to [[Phase 2.0]]. Project anchor: [[Cascadia dv.v]].
Validate the SC cross-component pipeline end-to-end on a small, known-good set of stations before scaling to multi-year production. This is a QC run, not a science run: we want to identify which stations produce a clean, stable Z–E Green's function in the 1–3 Hz band, and we want to lock in config choices (spectral whitening, time normalization, stacking) on real PNW data.
Autocorrelations are excluded from this pilot — we're isolating the cross-component pathway because it's the harder case and the one that most strongly filters unusable stations.
Input: data/inventory/suitable_1to3Hz_SC.csv (29 stations / 44 from the 2020–2026 full-coverage set, restricted to BH + HH because accelerometers have self-noise at or above ambient at 1–3 Hz).
Breakdown: 4 BH (IU.COR + CC.HUSB / WIFE / SHRK), 25 HH (CN, UO, UW across BC / OR / WA). Geographic coverage: BC + Vancouver Island, Three Sisters / Mt. Hood, Oregon Coast + Klamath + Basin&Range + Wallowas, WA Cascade foothills (both sides), WA eastern basin (Columbia plateau — dense).
Every combo has ≥95 % 3C co-availability every calendar year 2020–2026 per availability_matrix.parquet + availability_matrix_post2023.parquet , so data presence for January 2020 is essentially guaranteed.
Month: 2020-01-01 through 2020-01-31 (31 days).
Reason for January 2020: fully pre-pandemic (so the urban-noise anomaly that hit Q2 2020 is not in play yet), well inside PNWstore coverage (no mount issues), all 29 stations are known to have 3C data.
Per station, per day:
Load Z + E daily traces from PNWstore via /1-fnp/pnwstore1/p-wd00/PNW2020/{NET}/2020/{DOY}/{STA}.{NET}.2020.{DOY} .
Instrument response removal using local StationXML ( /1-fnp/pnwstore1/p-wd11/PNWStationXML/{NET}/{NET}.{STA}.xml ), output units = velocity.
Decimate to 20 Hz (we need > 6 Hz Nyquist for 3 Hz; 20 Hz gives 10 Hz Nyquist with a clean anti-alias).
Bandpass 0.5–5 Hz (one-octave padding around the 1–3 Hz science band).
Hourly segmentation — cc_len = 3600 s , step = 1800 s (50 % overlap) → 47 segments/day.
Per-segment preprocessing: Spectral whitening ( rma ) across the 1–3 Hz band.
One-bit time normalization.
Cross-correlation — Z·E in the frequency domain, maxlag = 60 s .
Daily stack — linear stack of all hourly ZE CCs for that day.
Month-level:
Reference stack — linear stack of all 31 daily stacks.
| Metric | How | Pass band |
|--------|-----|-----------|
| PPSD noise floor | obspy.signal.PPSD per component, report median PSD in dB ref 1 (m/s²)²/Hz averaged over 1–3 Hz | — |
| ZE coherence | scipy.signal.coherence on raw (pre-CC) 1-hour segments, averaged across segments then averaged across 1–3 Hz | 1–3 Hz |
| SC CC SNR | peak amplitude in coda window (|lag| ∈ [2, 30] s) divided by RMS in noise window (|lag| ∈ [40, 60] s) of the monthly reference stack | — |
| dv/v stability | stretching dv/v of each daily stack vs. monthly reference in coda window |lag| ∈ [2, 30] s, report std(dv/v) across the 31 days | 1–3 Hz |
Promotion criteria for Phase 2 (to be finalized after the pilot):
ZE coherence ≥ 0.3 (1–3 Hz)
SC CC SNR ≥ 5
dv/v stability std ≤ 0.5 %
Cascadia has 48 cores / 376 GB. Each station is independent. We use ProcessPoolExecutor with max_workers = 29 (one worker per station). Inside each worker: single-threaded numpy/scipy. Expected wall time: ~10–20 minutes.
Per-worker memory is small (one day ≈ 2 channels × 86400 samples × 8 B ≈ 1.3 MB raw; full month in memory per channel ≈ 40 MB; hourly CCs are small). Well within 376 GB / 29 workers.

This document captures the results of two pilot runs on the same 29 stations. Run 1 locked in the pipeline; Run 2 refined the coda window, added hourly dv/v, and restored per-day PSD plots. Artifacts from Run 1 live in data/phase13/old_stacks/ + qc_metrics_jan2020.prev.csv ; Run 2 artifacts overwrite the active paths.

Per station, per day in Jan 2020:
Load Z + horizontal (E, fallback to 1 for GSN convention) from /1-fnp/pnwstore1/p-wd00/PNW2020/{NET}/2020/{DOY}/{STA}.{NET}.2020.{DOY} .
Remove instrument response via local StationXML, output = velocity, pre_filt=(0.05, 0.1, 8, 10) .
Decimate to 20 Hz.
Bandpass 0.5–5 Hz (1-octave pad around the 1–3 Hz science band).
Split into hourly segments: cc_len=3600 s , step=1800 s (50 % overlap).
Per segment: Hann taper → spectral whitening on 1–3 Hz → one-bit time normalization.
Cross-correlate Z · E in frequency domain, maxlag=60 s , canonical length enforced at TARGET_FS=20 Hz .
Month-level:
Monthly reference = mean of all hourly CCs across the month (not mean-of-daily-means).
Daily stack = mean of that day's hourly CCs.
Hourly dv/v = stretching of each hourly CC vs monthly reference over coda window |lag| ∈ [2, 10 s] , STRETCH_EPS=0.03 , STRETCH_N=101 trial stretches. Two variants: raw, and QC'd (discard hours with stretching corrcoef < 0.5).
Daily dv/v = same stretching on each daily stack vs monthly reference.
SC SNR = max |ref| in |lag| ∈ [2, 10 s] / RMS |ref| in |lag| ∈ [40, 60 s] .

NaN in hourly-QC = fewer than 3 hours passed the stretching corrcoef ≥ 0.5 bar.
6 stations hit hourly-QC std ≤ 0.20 % (UW.RADR, UW.CINE, UW.CBS, UW.MDW, IU.COR, UO.MARQ, UW.TOLE via 0.23 %). These are genuinely usable for 1-hour-resolution dv/v without any post-hoc smoothing — strong enough coda coherence that individual hourly CCs stretch cleanly against the monthly reference.
~6 stations have NaN hourly-QC (CN.SYMB, UW.RPW2, UO.SISQ, UW.OT3, UO.DING, UW.WA2) — fewer than 3 hourly CCs passed stretching corrcoef ≥ 0.5. These are daily-only candidates; their hourly records are noise. Useful ranking: drop these from any hourly-resolution monitoring and keep only for daily dv/v.
The rest (~17 stations) fall between 0.25–0.70 % hourly-QC — usable for hourly monitoring but noisier. A 6- or 12-hour trailing stack will clean them up.
Across stations where both are well defined, hourly-raw std is 3–6× daily-raw std, matching the √24 ≈ 4.9 theoretical scaling from single-hour vs 24-hour stacking. Good sanity check on the pipeline — the stretching is not introducing non-statistical noise.
Rebuilding the reference from the full hourly tensor (Run 2) rather than mean-of-daily-stacks (Run 1) increased SNR across the board: CC.HUSB 50 → 61, CC.WIFE 22 → 27, UW.RADR 41 → 56, UW.CINE 43 → 46, UW.TOLE 24 → 40, UW.CBS 20 → 34, UO.MARQ 20 → 30. This is because the hourly CCs stack coherently without the intra-day-averaging penalty applied when short days already get partial stacking.
Both non-permanent HH stations with much higher SC SNR than expected from the day-count (24, 30 respectively). UW.RADR sits in the coast range (Naselle) and is at –160 dB on Z — moderately noisy — but produces SNR 55.5 and the best hourly-QC dv/v std of the whole set (0.15 %) . UW.CINE (Cinebar, western Cascade foothills) is quieter (–167 dB on Z) and delivers SNR 45.7 with hourly-QC 0.18 %. Both deserve priority in Phase 2 regardless of pedigree.
Raw-trace Z-E magnitude-squared coherence in the 1–3 Hz band was 0.04–0.19 across the whole set — with no clear separation between top-SNR and bottom-SNR stations. Consistent with the band being dominated by scattered, multi-mode wavefield where plane-wave coherence on 3600 s segments undersells the coda-domain coherence that actually matters for SC dv/v. Drop ZE coherence from the Phase 2 pass/fail set ; keep stretching corrcoef per CC as the primary coherence metric.
Tier A — hourly + daily dv/v (SNR > 30 AND hourly QC ≤ 0.25 %):
UW.RADR · UW.CINE · UW.CBS · UW.MDW · UW.TOLE · IU.COR · UO.MARQ
Three regions: western WA (CINE, CBS, MDW, TOLE — coast range / eastern basin), Oregon Willamette (MARQ), GSN (COR). UW.RADR outside the obvious "quiet-basin" archetype is the most interesting.

Phase 2 scope decision: pick Tier A + selected Tier B (8–15 stations) and extend to full multi-year (2020–2026) with monthly moving-reference stacks, to turn the pilot into a science run.
Cross-validate with stretching + MWCS on Tier A to confirm the hourly-QC std is method-limited, not noise-limited.

This methodology uses Tim Clements' exact workflow for California. This is Phase 2, replacing the earlier workflow in [[Phase 1.3 Plan]] / [[Phase 1.3 Results]]. Project anchor: [[Cascadia dv.v]].
Status: recipe frozen 2026-04-22. Target run: src/phase13_pilot.py on the 29-station Phase 1.3 pilot pool, January 2020, Z·E, 2–4 Hz.
[[Phase 1.3 Results]] produced a 29-station pilot pool at 1–3 Hz with a dv/v pipeline that hit a stretching-grid ceiling: the hourly-QC dv/v series quantized visibly around ±0.1 %. Phase 2 moves the science band to 2–4 Hz, adopts a more standard broadband-whitened preprocessing recipe, refines the stretching grid, adds MWCS as an independent method, and splits coda-domain dv/v measurements into positive-lag, negative-lag, and combined variants. The internals walkthrough is in [[04-28-26 Notes]]; the adaptive-coda extension (Phase 2.1) is in [[04-29-26 Notes]].
Executed once per trace (Z and E) per DOY before segmenting.
Taper gaps with a 100 s cosine window on each side of every zero-filled gap. After stream.merge(method=1, fill_value=0) , each zero run gets a cosine fade-out going in and fade-in coming out, to avoid spectral leakage from sharp data-to-gap transitions.
Demean + detrend ( obspy demean + linear ).
High-pass above 0.4 Hz (zerophase).
Instrument response removal to velocity, PRE_FILT = (0.05, 0.1, 18.0, 20.0) .
Resample to 40 Hz .
No per-day bandpass into the science band — whitening handles that.
30-min windows with step 7.5 min ( 75 % overlap , ~192 segments/day). For each segment:
Demean + light linear detrend.
20 s cosine taper on each side (flat middle).
Spectral whitening 0.5–19 Hz with cosine tapers outside.
One-bit time normalization.
Frequency-domain CC of Z · E, truncated to MAXLAG = 60 s → 4801-sample trace at 40 Hz.
Per station per month, build three CC tensors from the 30-min segments:
| Tensor | Size | Built from | Method |
|--------|------|------------|--------|
| 30min | (n_seg ≈ 31·192, 4801) | raw segments | primary |
| hourly | (≤ 31·24, 4801) | 30-min CCs whose midpoints fall in UTC-hour buckets | linear mean (non-overlapping) |
| daily | (n_days, 4801) | all 30-min CCs in each DOY | per-lag median (robust stack) |
Reference: monthly linear mean of all 30-min CCs.
Rationale for non-overlapping hourly buckets: the 24 hourly samples per day are then statistically independent, so np.std of hourly dv/v is an honest noise estimator. Smoothing (e.g. 24-h running median) is applied post-hoc on the dv/v series at plot time, not baked into the stored tensor.

All defined at the top of src/phase13_pilot.py .
| Constant | Value | Notes |
|----------|-------|-------|
| YEAR , DOYS | 2020, 1–31 | January 2020 pilot scope |
| TARGET_FS | 40.0 | Needed to whiten up to 19 Hz |
| HP_FREQ | 0.4 | Pre-response high-pass |
| GAP_TAPER_S | 100.0 | Cosine-taper half-width on each side of a gap |
| PRE_FILT | (0.05, 0.1, 18.0, 20.0) | remove_response pre-filter |
| FMIN , FMAX | 2.0, 4.0 | science band |
| WHITEN_FMIN , WHITEN_FMAX | 0.5, 19.0 | broadband whitening |
| SEG_TAPER_S | 20.0 | per-segment cosine taper half-width |
| CC_LEN , CC_STEP | 1800, 450 | 30-min window, 7.5-min step (75 % overlap) |
| MAXLAG | 60.0 | CC truncated to ±60 s |
| CODA_TBEG , CODA_TEND | 2.0, 8.0 | coda window |
| NOISE_TBEG , NOISE_TEND | 40.0, 60.0 | SNR noise window |
| STRETCH_EPS , STRETCH_N | 0.01, 401 | 0.005 %/step grid |
| STRETCH_USE_ABS | True | peak chosen by |corrcoef| |
| STRETCH_QC | 0.5 | |cc| threshold for hourly QC variant |
| MWCS_WIN_S , MWCS_STEP_S | 4.0, 2.0 | sub-window length / step |
Grid-search over 401 trial stretches in ±1 %. For each trial eps , resample cur(lag·(1+eps)) in the selected coda side and compute corrcoef(ref_coda, interp) . The peak is chosen by maximum |corrcoef| — ambient coda at 2–4 Hz is amplitude-dominant; signed correlation is brittle. The returned cc_best is the signed corrcoef at the peak.
QC variant (hourly only): discard measurements with |cc_best| < 0.5 .
Moving-window cross-spectral in-house. For each sub-window (width 4 s, step 2 s) inside the selected coda side:
Hanning taper, FFT both sub-windows.
Cross-spectrum cross = conj(Fref) · Fcur , phase φ(f) in 2–4 Hz.
Weighted linear fit φ(f) = 2π·f·Δt + φ₀ with weights |cross(f)| .
Record (lag_mid, Δt, σ_Δt) .
Then across all sub-windows, weighted regression through the origin of Δt = -(dv/v)·lag gives dv/v ± err . Returns (dvv, err, n_sub_windows_used) per trace.
Three sides per method per stack level:
pos : CODA_TBEG ≤ lag ≤ CODA_TEND
neg : -CODA_TEND ≤ lag ≤ -CODA_TBEG
both : |lag| ∈ [CODA_TBEG, CODA_TEND]
Pos vs neg asymmetry diagnoses source-side direction effects. both is the primary measurement.
Waveforms / stacks:
 30min.npy , 30min_times.npy , hourly.npy , hourly_times.npy ,
 daily.npy , daily_doys.npy , ref.npy , lags.npy , psd_z.npy , psd_e.npy

 dvv_{m}_{L}_{s}.npy , cc_{m}_{L}_{s}.npy 
(for MWCS the cc_* file holds the formal Δt error per measurement)
QC variants (stretching hourly only):
 dvv_stretch_hourly_{s}_qc.npy — raw dv/v with |cc|<0.5 set to NaN
4×2 grid:
| | left | right |
|---|---|---|
| (0) | reference stack ± PLOT_LAG with coda-pos/coda-neg/noise shaded | daily robust CC section (DOY vs lag) |
| (1) | per-day PSD Z / E | daily dv/v: stretching (solid) + MWCS (dashed, error bars) × 3 sides |
| (2) | hourly dv/v stretching, 3 sides + 24-h running median | hourly dv/v MWCS, 3 sides + running median |
| (3) | stretching |corrcoef| histogram, 3 sides | scatter stretching vs MWCS daily, color by side |
One row per station. Columns:
metadata: network, station, location, channel_band, state, site_name, status, error, elapsed_s
counts: n_days, n_segments_30min, n_hours
spectra: psd_z_db, psd_e_db
SNR: sc_snr_both, sc_snr_pos, sc_snr_neg
dv/v std (12 cols): dvv_std_pct_{m}_{L}_{s} for m ∈ {stretch, mwcs} , L ∈ {hourly, daily} , s ∈ {pos, neg, both}

Run these against the output CSV + a few station plots right after the full run:
Grid quantization resolved: dvv_std_pct_stretch_daily_both should not snap to multiples of 0.005 %. If it still quantizes visibly in the dv/v series plots, inspect the hourly corrcoef histogram — a long tail toward high |c| is expected; a narrow band clipped at some eps means the measurement is grid-bound.
Sides consistency: stretch_*_both should track stretch_*_pos and stretch_*_neg within ~2× on high-SNR stations. Large pos/neg asymmetry flags source-side direction effects or noise dominance on one side.
Method cross-check: On high-SNR stations, stretch_daily_both vs mwcs_daily_both should agree within ~1 grid step (0.005 %). Wider divergence on many stations → sub-window length or frequency fit range may need tuning.
Hourly independence: sqrt(24) × daily_std ≈ hourly_std within a factor of ~1.5 for well-behaved stations (from the Central Limit Theorem on 24 independent hourly samples).
PSD sensible: median Z PSD in 2–4 Hz should be in the −150 to −175 dB range for typical PNW short-period stations.

 Context: Codex was asked to produce a parallel list of currently-active PNSN stations from EarthScope. Its output lives in /home/seismic/Earthnote/codex/ . This note reconciles its results against the Earthnote Phase 1.2 pipeline (see [[PROJECT_PLAN]]; Phase 1.2 work in [[04-15-26 Notes]]).

The 679 number is not "all active." It's "active AND (qualifies for Phase 1.3 dv/v OR is a post-2023 deployment)." The ~114 stations in the gap:
Pre-2023 deployed, had PNWstore data, failed Phase 1.2b gap filter (no year with ≥90 % 3C uptime). Live on FDSN but not usable for historical dv/v.
Pre-2023 deployed, no PNWstore history at all (audit buckets B and C). Live on FDSN but missed by the 4-DOY PNWstore sample or never ingested.

Bbox labeling is brittle. Point-in-polygon on Natural Earth admin_1_states_provinces (10m) — what Earthnote uses — is more reliable than rectangular bounds + site-name string matching.
Network scope is narrow. Excluding NP, GS, IU, US drops some of the highest-value stations for dv/v (IU.COR has 20+ years of ≥90 % 3C uptime; GS post-2023 deployments are a growing chunk of the forward roster).
active_stations.csv is channel-metadata active, not availability-verified. Use shortlist_phase13.csv / pilot_pool_phase13.csv for delivery-verified counts.
